Father_Notes: Pietro Agnesi was a wealthy Milanese professor of mathematics at the University of Bologna who encouraged his daughter's scientific interests and established a cultural salon in his home.
Education_Notes: Educated at home by a series of distinguished professors secured by her father. Demonstrated exceptional linguistic ability, speaking French fluently by age five and mastering Greek, German, Spanish, and Hebrew by age eleven. Guided in advanced mathematics by Father Ramiro Rampinelli of the Olivetan Benedictines. No formal degree is recorded.
Religion_Notes: Expressed a strong desire to enter a convent in 1738; after her father's death in 1752 devoted herself to religious studies and social work. Became directress of the Pio Albergo Trivulzio, a home for the aged and indigent, in 1771.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Algebra; Geometry; Calculus; Analysis; Physics; Natural Philosophy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Solved difficult problems in analytic geometry and ballistics by age fourteen. Prepared a critical commentary on L'Hospital's Traité analytique des sections coniques. Her masterwork, the Istituzioni analitiche (1748), provided a comprehensive treatment of algebra, coordinate geometry, differential and integral calculus, infinite series, and differential equations. Known for the versiera (witch of Agnesi), a cubic curve with applications in physics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by her wealthy father Pietro Agnesi until his death in 1752. Received papal recognition and an honorary chair at Bologna (1750–1752) from Pope Benedict XIV, though she never taught. After 1752 devoted herself to religious studies and charitable work.
Patronage_Notes: Pope Benedict XIV provided the most significant recognition, sending congratulatory letters in 1749 and 1750, awarding a gold medal and precious-stone wreath, and appointing her to an honorary chair of mathematics and natural philosophy at Bologna.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Son of Berengar, lord of Le Pallet; came from a noble family with militaristic and governmental traditions.
Education_Institution: School of Roscelin; William of Champeaux's School; School of Anselme and Ralph of Laon
Education_Notes: Studied under Roscelin at Loches (ca. 1094–1096), then under William of Champeaux in Paris (ca. 1110), and later under Anselme and Ralph of Laon (ca. 1114). No formal degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: Loches, Unknown, France, 1094, 1096; Paris, Unknown, France, 1110, 1110; Unknown, Unknown, France, 1114, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Became a monk at the abbey of St. Denis (ca. 1118); later founded the convent of Paraclete; his theological doctrines were condemned at the Council of Soissons (1121) and the Council of Sens (1140) for his rationalist approach to faith.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in applying dialectical method to theology and philosophy. Developed systematic logic covering all recognized sections of the discipline. Made methodological contributions to the study of universals, language theory, and conditional propositions. Established critical rules for textual interpretation and the analysis of apparently contradictory authorities.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at various schools including his own on the Montagne Ste. Genevieve in Paris; served as abbot of St. Gildas in Brittany and as head of the Paraclete convent; received ecclesiastical benefices and monastic support.
Patronage_Notes: Peter the Venerable of Cluny persuaded him to accept the verdict of the Council of Sens and provided refuge at Cluny.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: University of Padua; University of Paris
Education_Notes: Completed early studies in Padua; lived in Constantinople; attended University of Paris around 1300, possibly teaching there; from 1307 taught philosophy and medicine at Padua. No degree is named.
Education_Locations: Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1300, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Accused of heresy for interpreting the birth and ministry of Christ as natural rather than miraculous; acquitted during his lifetime but condemned posthumously. His writings were found heretical and his remains were disinterred and burned approximately forty years after his death.
Scientific_Disciplines: Medicine; Philosophy; Natural History; Alchemy; Astronomy; Astrology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Author of the Conciliator, which reconciled medicine and philosophy through 120 disputed questions. Affirmed the brain as the seat of sensation and motion, opposing Aristotle. Possessed knowledge of anatomy from direct visualization. Treated astrology as comprising astronomy and judicial prediction concerning planetary influences on human events and conception.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught philosophy and medicine at Padua from 1307 for several years; possibly taught at Paris around 1300. Practiced medicine as a physician.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Disseminated oriental science in the West; understood prosodic rules and made known the Sind Hind astronomical tables, which influenced European astronomy. Attempted human flight and achieved a glide. Constructed a planetarium, clock, and armillary sphere. Introduced the cutting of rock crystal as an industry to Islamic Spain.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as court poet and astrologer to the emirs ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II and Muḥammad I.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by the emirs ʿAbd al-Raḥmān II and Muḥammad I of al-Andalus.
Instruments_Notes: Constructed a planetarium, a clock, and an armillary sphere. Attempted human flight, achieving a glide before a rough landing.

Father_Notes: None

Education_Notes: Studied under Oliver Wolcott Gibbs at City College of New York; worked with astronomer F.F.E. Brünnow at University of Michigan (1859–1860); studied with B.A. Gould at Cambridge, Massachusetts (1860–1864) while Gould was on detached duty with the Coast Survey; spent two years (1864–1866) at Pulkovo Observatory, Russia, under Otto Struve to improve his astronomical preparation. No formal degree is named.
Education_Locations: New York, New York, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Ann Arbor, Unknown, United States, 1859, 1860; Cambridge, Unknown, United States, 1860, 1864; Saint Petersburg, Unknown, Russia, 1864, 1866
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: First regular official weather forecaster of the U.S. government; promoted research in atmospheric physics; sought to apply astronomical methods to develop a physics of the earth; insisted on mathematical rigor and close attention to developments in physical sciences.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Director of Cincinnati Observatory (1868–1870); joined the Weather Service of the Signal Corps in 1871, the predecessor of the present Weather Bureau, where he served as the first regular official weather forecaster and established a laboratory and research center.
Patronage_Notes: Employed by the Weather Service of the Signal Corps, a U.S. government agency.

Father_Notes: Adam Abbe was a spinning-mill worker of modest means; his employers provided a scholarship enabling his son's education.
Education_Institution: Eisenach Gymnasium; University of Jena; University of Göttingen
Education_Notes: Studied physics at Jena and Göttingen; received doctorate from Göttingen on 23 March 1861 under the influence of mathematicians Riemann and physicist Wilhelm Weber. After a two-year interval with financial hardship, during which he taught at the Physikalischer Verein in Frankfurt am Main and did private tutoring, he became lecturer at Jena University in 1863.
Education_Locations: Eisenach, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1857; Jena, Unknown, Germany, 1857, Unknown; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1861
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in theoretical and practical optics; formulated the sine condition in radiational optics and developed the theory of image resolution in undulatory optics. His work on microscope design and the numerical aperture became foundational for optical science and later electron microscopy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer in mathematics, physics, and astronomy at Jena University from 1863; associate professor from 1870; full professor. Partner in the Zeiss Works from 1876, sharing in company profits and eventually becoming sole owner after Carl Zeiss's death in 1888.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and developed the apochromatic microscope objective, the Abbe refractometer, and illuminating apparatus for microscopes. His theoretical work on the sine condition and numerical aperture enabled systematic scientific production of optical instruments at the Zeiss Works.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: George M. Abel; family of Rhenish origin, moderately prosperous, owned a farm.
Education_Institution: University of Michigan; University of Leipzig; University of Strasbourg; University of Vienna; University of Berne; University of Leipzig
Education_Notes: Attended high school in Cleveland. Interrupted studies for three years (1883–1886) while serving as principal and superintendent of La Porte, Indiana public schools. Extensive postgraduate study in Germany 1884–1890 under leading physiologists and chemists including Carl Ludwig and M. von Nencki.
Education_Locations: Ann Arbor, Unknown, United States, 1876, 1883; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1884, 1886; Strasbourg, Unknown, Germany, 1886, 1888; Vienna, Unknown, Austria, 1888, 1889; Berne, Unknown, Switzerland, 1889, 1890; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1890, 1890
Scientific_Disciplines: Pharmacology; Biochemistry; Physiology; Chemistry; Medicine; Endocrinology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in establishing biochemistry and pharmacology as rigorous chemical disciplines in the United States. Major contributions include isolation and characterization of epinephrine, development of the artificial kidney and vividdiffusion apparatus, demonstration of free amino acids in blood, crystallization of insulin, and studies of pituitary hormones and tetanus toxin.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer in materia medica and therapeutics at University of Michigan (1891–1893); professor of pharmacology at Johns Hopkins University (1893–1932), also nominally in charge of physiological chemistry instruction until 1908. Maintained active laboratory research throughout career and after retirement.
Patronage_Notes: Victor Vaughan, his former teacher at Michigan, secured his initial teaching position there. A. A. Noyes of California Institute of Technology invited and subsidized his insulin crystallization work (1924–1926).
Instruments_Notes: Designed an apparatus of coiled collodion tubes surrounded by saline solution for removing and studying diffusible blood substances; arterial blood was shunted through the tubes and returned to the animal's vein. This vividdiffusion apparatus demonstrated the existence of free amino acids in blood and suggested clinical potential for managing renal failure.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Society of Biological Chemists; American Society for Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Principal organizer of the American Society of Biological Chemists (1906) and the American Society for Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics (1908). Instrumental in founding the Journal of Experimental Medicine (1896), the Journal of Biological Chemistry (1905), and the Journal of Pharmacology and Experimental Therapeutics (1909), which he edited until retirement.

Father_Notes: Lutheran minister, educated at University of Copenhagen; prominent in Norwegian nationalist movement; elected to the Storting in 1818; suffered from alcoholism and died in 1820, leaving the family in straitened circumstances.
Education_Notes: Received initial instruction from his father; attended Cathedral School in Christiania (Oslo) from 1815, where he studied under Bernt Michael Holmboe, who recognized his mathematical genius and guided his self-directed study of Euler, Lagrange, and Laplace. Entered University of Oslo in fall 1821 and completed the preliminary degree Candidatus Philosophiae within a year; thereafter pursued advanced research independently with no formal advanced courses available.
Education_Locations: Christiania, Unknown, Norway, 1815, 1821; Oslo, Unknown, Norway, 1821, 1822
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Proved the impossibility of solving the general quintic equation by radicals (Abel-Ruffini theorem); developed the theory of elliptic functions as a generalization of trigonometric functions, including double periodicity and addition theorems; made fundamental contributions to functional equations, power series, and the theory of equations solvable by radicals (Abelian equations); established Abel's theorem on sums of integrals of algebraic functions and introduced the genus of an algebraic function.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by professors at University of Oslo out of their own salaries during his studies; received a small stipend from the university upon his return in 1827; tutored schoolboys in Oslo during 1827–1828; served as substitute to Hansteen at the university and Norwegian Military Academy from 1828.
Patronage_Notes: Mentored and supported by Bernt Michael Holmboe and Christoffer Hansteen at the University of Oslo; received financial assistance and friendship from August Leopold Crelle in Berlin, who founded Crelle's Journal to publish Abel's work and attempted to secure him a position at a German university; supported by Legendre and other French mathematicians who petitioned the Swedish-Norwegian crown on his behalf.

Father_Notes: Teacher at the horticulture school and Dozent at the Institute of Agriculture in Vienna. Family had been gardeners for several generations; grandfather studied botany under Nicolaus Jaquin.
Education_Institution: University of Vienna; School of Mining
Education_Notes: Studied law at the Faculty of Law of the University of Vienna to please his parents, but devoted more time to natural sciences, especially botany. Took major examination in geology and paleontology in 1899. Attended the school of mining in Leoben briefly after receiving his Ph.D.
Education_Locations: Vienna, Unknown, Austria, Unknown, 1899; Leoben, Unknown, Austria, 1899, 1900
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founded paleobiology as a distinct discipline. Early work on orchids and fossil cetaceans; later focused on paleozoological reconstruction, vertebrate paleobiology, and cephalopod paleobiology. Conducted extensive paleozoological excavations in Austria and Greece.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at the Geological Institute of the University of Vienna from 1898; Mitarbeiter at the Imperial-Royal Geological State Institute in Vienna 1900–1907; Privatdozent in paleontology at the University of Vienna from 1901; associate professor from 1907; full professor from 1912; professor of paleobiology and director of the Paleobiological Institute from 1917. Accepted a post at the University of Göttingen in 1935 and spent five years there before retiring in 1940.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: President of the Paleontological Society from 1921. Member or honorary member of numerous scientific academies and learned societies. Honorary doctor of the universities of Cape Town and Athens.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Received a degree in civil engineering from the University of Padua in 1867, then abandoned engineering the following year to pursue astronomy.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Devoted his scientific activity to positional astronomy, making observations of small planets, comets, stellar occultations, and eclipses. Observed the transit of Venus in 1874 using the spectroscope for the first time. Determined geographic coordinates and longitude differences between Italian localities. Conducted precision studies on observational methods and least-squares equations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed astronomer of the University of Padua observatory in 1868, remaining until 1893. In 1894 appointed director of the Arcetri observatory and professor of astronomy at the University of Florence, holding the post until mandatory retirement in 1921. Continued research at the observatory from 1921 to 1928.
Instruments_Notes: Built an equatorial telescope in the shops of the Padua observatory and adapted the objective previously constructed by G.B. Amici (28 cm diameter). Equipped the Arcetri observatory with a Bamberg small meridian circle. Used these instruments for observations of small planets, comets, and fixed stars.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the Accademia Nazionale dei Lincei (Rome), associate member of the Royal Astronomical Society (London), and member of several other Italian academies.

Father_Notes: Wilhelm Abich was an official in the Department of Mines. Two uncles—Martin Klaproth, a chemist, and Julius Klaproth, an ethnographer and orientalist—significantly influenced his scientific interests.
Education_Notes: Began studies in law at Heidelberg, then transferred to physics and mathematics at Berlin, graduating in 1831. Defended a dissertation on spinel minerals. Teachers included Hegel, Humboldt, and Leopold von Buch.
Education_Locations: Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1831
Scientific_Disciplines: Geology; Mineralogy; Petrography; Geomorphology; Glaciology; Geobotany; Meteorology; Geography; Paleontology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in Caucasian geology; established stratigraphic sequences from Paleozoic to Quaternary; studied magmatic formations, tectonic structure, and mineral deposits. Discovered the Chiatura manganese deposit and developed the anticlinal theory for oil prospecting. Published over 200 works spanning geology, geomorphology, glaciology, meteorology, geography, geobotany, meteoritics, and archaeology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Extraordinary professor of mineralogy at Dorpat (Tartu) University from 1843; resigned to work full-time for the Corps of Mining Engineers and the viceregent of the Caucasus. Conducted extensive fieldwork in the Caucasus for nearly thirty-five years, retiring with a pension in 1876.
Patronage_Notes: Assigned to the headquarters of the Corps of Mining Engineers and detailed to the command of the viceregent of the Caucasus, where he conducted geological investigations and mineral surveys.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to membership in 1853; elevated to honorary membership in 1866.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Graduated from the Royal Military Academy; no university degree is named.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in quantitative sensitometry and photochemistry of photographic images; invented dry photographic emulsion and hydroquinone developer; first to photograph solar spectrum in infrared and to suggest detection of rapid stellar rotation via spectral broadening; studied color vision theory in later life.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served with Royal Engineers in India; chemical assistant at Chatham School of Military Engineering from 1869; supervisory career with Board of Education for England and Wales from 1877; held military rank of captain.
Patronage_Notes: Board of Education position from 1877 onward.
Instruments_Notes: Invented dry photographic emulsion (1874) and hydroquinone developer (1880); devised red-sensitive emulsion for spectroscopic work; used spectroscopy to analyze organic molecules and photograph solar spectrum in infrared.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Photographic Society; Royal Astronomical Society; Physical Society of London; Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of Royal Society (1876); president of Royal Photographic Society (1892–1894, 1896, 1903–1905); president of Royal Astronomical Society (1893–1895); president of Physical Society of London (1895–1897); awarded Rumford Medal by Royal Society (1882); knighted (1900).

Father_Notes: None

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Author of the Ḥibbūr ha-meshīḥah we-ha-tishboret, the earliest exposition of Arab algebra written in Europe and containing the first complete European solution of the quadratic equation. Introduced Arab trigonometry and Euclid's Book of Divisions to Europe. Wrote astronomical treatises on geography, stellar calculations, and astronomical tables following al-Battānī. Composed works on the calendar and philosophical subjects.

Father_Notes: Wealthy Jewish merchant family.
Education_Notes: Studied under Max Planck; completed doctoral dissertation in 1897.
Religion_Notes: Born to a wealthy Jewish merchant family.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Devoted his career to the explication and development of Maxwell's electromagnetic theory. Developed a theory of the electron based on electromagnetic mass calculations. Made significant contributions to vector notation in physics and authored the standard German textbook on electrodynamics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held positions as Privatdozent at Göttingen (1900–1909), professor at University of Illinois (1909), professor of rational mechanics at University of Milan (1909–1914), and professor of physics at Technische Hochschule Stuttgart (1918–1921). During World War I investigated theoretical problems in radio transmission for Telefunkengesellschaft.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Father had a friendship with Count Duarte de Castelo Branco, which aided Abreu's appointment as physician to the governor of Angola in 1594.
Education_Notes: Entered Évora University in 1577 and graduated as bachelor of arts about 1583. Studied medicine at Coimbra University on a royal scholarship and graduated as licentiate of medicine seven years later (ca. 1590).
Education_Locations: Évora, Unknown, Portugal, 1577, 1583; Coimbra, Unknown, Portugal, 1583, 1590
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of tropical medicine; described amoebiasis, yellow fever, scurvy, tungiasis, and Guinea worm infection based on his experience in Angola and Brazil. Authored the first text on tropical medicine.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine in Lisbon with limited success initially. Appointed physician to the governor of Angola in 1594 with annual salary of 24,000 reis. Served as surgeon during Dutch attack on Bahia. Appointed physician to treasury officials in 1612.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed physician to the governor of Angola through the patronage of Count Duarte de Castelo Branco, his father's friend.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Alt_Name: Hibat Allah; Awḥad al-Zamān Abu'l-Barakāt al-Baghdādī
Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: No formal institutional education is recorded. The entry indicates he acquired his philosophical learning through reading philosophical texts, particularly Avicenna's Kitāb al-Shifāʾ, and through personal reflection.
Religion_Notes: Born Jewish; converted to Islam late in life, reportedly either in reaction to social slight or to counter a threat to his life.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Physician to the caliph of Baghdad. Author of Kitāb al-Muʿtabar, a philosophical work consisting of critical remarks on philosophical texts, particularly Avicenna's work. Developed original theories in physics (time, space, projectile motion, acceleration of falling bodies) and psychology (nature of the soul, consciousness, psychic faculties) that departed significantly from Aristotelian and Avicennian traditions. Also wrote a philosophical commentary on Ecclesiastes and a treatise on the visibility of stars.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as physician to the caliph of Baghdad; engaged in philosophical writing and teaching.
Patronage_Notes: Physician to the caliph of Baghdad.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Member of the Ayyūbid princely family; family held estates in Syria.
Education_Notes: Participated in military campaigns from age twelve; no formal institutional education recorded.
Religion_Notes: Served as a vassal prince under the Mameluke sultanate.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Authored the Taqwīm al-buldān, a comprehensive geographical treatise with twenty-eight chapters covering rivers, lakes, oceans, mountains, and place coordinates. Also wrote the Mukhtaṣar taʾrīkh al-bashar, a historical work continuing Ibn al-Athīr's chronicle from pre-Islamic times through 1329.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as a vassal prince under the Mameluke sultanate after recovering his family estates in 1312; supported by his princely position and family wealth.
Patronage_Notes: Served the Mameluke court as a vassal prince; his position and resources enabled his scholarly work.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: In 1117 studied with Abū Bakr al-Ṭurṭūshī in Alexandria. No formal degree is recorded.
Religion_Notes: Born of Hispano-Arabic parents; undertook the pilgrimage to Mecca.
Scientific_Disciplines: Geography; Physical Geography; Astronomy; Astrology; Natural History; Zoology; Botany
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Traveled extensively through Eurasia and documented geographical, astronomical, and chronological observations. Authored the Muʿrib and Tuḥfa, influential works on cosmography, geography, and natural phenomena including descriptions of flora, fauna, seas, animals, and fossils.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by patrons during his travels and scholarly work; dedicated the latter part of his life to writing his two major geographical and cosmographical treatises.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Alt_Name: al-Ḥāsib al-Miṣrī; Abū Kāmil; Shujāʿ ibn Aslam
Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: No formal education is recorded. The entry indicates he was active in the intellectual ferment of the Islamic world in mathematics and sciences but provides no details of schooling or training.
Religion_Notes: Inferred from his position as a leading mathematician in the Islamic intellectual tradition of the ninth and tenth centuries.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: One of Islam's greatest algebraists following al-Khwārizmī. Advanced algebra through use of irrational coefficients, higher powers of unknowns, and systematic solutions to indeterminate equations. Integrated geometric and algebraic methods, drawing on Mesopotamian, Greek, and Indian traditions.
Means_of_Support_Notes: None
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Alt_Name: Jaʿfar Ibn Muḥammad; Albumasar; Abu Mashar
Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Began career in Baghdad probably at the beginning of al-Maʾmūn's caliphate (813–833) as an expert in ḥadīth. Around 825 became involved in a quarrel with al-Kindī that redirected his studies toward mathematics and philosophy. No formal degree is recorded.
Religion_Notes: Embedded in Islamic intellectual tradition; whipped once during the caliphate of al-Mustaʿīn (862–866) for his practice of astrology, but maintained strict adherence to Islamic tenets despite heretical philosophical views.
Scientific_Disciplines: Astrology; Astronomy; Mathematics; Philosophy; Natural Philosophy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Leading exponent of astrology in the Muslim world; synthesized Pahlavi, Sanskrit, Greek, and Syriac intellectual traditions. Developed philosophical justifications for astrology drawing on Aristotelian physics and Neoplatonic emanation doctrine. Composed works on astronomical tables, planetary conjunctions, nativities, and astrological history.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as leading astrologer at the court and in Baghdad's intellectual circles; advised caliphs and rebels; accompanied al-Muwaffaq on military expedition against the Zanj (880–883). Reputation as astrologer preserved him from persecution.
Patronage_Notes: Served under caliphs al-Maʾmūn and al-Mustaʿīn; accompanied al-Muwaffaq, a state military commander, on expedition. His great reputation as astrologer made him valuable to the caliphate despite his heterodox views.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Alt_Name: Muḥammad Ibn Muḥammad Ibn Yaḥyā Ibn Ismāʿīl Ibn Al-ʿAbbās; Abu'l-Wafa; Abul-Wafa
Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Moved to Baghdad in 959 where he studied and worked within the mathematics-astronomy school. No formal degree is recorded.
Religion_Notes: Inferred from cultural context of working in the Eastern Caliphate during the tenth century.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted astronomical observations at the Baghdad observatory. Authored practical arithmetic textbook and geometric constructions manual. Made significant advances in trigonometry, including improved sine tables and spherical trigonometry methods. Wrote commentary on works of Euclid, Diophantus, and al-Khwārizmī.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked within the Baghdad observatory and mathematics-astronomy school as part of the Eastern Caliphate's intellectual establishment.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by the Eastern Caliphate court, which maintained the Baghdad observatory and school.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Father Herz Marcus, a converted Jew, died in 1772. Family income came from a small soap-boiling business begun with his mother's dowry.
Education_Notes: Attended the respected local Gymnasium at Bückeburg, following the classical curriculum.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer work on gas-lighting technology and food adulteration. Undertook experimental work on gas-lighting processes and wrote the classic treatise on gas technology. Conducted sensational research on food adulteration that awakened public concern.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Established his own laboratory around 1800; served as assistant chemical operator to Humphry Davy (1800–1803); began public lecturing in 1802 with steady stream of laboratory pupils; manufactured and sold chemical apparatus; held two technical professorships in Berlin after 1820; authored multiple treatises and books.
Patronage_Notes: Early patronage from Anthony Carlisle and friendship of William Nicholson. Carlisle later pleaded on his behalf with the Royal Institution despite Accum's shortcomings.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and manufactured chemical apparatus; orders came from Harvard, Yale, and institutions in India, demonstrating the commercial success of his designs.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Institution; Royal Irish Academy; Linnean Society; Royal Academy of Sciences in Berlin
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Subscriber to the Royal Institution and member of the Royal Irish Academy and Linnean Society in England; corresponding member of the Royal Academy of Sciences in Berlin, a connection that continued after his move to Germany in 1820.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Arnold Thackray. Original works: System of Theoretical and Practical Chemistry, 2 vols. Father_Notes: Guillaume Achard was a minister; died when Franz Karl was two years old.
Education_Notes: No formal education is recorded. At age twenty he began his scientific career under the botanist J. G. Gleditsch and especially the chemist A. S. Marggraf, who trained him and introduced him to Berlin scientific circles.
Religion_Notes: Born of French Protestant émigré parents.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work on thermal expansion of gases and liquids, freezing-point depression, cooling by evaporation, electrical phenomena, and chemical subjects. Known for minor achievements in applied chemistry including a platinum-arsenic alloy and a process for fabricating lye. Best known for developing a practical method of extracting sugar from beets in large quantities, beginning experiments in 1786 and perfecting the process by 1799.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Admitted to the Berlin Academy in June 1776; succeeded Marggraf as director of the Class of Physics in 1782. Established and operated a beet-sugar refinery at Kunern, completed in 1801 and operational from 1802.
Patronage_Notes: Presented beet sugar and process description to Frederick William III in 1799; the king appointed a committee to investigate and provided financial aid to build the Kunern refinery. Received governmental financing under the Continental System.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Admitted to the Berlin Academy in June 1776; became director of the Class of Physics in 1782 following Marggraf's death.

Father_Notes: None

Education_Notes: Studied medicine at Uppsala and Lund; received M.D. from Lund in 1782. Last student to defend a thesis under Linnaeus (De planta Aphyteia, 1776).
Education_Locations: Uppsala, Unknown, Sweden, Unknown, Unknown; Lund, Unknown, Sweden, Unknown, 1782
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Devoted himself almost exclusively to the study and classification of lichens. Developed a rational system of lichen classification based on structure and morphological description. Described numerous new families and species, both Scandinavian and tropical. His terminology for lichen morphology remains largely valid in contemporary lichenology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine in Vadstena, Ostergotland, for the major part of his life. Pursued botanical research in his leisure time.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Graduated doctor of philosophy and medicine from the University of Bologna in 1484.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Known during his lifetime primarily as a philosopher. Remembered for significant anatomical research: described the veins of the arm, seven tarsal bones, brain fornix, cerebral ventricles, infundibulum, and trochlear nerve. Described the ducts of the submaxillary salivary glands and the ileocecal valve. First described the malleus and incus of the ear. Demonstrated errors in Galen's work.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed substitute lecturer of philosophy at the University of Bologna in 1484; taught medicine there after 1495. Taught philosophy at the University of Padua from 1506 to 1508, then returned to Bologna where he taught for three years until his death.

Education_Notes: Studied arts and medicine, most probably at Salamanca. No degree is named in the source.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Collected botanical specimens in India and made firsthand observations of Oriental drugs and plants. Author of the Tractado de las drogas, y medicinas de las Indias orientales, illustrated with woodcuts from his own accurate drawings, which surpassed García d'Orta's earlier work. Also wrote a major treatise on plants, fruits, and animals of the East Indies, Persia, and China, now lost.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed physician to the Royal Hospital in Cochin in 1569; practiced medicine in Burgos and served as the city's physician and surgeon from 1576 to 1587.
Patronage_Notes: Served under Luiz de Ataíde, viceroy of India, whom he rejoined in 1568.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Entered the Jesuit order at age fifteen in Medina del Campo and underwent rigorous theological and literary training. Was offered a chair of theology in Rome but declined to serve in the Americas instead.
Religion_Notes: Member of the Society of Jesus (Jesuits); served as historian of the third council of the church at Lima (1582–1583) and later as rector of the Jesuit college of Salamanca.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Provided detailed firsthand observations of the physical and human geography of Latin America, including altitude sickness, coca, crops, farm techniques, and domesticated animals. Described Inca and Aztec history, religious observances, folk customs, statecraft, Mexican ideograms, Peruvian quipu, and the Inca postal system. Considered the first true Americanist.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Member of the Jesuit order from age fifteen; lived at the Jesuit college on Lake Titicaca for many years; filled several important posts for the Jesuits in Spain; served as rector of the Jesuit college of Salamanca at his death.
Patronage_Notes: Served the Jesuit order in various capacities, including as historian of the third council of the church at Lima.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Studied astronomy under Jyeṣṭhadeva at Ālattūr. Jyeṣṭhadeva was a student of Nīlakaṇṭha Somasutvan and Dāmodara, continuing the Dṛggaṇita school of astronomy founded by Parameśvara.
Religion_Notes: Member of the Piṣāraṭi community, traditionally employed in temple affairs; inferred from cultural context.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Wrote nine works on astronomy and astrology, including treatises on planetary computation, eclipses, and astrological practice. Contributed to the Kerala school of astronomy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by patronage; also engaged in scholarly writing and teaching of astronomy and astrology.
Patronage_Notes: Patron was Ravivarman, King of Veṭṭattunād (r. 1595–1607), a scholar in grammar, poetics, medicine, astronomy, and astrology.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by David Pingree. S. Venkitasubramonia Iyer, 'Acyuta Piṣāroṭi; His Date and Works,' JOR Madras, 22 (1952–1953), 40–46. K. Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Doctor of arts and medicine at Basel, where he studied and practiced medicine.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Follower of Paracelsus' doctrines emphasizing the relationship between medicine and minerals, particularly metallic compounds. Developed strong interest in alchemical transmutation of base metals into gold and the philosophers' stone. Participated in translation, editing, and publication of Paracelsus' manuscripts and wrote introduction to Arnald of Villanova's Rosarium. Composed tracts on gout and the relation of herbs to zodiacal signs.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Doctor of arts and medicine at Basel; studied and practiced medicine there.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Pearl Kibre. Original works: numerous editions of Paracelsus' writings published 1556–1577 at Basel, Frankfurt, Strasbourg, and other centers; Isagoge in Arnaldi de Villanova Rosarium chymicum (Basel, 1559). (Frankfurt, 1706); Conrad Gesner, Historia animalium (Frankfurt, 1604).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Pearl Kibre.

Father_Notes: Father Noah Adams belonged to the distinguished Adams family of New England; family circumstances were comfortable.
Education_Institution: McGill University; Yale University; Heidelberg University
Education_Notes: Graduated with first rank honors in natural science from McGill University at nineteen, where he studied under J. W. Dawson and B. J. Harrington. Studied chemistry and mineralogy at Yale University (1878–1879). Attended sessions at Heidelberg University to master petrographic technique under H. Rosenbusch. Received Ph.D. summa cum laude from Heidelberg for thesis on anorthosites and Grenville rocks (1893).
Education_Locations: Montreal, Unknown, Canada, Unknown, 1878; New Haven, Connecticut, United States, 1878, 1879; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Deeply but quietly religious; devoted to Christ Church Cathedral, to which he dedicated his 1941 history of the cathedral.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in petrographic microscopy in Canada; established the igneous origin of anorthosites and sedimentary origin of Grenville crystalline rocks. Conducted groundbreaking experimental investigations into rock deformation under high pressure, demonstrating metamorphic processes and contributing to understanding of mountain building. Studied Precambrian rocks, the Monteregian Hills, and Haliburton and Bancroft areas. Published comprehensive geological report and map of Ceylon. Authored authoritative history of geological sciences.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Joined Geological Survey of Canada in 1880 as assistant chemist and lithologist, serving until 1890. Joined McGill as lecturer (1890–1893), then held the Logan chair of geology (1893–1924). Served as dean of the Faculty of Applied Science (1908–1922) and dean of the Faculty of Graduate Studies (11922–1924). Retired in 1924 after thirty-five years of service.
Patronage_Notes: Directed by A.R.C. Selwyn at the Geological Survey of Canada; granted leave of absence to study petrographic technique at Heidelberg.
Instruments_Notes: Became probably the first in Canada to use the petrographic microscope, mastering the technique at Heidelberg under H. Rosenbusch. Designed and operated a gigantic high-pressure press at McGill to subject rock cylinders to confining pressures up to 296,725 pounds per square inch, pioneering experimental investigation of rock deformation and metamorphic processes.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of London; Geological Society of America; Royal Society of Canada; Geological Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to Royal Society of London. President of Geological Society of America (1918). President of Royal Society of Canada (1913); awarded Flavelle Gold Medal (1937). Awarded Lyell Medal by Geological Society of London (1906) and Wollaston Medal (1939). President of the Twelfth International Geological Congress (Montreal, 1913). Received honorary degrees from McGill, Toronto, Queen's, Mount Allison universities, and Bishop's College.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Thomas H. Clark. Original works: Complete listings in United States Geological Survey Bulletins 746, 823, 937, 1049, 1195. Father_Notes: Thomas Adams was a tenant farmer and devout Wesleyan; family circumstances were modest but respectable.
Education_Notes: Early schooling in a farmhouse; tutored in calligraphy, Greek, and mathematics from 1827; attended his cousin's academy in Devonport from 1831, where he excelled in classics and self-taught advanced mathematics. Entered St. John's College, Cambridge in October 1839 on a sizarship; graduated in 1843 as senior wrangler in the mathematical tripos and first Smith's prizeman.
Religion_Notes: Son of a devout Wesleyan father; did not take holy orders, which caused his fellowship at St. John's to expire in 1852.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Predicted the existence and position of Neptune through analysis of Uranus's orbital perturbations (1843–1845); developed lunar theory and corrected Laplace's calculation of the moon's secular acceleration; analyzed the Leonid meteor shower; computed mathematical constants including Bernoullian numbers and Euler's constant to 263 decimal places.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Fellow and tutor of St. John's College, Cambridge (1843–1852); fellow of Pembroke College (1853 onward); professor of mathematics at University of St. Andrews (1858–1859); Lowndean professor of astronomy and geometry at Cambridge (1859–1892); director of Cambridge Observatory (1861–1892).
Patronage_Notes: Offered a knighthood by Queen Victoria in 1847, which he declined.
Instruments_Notes: In 1870 the Cambridge Observatory acquired a Simms transit circle, which Adams directed in a program to map a zone of the sky for the Astronomische Gesellschaft program, published in 1897.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected president of the Royal Astronomical Society in 1851 and again for a second term in 1874. Awarded the Copley Medal by the Royal Society in 1848 and a gold medal by the Royal Astronomical Society in 1866.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Morton Grosser. Original works: MSS on perturbations of Uranus, 1841–1846 (St. John's College Library, Cambridge); Lectures on the Lunar Theory (Cambridge, 1900); William Grylls Adams, ed., The Scientific Papers of John Couch Adams, 2 vols. (Cambridge, 1896–1900). Secondary: Morton Grosser, The Discovery of Neptune (Cambridge, Mass., 1962); W. M. Smart, "John Couch Adams and the Discovery of Neptune," Occasional Notes of the Royal Astronomical Society (London), 2 (1947), 33–88.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Morton Grosser.

Father_Notes: Lucien Harper Adams was a missionary in Syria; the family maintained a classical and historical library.
Education_Institution: Dartmouth College; University of Chicago; University of Munich
Education_Notes: Received early schooling from his mother and father's library in Syria. Graduated from Dartmouth College in 1898 with the A.B. degree. Studied at the University of Chicago under George Ellery Hale, earning his M.A. in 1900. Attended the University of Munich in 1901 before returning to Yerkes Observatory as a computer and general assistant.
Education_Locations: Hanover, Unknown, United States, Unknown, 1898; Chicago, Unknown, United States, 1898, 1900; Munich, Unknown, Germany, 1900, 1901
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in astrophysics and stellar spectroscopy. Developed the method of spectroscopic parallaxes for determining stellar distances. Conducted extensive studies of sunspot spectra, stellar atmospheres (Venus and Mars), white dwarfs, and interstellar gases. Investigated stellar motions, Cepheid variables, spectroscopic binaries, and novae.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as computer and general assistant at Yerkes Observatory from 1901. Joined Mount Wilson Solar Observatory in 1904 and remained there throughout his career, serving as acting director at various periods and as director from 1923 to 1946.
Patronage_Notes: Mount Wilson Solar Observatory was established by the Carnegie Institution of Washington in 1904, which provided institutional support for his research.
Instruments_Notes: Contributed significantly to the design of the 100-inch and 200-inch Hale telescopes on Palomar Mountain. Built the powerful Coudé spectrograph for the 100-inch telescope. Conducted pioneering observations with the Snow reflector, sixty-foot and 150-foot tower solar telescopes, and the sixty-inch reflecting telescope at Mount Wilson.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Astronomical Society; Astronomical Society of the Pacific; International Astronomical Union; American Philosophical Society; National Academy of Sciences; Royal Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: President of the American Astronomical Society (1931–1934) and the Astronomical Society of the Pacific (1923). Vice-president of the International Astronomical Union (1935–1948) and acting secretary (1940–1945). Elected to the American Philosophical Society (1915) and the National Academy of Sciences (1917). Foreign member of the Royal Society of London and foreign associate of academies of science in France, Sweden, and the Soviet Union.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Helen Wright. Original works: 270 papers listed in Joy's biographical article, including 'The Polar Compression of Jupiter' (Astronomical Journal, 1899); 'Radial Velocities of Twenty Stars Having Spectra of the Orion Type' (Publications of the Yerkes Observatory, 1904, with E.B. Frost); 'Photographic Observations of the Spectra of Sunspots' (Astrophysical Journal, 1906, with G.E. Hale); 'A Spectroscopic Method of Determining Parallaxes' (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 1916); 'The Relativity Displacement of the Spectral Lines in the Companion of Sirius' (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 1925); 'Absorption Bands in the Spectrum of Venus' (Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific, 1932, with Theodore Dunham, Jr.); 'Early Days at Mount Wilson' (Publications of the Astronomical Society of the Pacific, 1947); and many others. Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: Plessis Sorbon; Collège Royal; Jardin du Roi
Education_Notes: Educated at the Plessis Sorbon, the Collège Royal, and Jardin du Roi. Studied under Pierre Le Monnier, Réaumur, G.-F. Rouelle, and Antoine and Bernard de Jussieu. No formal degree is named.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Botany; Zoology; Physics; Electricity; Philosophy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered natural classification of mollusks based on anatomical structure of living animals; developed a natural plant classification system based on all characters rather than arbitrarily selected ones, challenging Linnaeus's system. Studied static electricity in torpedo fish and tourmaline; investigated microscopic organisms, sap circulation in lower plants, and regeneration in frogs and snails. Contributed extensively to Buffon's Histoire naturelle générale and introduced modern statistical methods into systematic botany.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Elected adjoint botaniste (1759), associé botaniste (1773), and académicien pensionnaire (1782) at the Académie des Sciences. Received a life annuity in the 1760s when his natural history collection became part of the Cabinet du Roi. Conducted scientific expeditions on behalf of the Compagnie des Indes. Made a member of the Institut de France upon its creation and later appointed to the Legion of Honor by Napoleon.
Patronage_Notes: Patronage obtained by friends; supported by the Cabinet du Roi through a life annuity. Corresponded with and was influenced by Bernard de Jussieu and other leading naturalists of Europe.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Royal Society of London; Institut de France
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of the Académie des Sciences (24 July 1750); elected foreign member of the Royal Society of London (1761); immediately selected as a member of the first college of the Institut de France upon its creation.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by J. P. Nicolas. Original works: Histoire Naturelle du Sénégal. Coquillages (Paris, 1757); Familles des plantes, 2 vols. Father_Notes: Father Joseph Addison wished Thomas to become a lawyer but did not prevent his medical studies.
Education_Institution: Grammar School; University of Edinburgh; Guy's Medical School
Education_Notes: Attended grammar school at Newcastle-on-Tyne; entered University of Edinburgh as medical student in 1812 and graduated in 1815 with M.D., thesis titled 'De syphilide et hydrargyro.' Became perpetual Physician's Pupil at Guy's Medical School in December 1817.
Education_Locations: Newcastle-on-Tyne, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, 1812, 1815; London, Unknown, England, 1817, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Clinical studies on fatty liver degeneration, appendicitis, pneumonia, phthisis, and xanthoma. Described pernicious anemia in 1849 and discovered Addison's disease (suprarenal insufficiency) in 1855, laying the foundation for modern endocrinology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: House surgeon at Lock Hospital (1815); assistant physician to Guy's Hospital (1824); lecturer on materia medica (1827); joint lecturer on medicine with Richard Bright (1835); physician to Guy's Hospital (1837); sole lecturer on medicine (1840–1854 or 1855).
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Obtained licentiateship in the Royal College of Physicians on 22 December 1819; elected fellow on 4 July 1838.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: Cathedral School of Tours; Cathedral School of Laon
Education_Notes: Studied at Tours and taught at Laon in France. Traveled widely for seven years visiting Salerno, Sicily, Cilicia, Syria, and possibly Palestine; likely spent time in Spain. Learned Arabic during his travels, possibly in Sicily or through contact with other Arabists.
Education_Locations: Tours, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Laon, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Astronomy; Astrology; Philosophy; Natural Philosophy; Geometry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Foremost medieval translator of Arabo-Greek learning into Latin. Translated astronomical tables of al-Khwārizmī and works on astrology. Composed treatises on the astrolabe, arithmetic, and geometry. Wrote philosophical works on universals and natural questions covering plants, animals, meteorology, and physics. Pioneered full Latin versions of Euclid's Elements from Arabic sources.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Laon in France. Received payment from the sheriff of Wiltshire in 1130 (4s. 6d.). Indications of association with the royal court; dedicated his Astrolabe to a young Henry (regis nepos).
Patronage_Notes: Dedicated his Astrolabe to a young Henry, identified as regis nepos (king's nephew), suggesting royal patronage or connection. Received payment from royal sources in 1130.
Instruments_Notes: Composed a tract on the astrolabe, continuing a line of work begun with earlier Arabic translations. Cited his own translation of al-Khwārizmī's Tables and Euclid's Elements in this work.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Docteur-régent of the Faculty of Medicine in Paris; no other formal education is named.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Keen supporter of antiphlogistic chemistry from his early years. Participated in founding Annales de chimie (1789) and served as editor. Proposed a new system of chemical symbols with Hassenfratz to indicate substance identity, physical state, oxygen content, and degree of acid neutralization. Investigated stannic chloride, pineapple juice, and acetic acids; concluded that acetous and acetic acids differed only in water content, a conclusion later confirmed by Proust.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held position as docteur-régent of the Faculty of Medicine in Paris. Became colonial administrator in Santo Domingo (1791) and later prefect of the Niévre (after 1803). Served as editor of Annales de chimie for several years and published translations and original works.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Educated in Ireland; no formal degree recorded. Emigrated to America in 1798 following the Irish rebellion.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering American mathematician; published early work on the normal law of errors (1808), predating Gauss's published work; studied isotomous curves, catenaria volvens, Diophantine algebra, and the figure of the earth. Shared with Nathaniel Bowditch the distinction of being a creative mathematician in early American science.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Master at Princeton Academy; principal of York County Academy in York, Pennsylvania (1798–1805); principal of Reading Academy (1805–1809); professor of mathematics at Queen's College, New Brunswick (1809–1813); professor at Columbia College, New York (1813–1826); taught at University of Pennsylvania (1827–1834), becoming vice-provost in 1828; taught at Columbia College grammar school (1836–1840).
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of the American Philosophical Society in 1812; published papers in its Transactions (1818).

Father_Notes: Father held the chair of theology at the University of Rostock.
Education_Institution: University of Jena; University of Rostock
Education_Notes: Studied medicine and mathematics at Jena under G.E. Hamberger and at Rostock, where he received his M.A. in 1747 with a dissertation on the paths of falling bodies.
Education_Locations: Jena, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Rostock, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1747
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Physics; Electricity; Magnetism; Astronomy; Optics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work on algebraic equations, partial differential equations, and negative numbers. Pioneering research on thermoelectric properties of tourmaline and the analogy between electricity and magnetism. Masterwork Tentamen theoriae electricitatis et magnetismi (1759) established action-at-a-distance theory of electrical phenomena. Contributions to astronomy and optics were competent but not outstanding.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught mathematics at Rostock as junior lecturer until 1755. Director of the Berlin Observatory and member of the Academy of Sciences (1755–1757). Director of the observatory and professor of physics at the Imperial Academy of St. Petersburg (1757–1760s). Instructor to the Corps of Imperial Cadets (1760 or 1761 onward). Later became preceptor to the crown prince, diplomat, courtier, and privy councillor.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed to Berlin Observatory and Academy by Frederick II. Recommended by Euler for position at Imperial Academy of St. Petersburg. Later became member of the Order of St. Anne and served as preceptor to the crown prince.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences, Berlin; Imperial Academy of Sciences, St. Petersburg
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the Berlin Academy of Sciences from 1755. Member of the Imperial Academy of St. Petersburg from 1757.

Evaluated sources using his own experience and judgment despite later claims of unoriginality.

Religion_Notes: Accepted the bishopric of Karlstad diocese in 1835, suggesting Lutheran affiliation, but the entry does not explicitly state his religious belief.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Renowned for contributions to algal taxonomy and classification. Authored foundational works on algal systematics including Synopsis algarum Scandinaviae and Systema algarum. Also contributed to plant classification systems, plant anatomy, and plant physiology, influenced by Romantic Naturphilosophie.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor at the University of Lund from 1812 to 1835. In 1835 accepted the bishopric of Karlstad diocese and ceased botanical writing.

Father_Notes: Father was the prominent botanist Carl Adolph Agardh; Jacob accompanied him on an algological expedition to the Adriatic at age fourteen.
Education_Notes: Acquired scientific experience at an early age under his father's guidance; accompanied his father on an algological expedition to the Adriatic at age fourteen; undertook extensive field trips to the Mediterranean and studied herbarium collections at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle in Paris.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in sea algae and algology, particularly the Florideae (red algae) and Fucaceae (brown algae). Pioneered systematic and morphological approaches to algal taxonomy. Studied germination processes, swarm spores, and the influence of environmental conditions on algal species. Developed comprehensive taxonomic classification in Species, genera et ordines algarum. Also worked on plant systematics and the philosophy of plant classification.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Active as a teacher at the University of Lund from 1834 and served as professor of botany from 1854 to 1879.

Father_Notes: Louis Agassiz, a prominent naturalist; mother was Cecile Braun Agassiz, sister of botanist Alexander Braun.
Education_Institution: Harvard College; Lawrence Scientific School; Lawrence Scientific School
Education_Notes: Lived at Freiburg im Breisgau 1847–1849 under the influence of his uncle. Graduated from Harvard College in 1855; earned engineering degree from Lawrence Scientific School in 1857 and zoology degree from Lawrence Scientific School in 1862.
Education_Locations: Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States, Unknown, 1855; Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States, 1855, 1857; Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States, 1857, 1862
Scientific_Disciplines: Zoology; Oceanography; Marine Zoology; Echinoderms; Engineering
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work focused on New England shore animals, especially echinoderms, culminating in Revision of the Echini (1872–1874). Shifted to deep-sea dredging and abyssal fauna from 1877 onward. Major interest from 1892 in coral atoll formation, questioning Darwin's subsidence theory through comparative study of Caribbean, Hawaiian, and Pacific islands. Later work bridged classical zoology and modern oceanography.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant to his father at the Museum of Comparative Zoology from 1859, serving chiefly as director for the rest of his life. Managed Calumet and Hecla copper mines in Michigan from 1866, accumulating a fortune by 1869 that he invested in scientific research. Supported himself through inherited and accumulated wealth while funding expeditions and publications.

Father_Notes: Minister father; family enjoyed prosperity and status in Swiss cantons.
Education_Institution: University of Zurich; University of Heidelberg; University of Munich; University of Erlangen
Education_Notes: Attended universities of Zurich, Heidelberg, and Munich. Earned doctorate in philosophy from Munich and Erlangen in 1829; earned doctor of medicine degree from Munich in 1830. Studied under Baron Georges Cuvier in Paris.

Religion_Notes: Embraced Protestant pietism of his minister father; devoted to idealistic romanticism seeing Creator's power in nature; never identified with sectarian religious persuasion.
Scientific_Disciplines: Ichthyology; Geology; Paleontology; Zoology; Embryology; Marine Biology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in paleoichthyology with Poissons fossiles describing over 1,700 ancient fish species with comparative anatomy reconstructions. Developed Ice Age theory through glacial research in Switzerland and Europe, explaining Continental natural history through glaciation. Established Museum of Comparative Zoology at Harvard as center for natural history research. Opposed Darwin's evolution theory, asserting permanent species and multiple separate creations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor at College of Neuchâtel from 1832; lectured at Lowell Institute in Boston from 1846; professor at Lawrence Scientific School of Harvard University from 1847 until death. Founded and directed Museum of Comparative Zoology at Harvard College from 1859.
Patronage_Notes: Studied under Baron Georges Cuvier in Paris; admired by Alexander von Humboldt and Sir Charles Lyell. Advised federal government on U.S. Coast Survey and Smithsonian Institution. Received support from private gifts and Massachusetts state funds for museum.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Geological Society of London; Royal Society of London; National Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Received Wollaston Medal from Geological Society of London and Copley Medal from Royal Society of London. Helped establish National Academy of Sciences in 1863.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Practitioner and founder of the episynthetic (eclectic) school of medicine. Wrote on the pulse, fever (especially semitertian fever), and hellebore. Emphasized empirical verification and intellectual unity of medicine.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a physician in Rome and founded his own medical school with many disciples.

Father_Notes: Pietro Agnesi was a wealthy Milanese professor of mathematics at the University of Bologna who established a cultural salon in his home and secured distinguished tutors for his daughter.
Education_Notes: Educated at home by a series of distinguished professors secured by her father. Demonstrated exceptional linguistic ability, speaking French fluently by age five and mastering Greek, German, Spanish, and Hebrew by age eleven. Studied mathematics under Father Ramiro Rampinelli of the Olivetan Benedictines. No formal degree is recorded.
Religion_Notes: Expressed a strong desire to enter a convent in 1738; after her father's death in 1752 devoted herself to religious studies and social work. Became directress of the Pio Albergo Trivulzio, a home for the aged, ill, and indigent, in 1771.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Algebra; Geometry; Calculus; Analysis; Physics; Natural Philosophy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Demonstrated early interest in analytical geometry and ballistics by age fourteen. Prepared critical commentary on L'Hospital's Traité analytique des sections coniques. Her masterwork, the Istituzioni analitiche (1748), provided comprehensive treatment of algebra, coordinate geometry, differential and integral calculus, infinite series, and differential equations. Also known for the versiera (witch of Agnesi), a cubic curve with applications in physics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by her wealthy father Pietro Agnesi throughout her life. Received papal recognition and an honorary chair at the University of Bologna from 1750 to 1752, which she did not actively teach.
Patronage_Notes: Pope Benedict XIV provided the most significant recognition, sending congratulatory letters in 1749 and 1750, awarding a gold medal and precious-stone-adorned wreath, and appointing her to the chair of mathematics and natural philosophy at Bologna in 1750.

Father_Notes: Gregor Bauer was a dyer and woolen draper.
Education_Institution: Leipzig University; University of Bologna; University of Venice
Education_Notes: Attended schools in Glauchau, Zwickau, and Magdeburg before entering Leipzig University in 1514. Received B.A. in 1515 and remained as lecturer in elementary Greek. Studied medicine at Leipzig under Heinrich Stromer von Auerbach from 1523, supported by a prebend. Spent three years at Bologna and Venice (1523–1526) as member of the Aldina editorial staff for classical medical texts.
Education_Locations: Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1514, 1517; Bologna, Unknown, Italy, 1523, 1526; Venice, Unknown, Italy, 1523, 1526
Religion_Notes: Roman Catholic; believed reform was necessary but opposed revolutionary aspects of the Reformation. Served as one of few Catholic representatives at the Protestant court of Moritz, duke of Saxony. After his death, Protestant clergy refused him burial in the parish church, and he was interred in the cathedral at Zeitz through intervention of the Catholic bishop Julius von Pflug.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mining; Metallurgy; Geology; Mineralogy; Medicine; Pharmacology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in systematic study of mining and metallurgy, recording observations from St. Joachimsthal mines and smelters. Compiled comprehensive inquiries on principles of geology and mineralogy over fifteen years, culminating in De re metallica libri XII. Studied pharmaceutical uses of minerals and smelting products, and occupational diseases of miners and smelters. Also published on weights and measures, and plague medicine.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer in Greek at Leipzig (1515–1517); town physician and apothecary of St. Joachimsthal (1527–1533); town physician of Chemnitz (1533 onward); profited from mining shares and partnerships, becoming one of the twelve richest inhabitants of Chemnitz by 1542; served as mayor of Chemnitz and councillor to the court of Saxony; appointed historiographer of the court of Saxony in 1534.
Patronage_Notes: Nominated historiographer of the court of Saxony by Georg the Whiskered, duke of Saxony, in 1534. Served as councillor to the court of Saxony and ambassador to Emperor Charles V and Ferdinand, king of Bohemia, during the Schmalkaldic War (1546–1548). Erasmus contributed a letter of recommendation for Bermannus.

Education_Notes: Enrolled at University of Cologne in 1499, where he studied law, medicine, magic sciences, and theology under Peter Ravenna. Made a trip to Paris at age twenty to study. Gave lectures on Reuchlin's De verbo mirifico at Dôle. Held theological disputations at Cologne in 1510. Taught theology at Turin and expounded Hermetic writings at Pavia in 1515. No degree is named.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Author of De occulta philosophia, a foundational work on magic and Neoplatonic mysticism combining metaphysical speculation with Hermetic and Cabalistic thought. Wrote De incertitudine et vanitate scientiarum, a polemic on the limits of human knowledge and the vanity of the sciences. Worked as court astrologer and physician. His thought synthesized Platonic, Neoplatonic, and Hermetic influences with Renaissance skepticism.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served in the army of Emperor Maximilian I. Public advocate in Metz in 1518. Town physician in Fribourg, Switzerland during 1523–1524. Personal physician to the queen mother and court astrologer at the court of Francis I in Lyons after 1524. Historian and librarian to Margaret of Austria in Antwerp from 1528. Constantly in monetary difficulties.
Patronage_Notes: Served Emperor Maximilian I in military capacity. Employed by Francis I as personal physician to the queen mother and court astrologer in Lyons. Summoned by Margaret of Austria, regent of the Netherlands, to serve as historian and librarian in Antwerp.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by the Jesuit order; taught syntax, logic, and theology; charged with organizing the teaching of exact sciences in Belgium.

Father_Notes: Yūsuf ibn Ibrāhīm, sometimes called al-ḥāsib (the reckoner), was a learned and influential scholar. Works on the history of medicine, history of astronomy, and astronomical tables are attributed to him, though none survive.
Education_Notes: No formal institutional education is recorded. The entry indicates he was influenced by Greek mathematical and astronomical works, particularly Euclid, Ptolemy, Archimedes, Hero, Plato, Empedocles, and Apollonius.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal work was a treatise on ratio and proportion, expanding Euclid's definitions through dialectic argument and identifying eighteen cases of proportional relationships. Also wrote on similar arcs, a commentary on Ptolemy's Centiloquium, and a work on the astrolabe.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as a private secretary to the Ṭūlūn family, which ruled Egypt from 868 to 905, likely under Abū'l-Baqāʾ Hudā ibn Aḥmad ibn Ṭūlūn.
Patronage_Notes: Employed by the Ṭūlūn family, the ruling dynasty of Egypt during his active period.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed simplified symbolic notation for geometry problems; worked on ellipses, spheres, circles, and regular polygons; created a logarithm table to base two; contributed to number theory through continued fractions and integral solutions of polynomial equations; founder of the Saijyo school of mathematics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as field supervisor of engineering, river improvement, and irrigation under the Edo shogunate until 1788; subsequently lived on savings while teaching mathematics to numerous pupils and publishing mathematical works.

Education_Notes: Studied at the College of Navarre of the University of Paris, receiving his doctorate of theology in 1381.
Religion_Notes: Bishop of Le Puy from 1395, bishop of Cambrai from 1397, and cardinal from 1411. Active in the conciliar movement.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Wrote commentaries on Aristotle's De anima and Meteorologica. Composed astronomical and astrological treatises, including a commentary on Sacrobosco's De sphaerae. His principal work, Imago mundi, is a collection of sixteen treatises on geography, astronomy, and the concordance of astrology, astronomy, and theology with historical events. Concerned with calendar reform and wrote on this subject for the Council of Constance (1414). Adopted a nominalist philosophical outlook.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Grand master of the College of Navarre from 1384 to 1389; chancellor of the University of Paris from 1389 to 1395. Held ecclesiastical positions as bishop of Le Puy (1395) and bishop of Cambrai (1397), and was created cardinal in 1411.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by the Church hierarchy; his ecclesiastical advancement culminated in his cardinalate.

Father_Notes: William Airy was a farmer who through self-education acquired posts in the Excise; he later lost his Excise post due to financial difficulties.
Education_Institution: Byatt Walker's School; Trinity College, Cambridge
Education_Notes: Attended Byatt Walker's school at Colchester from age ten, where he learned arithmetic, bookkeeping, and the slide rule. Entered Trinity College, Cambridge in October 1819 as a sizar. Graduated as Senior Wrangler in 1823, outdistancing all men of his year. Elected fellow of Trinity College in 1824.
Education_Locations: Colchester, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1819, 1823
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primarily an observational astronomer and organizer of astronomical institutions. Made contributions to optics, both practical and theoretical, including the invention of a cylindrical lens to correct astigmatism. Undertook numerical lunar theory based on Delaunay's equations. Published extensively on practical astronomy, optics, and mathematical topics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held the Lucasian professorship at Cambridge (1826) and the Plumian professorship with directorship of the Cambridge Observatory (1828–1835). Served as Astronomer Royal at the Royal Greenwich Observatory (1835–1881). Also undertook numerous government tasks beyond astronomy.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed Astronomer Royal by the Admiralty, which had interest in navigational applications of astronomical observations. Served as a prototype of the modern government scientist.
Instruments_Notes: Invented a cylindrical lens to correct astigmatism in his own eyesight; the method is still used.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Outstanding observer of double stars; conducted systematic surveys of double stars and published statistical investigations; compiled and revised catalogs of double stars, producing the New General Catalogue of Double Stars Within 120° of the North Pole (1932), still a standard work.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of mathematics at the University of the Pacific (1891); assistant astronomer, astronomer, associate director, and director at the Lick Observatory (1895–1935).
Instruments_Notes: Worked with a six-inch Clark refractor at the University of the Pacific observatory and conducted observations at the Lick Observatory using its telescopes.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Trained as a gardener; became assistant to Philip Miller at Chelsea Physic Garden in 1755, where he greatly enlarged his botanical knowledge under Miller's influence.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Superintendent of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew from 1783; compiled Hortus Kewensis (1789), a three-volume catalog of approximately 5,500 cultivated plants with descriptions of new species, provenance, and introduction dates. Recognized for superior practical knowledge of living plants.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Engaged by Princess Augusta in 1759 to establish and manage the botanical garden at Kew House; assumed full control of the gardens in 1783 under royal patronage.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Princess Augusta (1759–1772), who engaged him to plant Kew; later supported by John Stuart, third earl of Bute, a knowledgeable botanist who encouraged him; subsequently befriended and supported by Sir Joseph Banks, royal adviser on Kew.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by George Taylor. Aiton, Hortus Kewensis; or, a Catalogue of the Plants Cultivated in the Royal Botanic Garden at Kew, 3 vols. (London, 1789). Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by George Taylor.

Father_Notes: William Aiton was in charge of the living collections at the Royal Botanic Garden, Kew, and styled himself "Gardens to His Majesty."
Education_Notes: Attended school at Chiswick until age thirteen, then transferred to a school at Camberwell. At age sixteen entered Kew as assistant to his father, gaining practical knowledge of horticulture and experience with living plants.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Director-general of the royal gardens at Kew, Richmond, Kensington, Buckingham Palace, Brighton, and Windsor. Succeeded his father in 1793 and oversaw the enrichment of Kew's plant collections. Collaborated on the second edition of Hortus Kewensis and published works on exotic plants and practical gardening.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as director-general of the royal gardens from 1793 onward, managing collections at multiple royal properties. Also worked as a landscape gardener, receiving commissions from the Duke of Kent and other nobility.
Patronage_Notes: Served under George IV and William IV as director of royal gardens. Received invaluable patronage and advice from Sir Joseph Banks, whom he consulted on enriching Kew's collections.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: One of seven gentlemen who founded the Royal Horticultural Society on 7 March 1804 at Mr. Hatchard's House, on the initiative of John Wedgwood.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Studied mathematics under Masatada Irie of the Nakanishi school in his youth. Later studied mathematics and astronomy under Nushizumi Yamaji, who initiated him into the secret mathematical principles of the Seki school; he was apparently over thirty when he began with Yamaji. No formal degree is recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed innovative geometry within the algebraic and numerical tradition of the Seki school. Refined the yenri method for determining areas of circles, spheres, and curved figures by dividing the diameter or chord into equal segments, initiating a technique similar to definite integration. Discovered a method for obtaining the volume common to two intersecting cylinders using double integration. Constructed logarithmic tables to twelve places and worked on yo jutsu problems involving circles inscribed in triangles and squares, including the problem later attributed to Malfatti.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as a retainer of the Shinjo clan, stationed in Edo throughout his life.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Shin'ichirō Oya. Works: Fukyu sampo; Kohai jutsu kai; Enchu kokuen jutsu.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Shin'ichirō Oya.

Alt_Name: Alanus de Insulis; Alain de Lille
Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: University of Paris; University of Montpellier
Education_Notes: Taught theology at Paris and Montpellier; later joined the Cistercian order. No formal degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Member of the Cistercian order; wrote against the Albigensians.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Attempted to construct a deductive theology derived from axioms in the manner of mathematics. Works reveal Neoplatonic influences and employ materials from Boethius and pseudo-Hermetic sources. Alluded to astronomical concepts including the eccentric and possibly the equant; mentioned Ptolemy and Abū Maʿshar by name.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught theology at Paris and Montpellier; subsequently became a member of the Cistercian order.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Son of Charles III of Monaco (Honoré Grimaldi), a ruling prince; inherited the principality in 1889.
Education_Notes: No formal education is recorded. Trained as a naval officer; served as lieutenant-commander in the French navy during the Franco-Prussian War (1870).
Scientific_Disciplines: Oceanography; Physical Oceanography; Marine Biology; Zoology; Anthropology; Paleontology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer oceanographer who conducted systematic studies of ocean currents, especially the Gulf Stream; investigated water temperature and salinity at various depths; studied plankton and deep-sea fauna; conducted physiological research on marine toxins (hypnotoxin from Physalia); founded major oceanographic institutions and publications.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Reigning Prince of Monaco from 1889; financed his oceanographic research through personal wealth and princely resources; established and maintained research vessels and institutions.
Instruments: Hirondelle; Hirondelle II; Princesse Alice I; Princesse Alice II; Richard bottle; Polyhedral nets
Instruments_Notes: Designed and commissioned a series of research vessels for oceanographic cruises spanning four decades. Used the Richard bottle to collect water samples at depth; employed baited polyhedral nets to sample bathypelagic fauna; established observation centers in the Azores for meteorological study.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences, Paris; Académie de Médecine; Académie d'Agriculture
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Corresponding member of the Académie des Sciences; foreign associate member from 1909, succeeding Lord Kelvin; foreign associate member of the Académie de Médecine; member of the Académie d'Agriculture for model farming practices at Marchais, Aisne.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Georges Petit.
