Established stratigraphic chronology with the four-order system (Primary, Secondary, Tertiary, Quaternary). Studied fossil species variation, magmatic rocks, and volcanic origins. Precursor of actualism in geology.

Appointed by Venetian Senate in 1769 to office overseeing agriculture and industry development. Conducted research in chemistry and metallurgy for state purposes.
Patronage_Notes: Early patronage by Marchese Andrea Carlotti enabled his education. Later supported by Venetian Senate, which commissioned mining studies and appointed him to state office in 1769.

Father_Notes: Johann Gottlieb Argelander was a wealthy merchant from Finland.

Entered University of Königsberg in 1817 to study political economy and political science, but was won over to astronomy by Friedrich Wilhelm Bessel. Earned doctorate in 1822 with dissertation on Greenwich observations.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in systematic observation of stellar positions and proper motions. Developed method for estimating stellar magnitudes without instruments. Created the Bonner Durchmusterung, a comprehensive catalog of 324,198 stars with positions and magnitudes. Investigated the motion of the solar system through space using proper motions of stars.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at Königsberg Observatory from 1821; observer at Åbo Observatory from 1824; full professor at University of Helsinki from 1828; professor of astronomy at University of Bonn from 1836 until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Formed lasting friendship with Crown Prince Friedrich Wilhelm (later Friedrich Wilhelm IV) during childhood when the royal family fled to Memel. The crown prince, after ascending the throne, supported the construction of the new observatory at Bonn.

Instruments_Notes: Used transit circle at Königsberg and Helsinki to measure stellar positions. Developed the method of 'estimation by steps' for measuring stellar magnitudes without a photometer.

Father_Notes: Father Antoine Dezallier owned the d'Argenville estate near Bezons and Versailles.
Education_Notes: Studied at the Collège du Plessis; trained in the fine arts under the engraver Bernard Picart, the painter Roger de Piles, and the architect Alexandre Le Blond. Also developed interests in natural science.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Geology; Conchology; Art History; Engraving
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Published L'histoire naturelle éclaircie dans deux de ses parties principales, la lithologie et la conchyliologie (1742), a successful work on mineralogy and shell collecting illustrated with fine plates. Also authored Abrégé de la vie des plus fameux peintres (1745–1752), a biographical dictionary of painters. Contributed to eighteenth-century natural history vogue through descriptions of notable natural history collections.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Purchased the post of secretary to the king in 1716; named maître des comptes in 1733 and counsellor to the king in 1748. Also supported by personal wealth as a collector and scholar.
Patronage_Notes: Held posts as secretary to the king (1716), maître des comptes (1733), and counsellor to the king (1748).
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Société Royale des Sciences de Montpellier; Royal Society of London; Académie de La Rochelle
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Société Royale des Sciences de Montpellier in 1740, the Royal Society of London in 1750, and the Académie de La Rochelle in 1758.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Yves Laissus. (Paris, 1780). Manuscripts at Bibliothèque Nationale, Paris and Bibliothèque d'Avignon. Father_Notes: Father was Octavio Argoli, a lawyer.
Education_Notes: Evidence suggests study with Magini around 1600 in Padua, though dates are uncertain. No degree is named.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Produced extensive astronomical ephemerides based on the Prutenic Tables and later on Tycho Brahe's observations. Proposed a geocentric system in which Mercury and Venus orbit the sun while Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn orbit the earth, with the earth rotating on its axis. Wrote on astrological medicine and general astrology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held the chair of mathematics at the Sapienza in Rome from 1622 to 1627, losing the post apparently due to his enthusiasm for astrology. From 1632 onward served as professor of mathematics at Padua.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: None
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed conic section theory as loci; introduced terminology for sections of acute-angled, right-angled, and obtuse-angled cones; treated the locus problem with respect to three or four lines, vergings by conic sections, angle trisection, and the focus-directrix property of conics. His work influenced Euclid and was foundational to later developments by Apollonius.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Studied under Strato of Lampsacos, third head of the Lyceum; likely studied at Alexandria rather than Athens after Strato assumed the headship in 287 B.C.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Propounded the first heliocentric theory, eighteen centuries before Copernicus. Authored On the Sizes and Distances of the Sun and Moon, the first attempt to determine astronomical distances and dimensions by mathematical deduction. Developed geometric procedures for approximating sines of small angles, anticipating trigonometric methods.
Means_of_Support_Notes: None
Instruments_Notes: Invented the skaphē, a widely used sundial consisting of a hemispherical bowl with a vertically erected needle to cast shadows.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Served as personal physician to Amyntas II of Macedon, grandfather of Alexander the Great. Died while Aristotle was a boy.
Education_Notes: Joined Plato's Academy in Athens around 367 B.C. at age seventeen and remained for twenty years. Studied under Plato. Later served as tutor to the young prince Alexander in Macedon from 342 B.C. No formal degree is recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Natural Philosophy; Astronomy; Meteorology; Biology; Zoology; Anatomy; Physiology; Psychology; Mathematics; Mechanics; Optics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Most influential ancient exponent of scientific methodology and division of sciences. Made foundational contributions to physics, cosmology, natural history, and zoology. Developed theories of motion, elements, causation, and teleology. Advanced understanding of animal anatomy and behavior through dissection and observation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Plato's Academy for twenty years (367–347 B.C.). Served as tutor to Prince Alexander in Macedon (342–335 B.C.). Upon return to Athens in 335 B.C., lectured at the Lyceum and organized research programs with students and associates.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by Hermeias, ruler of a court across the Aegean, who became his father-in-law. Employed as tutor to Prince Alexander of Macedon (342 B.C. onward), a position of significant patronage.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Joined Plato's Academy in Athens as a young man; studied there for approximately twenty years before Plato's death. Later founded his own school, the Lyceum, in Athens.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural Philosophy; Zoology; Biology; Anatomy; Physiology; Philosophy; Logic; Metaphysics; Natural History
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted systematic zoological research, particularly during his years on Lesbos (344–342 B.C.). Authored the Historia animalium, De partibus animalium, De generatione animalium, and other biological treatises. Developed theories of form and matter, actuality and potentiality, and teleological explanation applied to animal reproduction, growth, and classification. Integrated biological observation with philosophical framework.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Studied at Plato's Academy; founded and directed the Lyceum in Athens, where he taught and conducted research.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: None
Scientific_Disciplines: Anatomy; Physiology; Natural History; Medicine; Zoology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted detailed dissections of animals and gave one of the earliest systematic accounts of the cardiovascular system, including the heart, blood vessels, and blood. Studied embryonic development in the chick. Interpreted respiration and the role of heat in the body. Distinguished animals with blood from those without blood.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Ancient Greek philosopher whose works span logic, metaphysics, natural philosophy, physics, biology, and rhetoric. His writings formed the foundation of Western philosophy and science.

Father_Notes: Father was either Mnaseas or Spintharus; Spintharus was certainly his teacher, a musician whose acquaintance included Socrates, Epaminondas, and Archytas.
Education_Notes: Studied at Mantinea, an Arcadian city with a strong conservative musical tradition. Later became a pupil of Aristotle in Athens and held a position in the Lyceum, hoping to become head of the school upon Aristotle's death in 322 B.C.
Education_Locations: Mantinea, Unknown, Greece, Unknown, Unknown; Athens, Unknown, Greece, Unknown, 322
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Most famous and influential musical theorist of antiquity. Developed a descriptive system of harmonic theory based on the ear as the sole criterion of musical phenomena, rejecting the Pythagorean mathematical approach to musical intervals. Also wrote on rhythm, educational and political theory, Pythagorean doctrine, and biographies.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held a position in Aristotle's Lyceum in Athens.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: None

His observations, made approximately a century before Hipparchus, were used by Hipparchus to discover the precession of the equinoxes. Wrote in prose on astronomical topics including the polar stars and commentary on Aratus.

Father_Notes: Died when Vladimir was young; mother worked in a library.
Education_Notes: Attended Gymnasium, graduating in 1904. Entered Physics and Mathematics Faculty of Moscow University in 1904, where he studied under P.N. Lebedev and N.A. Umov. No degree is named in the source.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered experimental study of ferromagnetism in high-frequency fields; discovered ferromagnetic resonance (1913); developed theory of magnetodynamics and magnetic viscosity; studied diffraction of light on large objects; constructed high-tension impulse (lightning) generator; demonstrated levitation of permanent magnet above superconductor.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Studied at Moscow University under Lebedev from 1904. Left Moscow University in 1911 in protest and transferred to Shanyavsky Municipal University with Lebedev. Returned to Moscow University after October Revolution and organized and headed a large laboratory for electromagnetic research until his death.
Instruments: Lightning Generator; Electromagnetic Spectrograph; Photographic Plate for Centimeter Waves
Instruments_Notes: Constructed high-tension impulse generator (lightning generator) in 1925. In 1922 proposed a generator enabling his wife A.A. Glagoleva-Arkadieva to obtain first electromagnetic spectra in centimeter to 0.080 millimeter wavelength range. Developed photographic plate sensitive to centimeter-length waves in 1934.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences of the U.S.S.R.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Chosen associate member of the Academy of Sciences of the U.S.S.R. in 1927.

Father_Notes: Partner in the family brewery at Kingsdown, Wiltshire; family had established commercial interests.
Education_Notes: Graduated in geology from New College, Oxford in 1925 after three years of study; awarded the Burdett-Coutts research scholarship.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on Jurassic stratigraphy and ammonite classification; developed systematic framework for Jurassic zones and stages; published comprehensive synthesis of world Jurassic geology; contributed to standardization of stratigraphical nomenclature.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer at New College, Oxford from 1929; senior research fellow at New College 1933–1940; principal in the Ministry of War Transport 1941; senior research fellow at Trinity College, Cambridge from 1947.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of London; Linnean Society of Normandy; Geological Society of London; Geological Societies of France, Germany, and Egypt; Paleontological Society of America
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society of London in 1947; honorary member or correspondent of multiple geological and paleontological societies.

Father_Notes: Father was Henry Edward Armstrong, a fellow of the Royal Society.
Education_Notes: Trained in inorganic chemistry with Claisen and physical chemistry with van't Hoff at the University of Berlin, receiving Ph.D. in 1901. Conducted research with Emil Fischer. Received the first D.Sc. by research of the University of London for work on disaccharides, glucosides, and enzymes at Central Technical College.
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Organic Chemistry; Physical Chemistry; Catalysis; Biochemistry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on carbohydrates, disaccharides, glucosides, and enzymes. Extensive research on heterogeneous catalysis, including large-scale catalytic production of acetic acid and acetone from ethyl alcohol during World War I. Published monograph on carbohydrates in 1910.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Conducted research at Central Technical College in London. From 1905 entered the chemical industry while continuing research; from 1928 served as consultant to the chemical industry. Involved in formation of Imperial Chemical Industries, Ltd.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society of London and was active in its affairs.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Conrade E. Ronneberg. Father_Notes: John Armstrong was a publisher who became vice-president in charge of the American branch of Oxford University Press.
Education_Notes: Studied electrical engineering at Columbia University under Michael Idvorsky Pupin, graduating in 1913. Became interested in radiotelegraphy while in high school in Yonkers.
Education_Locations: New York, Unknown, United States, Unknown, 1913
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering inventor in radio engineering and electronic communication. Developed the triode feedback (regenerative) circuit, super-heterodyne circuit, superregeneration, and frequency modulation (FM). Made four particularly significant inventions that transformed radio technology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as assistant at Columbia University; sold feedback and superheterodyne patents to Westinghouse Electric & Manufacturing Company with royalty-earning licensing rights; became a millionaire through RCA's acquisition of superheterodyne rights via cross-license with Westinghouse.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Institute of Electrical Engineers; Institute of Radio Engineers
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Received Edison Medal from American Institute of Electrical Engineers (1942) and Medal of Honor from Institute of Radio Engineers (1918, reaffirmed 1934).
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Charles Süsskind. See also obituaries in New York Times (2 Feb. 1954), p. 27; and in Proceedings of the Institute of Radio Engineers, 42 (1954), 635.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Charles Süsskind.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: Royal College of Chemistry; University of Leipzig
Education_Notes: Entered Royal College of Chemistry, London in 1865; studied under A.W. Hofmann and John Tyndall; conducted research under Edward Frankland; studied under Hermann Kolbe at Leipzig; awarded Ph.D. in 1870.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, 1865, Unknown; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1870
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Organic Chemistry; Chemistry Education; Crystallography; Chemical Engineering
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer work on benzene structure and centric formula; research on naphthalene structure and reactions with W.P. Wynne, advancing the dye industry; quinonoid theory for color of organic compounds; reactions of camphor and terpenes; enzyme reaction mechanisms; significant crystallography research predating X-ray diffraction; early advocate of Mendeleev's periodic table and spatial molecular configuration; devised curricula relating chemistry and engineering, regarded as father of chemical engineering.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Teaching combined with research from 1870; professor of chemistry at Central Institution, South Kensington from 1884 (merged with Imperial College in 1907); retired from teaching in 1911. Practiced chemistry research throughout his career.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of London; Chemical Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Royal Society of London at age twenty-eight; served Chemical Society of London as secretary, president, and vice-president. Regarded as doyen of British chemists between 1890 and 1935.

Alt_Name: Arnau de Vilanova; Arnaldus de Villanova
Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Student at Montpellier ca. 1260. Studied for six months with the Montpellier Dominicans. By 1291 was a medical master at Montpellier's newly chartered studium generale. No formal degree is recorded.
Religion_Notes: Influenced by Joachimite Peter John Olivi and the spiritual-Franciscans. Wrote prophetic and mystical theological works; his De adventu antichristi was condemned in 1299. Tolerated by popes Boniface VIII and Benedict XI as a physician but not for his theology. Gained papal patronage under Clement V in 1305. In 1309 made statements that questioned James II's orthodoxy.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Physician to Peter III and Alfonso III of Aragon, and later to James II. Principal figure in fusing Western empirical tradition with Greek and Arab medical philosophy at Montpellier. Translated Avicenna's De viribus cordis and Galen's De rigore from Arabic into Latin. Lectured extensively on Hippocratic and Galenic works. Developed systematic medical theory based on complexio (qualitative medicine); established mathematical pharmacy in Aphorismi de gradibus. Wrote on astrology and oneiromancy; his heterodoxy led to attribution of alchemical texts, though he considered alchemists ignorant.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Physician to the Aragonese royal family from 1281 onward, serving Peter III, Alfonso III, and James II. Medical master at Montpellier from ca. 1291, where he taught and wrote extensively on medical theory and practice.
Patronage_Notes: Served as physician to Peter III of Aragon (from 1281), Alfonso III, and James II. Received royal support for his developing religious views. Gained papal patronage under Clement V from 1305. Supported by William of Nogaret, Philip IV's minister, who intervened to spare him imprisonment in 1299. Later attached himself to Frederick I of Trinacria.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Father was a lawyer who defended the University of Paris against the Jesuits in 1594; Antoine was the youngest of twenty children.
Education_Notes: Ordained a priest; received doctorate in theology in 1641; entered the Sorbonne in 1643 after the death of Richelieu.
Religion_Notes: Ordained a priest; held Jansenist views and was expelled from the Sorbonne in 1656 for these beliefs; spent much of his later life in theological dispute.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Contributed to mathematical pedagogy through the Éléments (1667), a reworking of Euclidean theorems emphasizing clarity and fresh exposition. Developed Port-Royal Logic with Pierre Nicole, elaborating the theory of clear and distinct ideas and giving the first account of Pascal's method. Co-authored Port-Royal Grammar, which treated linguistic and mental processes as virtually identical and anticipated modern linguistic theory through its analysis of signs and universal grammar.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Entered the Sorbonne in 1643 as a theologian; ordained a priest; spent latter part of life in self-imposed exile in Brussels.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the development of reliable triode designs for long-distance telephony by recognizing the importance of high vacuum; contributed to magnetic alloys for sound reproduction and electroacoustics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked for Bell Telephone Laboratories from its inception; served as the first director of research when the laboratories were formally established in 1925, a position he held until his death.
Instruments_Notes: Developed designs utilizing reliable triodes that made long-distance telephony possible; earlier experimented with mercury-arc repeaters for telephone signal amplification.

Education_Institution: Not Specified; Not Specified; University of Padua
Education_Notes: Studied philosophy and medicine at Perugia, Montpellier, and Padua, where he attended Fabricius' lectures. Graduated M.D. in 1605.

Religion_Notes: Buried in the Church of Saint Luke in Venice; declined invitation to serve Pope Urban VIII.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Advanced the hypothesis of preformation of the germ in plant and animal generation. Published the Epistola de generatione plantarum ex seminibus (1625), which posited that seeds contain a miniature germ and nutritive matter. Investigated the permeability of the interventricular septum of the heart, though no writings on this survive.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine in Venice from 1610. Also engaged in literary scholarship and debate.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Attended Angerburg elementary school and Gymnasium in Rastenburg; after father's death, mother moved to Königsberg where he attended Gymnasium and graduated in 1841. Studied mathematics and natural sciences at University of Königsberg 1841–1845 under Bessel, Jacobi, Richelot, Hesse, and Franz Neumann. Followed Jacobi to Berlin and studied under Dirichlet, Steiner, Gustav Magnus, and Dove. Did not take state examinations; awarded Doctor honoris causa by University of Königsberg in 1851 for treatise on algebraic principles.
Education_Locations: Rastenburg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Königsberg, Unknown, Germany, 1841, 1845
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in the theory of invariants in Germany; developed a distinctive method for studying functions unchanged under linear substitutions. Established foundational principles of invariant theory and derived characteristic partial differential equations (Aronhold's differential equations). Worked on plane curves, completing Plücker's problem of nine inflection points on third-order curves and formulating theorems on fourth-order plane curves.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Artillery and Engineers' School in Berlin 1852–1854; taught at Royal Academy of Architecture from 1851, appointed professor in 1863. Joined Royal Academy for Arts and Crafts in 1860; took over Weierstrass's teaching schedule in 1862 and was appointed professor in 1864.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Appointed corresponding member of the Academy of Sciences in Göttingen in 1869.

Father_Notes: Father was an accountant of Huguenot descent.
Education_Institution: Collège Français; University of Berlin; University of Leipzig
Education_Notes: Attended Collège Français in Berlin before entering University of Berlin in 1839 as a promising graduate student with early publications. Received Ph.D. from University of Leipzig in 1850.
Education_Locations: Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1839, Unknown; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1850
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Diligent investigator of comets, asteroids, and nebulae. Discovered comet 1845 I, comet d'Arrest (1851 II), comet 1857 I, and asteroid (76) Freia. Made accurate measurements of nebulous objects and extended observations to 1,942 nebulae. First to note in 1873 that gaseous nebulae were preferentially located near the plane of the Milky Way. Began spectroscopic observations following William Huggins.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked at Leipzig Observatory under August Ferdinand Möbius from 1848. Became professor at University of Copenhagen in 1858 and director of its new observatory.
Instruments_Notes: Used an eleven-inch telescope for nebular observations and a sixteen-foot Merz telescope for extended nebular survey work.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected foreign associate of the Royal Astronomical Society of London in 1848. Received the Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society in 1875.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Sally H. Dieke. Father_Notes: Svante Gustav Arrhenius was a surveyor and later supervisor of the University of Uppsala, and overseer of the estate of Vik.
Education_Notes: Attended Cathedral School in Uppsala; entered University of Uppsala at age seventeen, studying mathematics, chemistry, and physics; passed candidate's examination in 1878; chose physics as principal subject for doctoral study; worked under Erik Edlund in Stockholm from 1881; defended dissertation in May 1884.
Education_Locations: Uppsala, Unknown, Sweden, Unknown, Unknown; Uppsala, Unknown, Sweden, 1876, 1884
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Physical Chemistry; Physics; Meteorology; Cosmic Physics; Immunology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founder of modern physical chemistry; developed theory of electrolytic dissociation; studied conductivity of electrolytes and reaction velocity; investigated cosmic and meteorological phenomena including glacial periods, volcanic physics, radiation pressure, and panspermic theory; applied physical chemistry to toxins and antitoxins.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed lecturer in physical chemistry at University of Uppsala in November 1884; professor of physics at Technical High School in Stockholm from 1895; rector of Technical High School 1896–1905; director of physical chemistry department at Nobel Institute in Stockholm until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Received travel grant from Swedish Academy of Sciences enabling work in laboratories of Ostwald, Kohlrausch, Boltzmann, and van't Hoff (1886–1890); Wilhelm Ostwald offered him a docentship in Riga in 1884 after reviewing his dissertation.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Swedish Academy of Sciences; Deutsche Elektrochemische Gesellschaft; Deutsche Chemische Gesellschaft; Royal Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected honorary member of Deutsche Elektrochemische Gesellschaft in 1895; appointed to Swedish Academy of Sciences in 1901 over strong opposition; elected honorary member of Deutsche Chemische Gesellschaft in 1905; became foreign member of Royal Society of London in 1911.

Father_Notes: Member of ancient French nobility with land and wealth in Limoges for centuries.
Education_Institution: Lycée Impérial de Limoges; Collège Ste.-Barbe; Université de Poitiers
Education_Notes: Studied classics at Lycée Impérial de Limoges and Collège Ste.-Barbe; received baccalaureate from Université de Poitiers in 1869. Medical studies began at Limoges, continued in Paris after 1870. Became préparateur to Claude Bernard from 1873 to 1878, which constituted his principal scientific training.
Education_Locations: Limoges, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Poitiers, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1869
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in biophysics and electrophysiology; studied electrical properties of muscle contraction and animal electricity. Developed calorimetric methods for measuring animal heat and body temperature. Invented high-frequency electrotherapy apparatus and founded the paramedical field of physiotherapy. Contributed to understanding of endocrine extracts and hormone theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Préparateur to Claude Bernard (1873–1878); assistant to C. Brown-Séquard at Collège de France; directed the laboratory for biophysics at rue St.-Jacques (1882–1910) and the laboratory at Nogent-sur-Marne (1910–1931). Also served as government science consultant during World War I.
Patronage_Notes: Paul Bert, as Minister of Public Education, assisted in establishing the laboratory for biophysics at the Collège de France in 1882. Claude Bernard's mentorship was instrumental in directing his career toward physiological research.
Instruments: Calorimeter; Thermoelectric Needles; Galvanometer; Electrodes; Myographic Equipment; High Frequency Oscillator; Electrotherapy Apparatus; Electrocoagulation Apparatus; Temperature Incubator
Instruments_Notes: Designed a double-chambered calorimeter with constant interior temperature maintained by circulating ice water, achieving remarkable accuracy. Invented thermoelectric needles for simultaneous temperature measurement of tissue and blood. Developed nonpolarizable silver chloride electrodes and refined carbon-rod microphones. With Deprez, invented the mobile circuit galvanometer (1882). With Marey, invented myographic equipment. Designed the first electrically controlled constant temperature incubator for embryological and bacterial research. Developed high-frequency heat therapy apparatus and electrocoagulation equipment for surgical use.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences; Academy of Medicine; Society of Biologists; International Society for Electrical Science; International Society for Cryogenic Studies
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to Academy of Sciences in 1894 and Academy of Medicine in 1888. Instrumental in founding the national society for electrical science (1881) and international society for electrical science (1897). Founded international society for cryogenic studies (1908). Active member of societies for electrotherapy, physics, electronics, civil engineering, electroceramics, and soldering.

Alt_Name: Petrus Arctaedius Angermannus; Petrus Arctelius Angerm.; Peter Arctaedius
Father_Notes: Father Olaus Arctaedius was a curate appointed to the living of Nordmaling in 1716; grandfather was also a clergyman.
Education_Notes: Attended school at Hernösand from autumn 1716, excelling in studies and pursuing ichthyological interests outside school hours. Matriculated at Uppsala University on 30 October 1724. Studied chemistry and natural history in the medical faculty under Lars Roberg and Olof Rudbeck. Sought to qualify for a doctor's degree in medicine at Leiden but did not complete it before his death.
Education_Locations: Hernösand, Unknown, Sweden, 1716, Unknown; Uppsala, Unknown, Sweden, 1724, 1729
Religion_Notes: Son of a curate and grandson of a clergyman; embedded in Swedish Lutheran clerical culture, though he chose natural history over the clergy.
Scientific_Disciplines: Biology; Ichthyology; Zoology; Botany; Mineralogy; Alchemy; Anatomy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of ichthyology and the first to establish the notion of genus in zoology and the distinction between species and variety. Studied fishes, amphibians, and mammals with comparative anatomical methods. Specialized in the Umbelliferae in botany. Examined seventy-two fish species through dissection and live observation. Studied mineralogy and medieval alchemical writings.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Studied at Uppsala University and later worked on scientific manuscripts with financial support from his brothers-in-law for travel to England. Supported by chemist Albert Seba of Amsterdam, who entrusted him with studying fishes for his Thesaurus.
Patronage_Notes: Received financial aid from brothers-in-law for travel. Supported by Albert Seba, a chemist and collector in Amsterdam, who employed him to study fishes for his Thesaurus. Benefited from the patronage of Sir Hans Sloane, president of the Royal Society, during his stay in England.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Sir Hans Sloane, president of the Royal Society, provided assistance during Artedi's studies in England.

Contributed to abstract algebra, formal-real fields, hypercomplex numbers and algebras of associative rings, braid theory, and the theory of Artin rings. Lectured on mathematics, mechanics, and relativity theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer at University of Hamburg (1923), extraordinary professor (1925), ordinary professor (1926). Taught at University of Notre Dame (one year), Indiana University Bloomington (1938–1946), Princeton University (1946–1958), and returned to University of Hamburg (1958–1962).

Father_Notes: Ayabe Yasumasa was a Confucian scholar-administrator of the Kizuki fief government.
Education_Notes: Self-taught in medicine and astronomy. Read Chinese calendrical works and possibly Jesuit missionary writings. No formal institutional education is recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in introducing Western observational methods and instruments to Japanese astronomy. Developed techniques for precise observation, ground lenses, and made telescopes. Studied Jupiter's satellites and lunar eclipses. Formulated cyclic variation of astronomical parameters and investigated Kepler's third law. Synthesized Chinese and Western astronomical traditions.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed physician of the Kizuki fief government in 1767. Deserted his fief in 1772 and practiced medicine in Osaka to support himself while pursuing astronomy. Taught and educated numerous pupils who became prominent astronomers.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by wealthy Osaka merchant Hazama Shigetomi (1756–1816), one of his most able pupils, who sponsored instrument-making and astronomical observation. Also received annual monetary gifts from his eldest brother after deserting his fief.
Instruments_Notes: Ground lenses and made a telescope to observe Jupiter's satellites. Hazama Shigetomi, his pupil, showed greatest talent for inventing and improving instruments, conducting systematic observations with modern equipment.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Rejected humoralism in favor of solidism based on atomism and Epicurean philosophy. Developed a mechanistic medical system emphasizing diet, exercise, massage, and baths. Opposed anatomical study. Influenced the methodist school of medicine through his pupil Themison of Laodicea.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Distinguished himself in anatomical studies and surgical practice. Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced surgery in Milan and was appointed first surgeon of the Spanish army in Italy from 1612 to 1620. Continued anatomical research in Milan and delivered lectures on the chylous vessels in 1625.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed first surgeon of the Spanish army in Italy (1612–1620). Received honorary citizenship of Milan for his anatomical contributions.

Father_Notes: Simon Ashmole was a saddler of Lichfield; the family held a humble social position.
Education_Notes: Educated at Lichfield Grammar School in expectation of entering a craft; obtained legal training in London.
Religion_Notes: In religious and political matters he was excessively conservative and orthodox.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural Philosophy; Alchemy; Astrology; Botany; Medicine; Heraldry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Deeply influenced by mathematicians and astrologers during the Civil War; formed significant astrological friendship with William Lilly; extended interests to botany, medicine, and stenography; became pupil of William Backhouse in alchemy; published major alchemical collections including Fasciculus chemicus (1650) and Theatrum chemicum Britannicum (1652); regarded occult sciences and experimental natural philosophy as complementary means of discovering natural principles; founding fellow of Royal Society (1660); devoted intellectual energies to heraldry and compiled comprehensive history of the Order of the Garter.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Established law practice in 1638 but practiced sporadically; appointed comptroller of the excise and Windsor herald by Charles II in 1660, the former providing large income; marriage provided independent means; appointed keeper of the Ashmolean Museum and first professor of chemistry at Oxford (Robert Plot, his protégé, held this post).
Patronage_Notes: Rewarded by Charles II with offices of comptroller of the excise and Windsor herald in 1660; married Elizabeth Dugdale, daughter of Sir William Dugdale, a prominent antiquarian and friend; associated with eccentric collectors and patrons of alchemical and astrological pursuits.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Became founding fellow of the Royal Society in 1660; made significant bequests to the society's museum.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of Trinity College, Cambridge (1919); received medals from many scientific institutions; chairman of the Committee on Atoms of the International Union of Chemistry (1936–1945); awarded the Nobel Prize for Chemistry in 1922.

Father_Notes: Protestant clergyman, probably of Jewish ancestry who renounced that religion rather than leave France.
Education_Notes: Received doctorate in medicine at Montpellier in 1703; passed competitive examination of the Faculty of Medicine of Toulouse in 1711.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Comprehensive medical educator covering anatomy, physiology, psychology, gerontology, pathology, therapy, venereology, gynecology, neurology, and pediatrics. Pioneered description of septicemia from uterine infections and puerperal fever; described extrauterine pregnancies and lithopedions. Intuited reflex action in 1743. Treatise on venereal diseases included first Western reproduction of Chinese medical terminology in printed Chinese characters. Biblical scholar whose Conjectures sur la Genèse applied textual criticism to the Old Testament using divine names as dating keys.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Occupied chairs of medicine at Montpellier (1716–1728) and at the College Royal (1751); general physician to the duke of Orleans from 1728; chief physician to Augustus II of Poland from 1729; king's counsellor and physician from 1730; inspector general of mineral waters of Languedoc from 1721; municipal magistrate of Toulouse from 1730.
Patronage_Notes: Served as general physician to the duke of Orleans and chief physician to Augustus II of Poland. Received royal pension in 1720 and was named king's counsellor and physician in 1730. Mme. de Tencin, a patient, assisted in arranging his daughter's marriage and remembered him in her will.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in precise observation and calculation of stellar positions, proper motions, and parallaxes. Derived orbits of double stars Sirius and Procyon; conducted meridian observations and created fundamental star catalogs. Participated in Venus transit expeditions and determined solar parallax.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at Königsberg Observatory (1859–1862); spent four years at Gotha Observatory under Hansen; appointed astronomer of the Berlin Academy in 1866, where he remained for five decades; served as permanent secretary of the Academy from 1878 until his death; elected secretary of the Astronomical Society at its first meeting and served as its president from 1881 to 1889.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected secretary of the Astronomical Society at its first meeting (founded 1865); served as president from 1881 to 1889.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Master organic chemist who investigated structural theory for over fifty years. With Victor Meyer, substituted the term stereochemistry for van't Hoff's chemistry in space in 1888. Studied geometrical isomerism, particularly in benzildioxime and oxime compounds. Mastered the assignment of configuration to stereoisomers and established the configuration of crotonic acids. Investigated spectrochemistry of organic compounds, the relation of physical properties to molecular structure, and molecular rearrangements, including determination of keto-enol proportions in tautomeric mixtures.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Director of the chemical institute at the University of Marburg. Published over 500 papers in German journals from 1884 to 1938.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Designed vacuum experiments to demonstrate air pressure on barometers; made significant contributions to the development of the micrometer and telescopic sights for astronomical instruments; criticized mathematical treatises and prepared work on proportions.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Member of the Académie des Sciences until his withdrawal in 1668; supported by patrons whose identities are not specified in the entry.
Instruments_Notes: Perfected the micrometer by modifying Malvasia's lattice design with two parallel hairs separated by a variable distance, controlled by a precision screw; developed systematic use of telescopic sights in place of open sights during 1667–1671 in collaboration with Picard and Roberval.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on the immunological specificity of pneumococcus and the chemical nature of soluble specific substances. Demonstrated that DNA, not protein, is the active agent in bacterial transformation, establishing the molecular basis of heredity and laying the foundation for modern molecular biology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked briefly in clinical medicine; joined Hoagland Laboratory as researcher and lecturer in bacteriology and immunology; member of the Rockefeller Institute Hospital staff from 1913 to 1948.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Royal Society, as indicated by biographical memoir publication.

Father_Notes: Count Filippo Avogadro was a distinguished lawyer and higher civil servant who became a senator of Piedmont in 1768 and was appointed advocate general to the senate of Vittorio Amedeo III in 1777. He reorganized the senate under French rule and became its president.
Education_Notes: Received early education at home, then attended grammar school in Turin for secondary education. Became a bachelor of jurisprudence in 1792 and gained a doctorate in ecclesiastical law in 1796. From 1800 studied mathematics and physics privately.
Religion_Notes: Described after his death as religious but not a bigot.
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Chemistry; Physical Chemistry; Electricity; Thermodynamics
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Formulated Avogadro's hypothesis distinguishing atoms and molecules, fundamental to nineteenth-century chemistry. Conducted research on electricity, specific heats of gases, atomic volumes, chemical affinity, and the relationship between physical properties and chemical composition. Applied mathematical and physical approaches to chemical problems.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed secretary to the prefecture of the department of Eridano in 1801. Demonstrator at the college attached to the Academy of Turin in 1806. Professor of natural philosophy at the College of Vercelli from 1809. Held the first chair of mathematical physics at Turin from 1820 (with salary of 600 lire), lost it in 1822 due to political changes, received honorary title of professor emeritus in 1823, and was reappointed in 1834 until retirement in 1850. Served on government commissions on statistics, weights and measures, and public instruction.
Patronage_Notes: Benefited from government appointments and academic positions under the Piedmontese state.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of the Academy of Sciences of Turin on 5 July 1804 and became a full member on 21 November 1819. Notably absent from foreign membership of the Paris Academy of Sciences and the Royal Society of London.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Infantry cadet from 1764; second lieutenant assisting in hydrographic surveys near Madrid by 1769; taught mathematics in the army until 1774; captain of a frigate appointed by the Spanish viceroy; served as mayor of Huesca in later life.
Patronage_Notes: Commissioned by the Spanish crown in 1781 to establish the frontier between Brazil and Spanish colonies; appointed captain of a frigate by the Spanish viceroy; declined appointment as viceroy of Mexico.

Father_Notes: Konrad Baade was a schoolteacher; his wife Charlotte Wulfhorst was Protestant and the family initially planned a theological career for Wilhelm.

Education_Notes: Attended Friedrichs-Gymnasium in Herford from 1903 to 1912. Studied at University of Münster briefly, then transferred to Göttingen in Easter term 1913, where he remained throughout World War I. Gained competence in the observatory under Leopold Ambronn and served three years as assistant to mathematician Felix Klein. Passed doctoral examination in July 1919; dissertation on spectroscopic binary star β Lyrae written under Johannes Hartmann.
Education_Locations: Herford, Unknown, Germany, 1903, 1912; Münster, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1913; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, 1913, 1919
Religion_Notes: Protestant; family initially planned his career in theology.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering observational astronomer whose work on stellar populations fundamentally changed understanding of galactic structure and the scale of the universe. Discovered asteroids and comets; conducted spectroscopic studies of binary stars, supernovae, and distant galaxies. Identified two stellar populations (Type I and Type II) based on color and location. Resolved stars in Andromeda galaxy nucleus and determined the galaxy's greater distance, effectively doubling the known size of the universe.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Scientific assistant at University of Hamburg's Bergedorf Observatory (1919–1931); promoted to observer (1927); Privatdozent at Hamburg (1928–1931); staff member at Mt. Wilson Observatory (1931–1958); Gauss professor at Göttingen (1958–1960).
Instruments_Notes: Conducted lifetime of telescopic observations using progressively larger instruments, including the 39-inch telescope at Bergedorf, the 100-inch telescope at Mt. Wilson, and the 200-inch Palomar telescope. Worked with spectroscopic equipment for binary star and supernova analysis. Collaborated with Bernard Voldemar Schmidt on the design of Schmidt wide-angle telescopes.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Philosophical Society; Academy of Sciences of Amsterdam; Academy of Sciences of Göttingen; Academy of Sciences of Lund; Academy of Sciences of Munich; Academy of Sciences of Mainz
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the American Philosophical Society and scientific academies in five European cities.

Father_Notes: Parents were affluent.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in mechanization of computation and the design of calculating machines (Difference Engine and Analytical Engine). Wrote on applied mathematics, functions, mass production principles, operational research, and engineering notation. Diverse interests included cryptanalysis, probability, geophysics, astronomy, altimetry, ophthalmoscopy, statistical linguistics, meteorology, actuarial science, and lighthouse technology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Elected Lucasian professor of mathematics at Cambridge in 1827 and held the position for twelve years, though he never functioned as professor. Received government subsidy for his calculating engine projects.
Patronage_Notes: Received government subsidy for the Difference Engine project, though it proved insufficient to complete the work.
Instruments_Notes: Designed the Difference Engine, which would calculate functions and print results using the method of differences; the unfinished Difference Engine Number One became a museum piece. Conceived the Analytical Engine, inspired by Jacquard's punched cards, featuring a mill with 1,000 columns of geared wheels capable of performing arithmetic operations and incorporating decision-making logic units; it remained a paper project but foreshadowed modern computing.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Astronomical Society; British Association; Statistical Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Royal Society from 1816. Helped found the Astronomical Society (1820), the British Association (1831), and the Statistical Society of London (1834). Criticized unprogressive learned societies and advocated for scientific reform.

Father_Notes: Jean Babinet was mayor of Lusignan; mother was daughter of a lieutenant-general.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work in diffraction theory and the wave theory of light; formulated Babinet's principle relating diffraction phenomena to transparent and opaque systems. Extensive research in meteorological optics including rainbows, coronas, atmospheric refraction, and polarization of skylight. Also worked in mineralogy and astronomy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held professorships at Fontenay-le-Comte and Poitiers after graduation from École Polytechnique; became professor of physics at Collège Louis-le-Grand in Paris in 1820; appointed librarian at the Bureau of Longitudes in 1841.
Instruments_Notes: Constructed a portable goniometer for measuring angles of refraction in mineralogical experiments, improving upon Malus' design. Invented the Babinet compensator to produce or analyze arbitrarily polarized light.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of the physics section of the Académie des Sciences in 1840.

Father_Notes: A keen amateur botanist who influenced his son's devotion to natural history.
Education_Notes: Attended private schools and Charterhouse before entering St. John's College, Cambridge in 1826. Graduated B.A. in 1830 and received M.A. in 1833. Established an enduring friendship with J.S. Henslow, professor of botany, whose enthusiasm confirmed his lifelong devotion to botany.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Leading botanist and taxonomist. Published Flora Bathoniensis (1834), Primitiae florae Sarnicae (1839), and Manual of British Botany (1843), considered his magnum opus and the first complete guide to British plants arranged according to a natural system. Insisted upon critical delimitation of species, demonstrated in British Rubi (1869). Made significant additions to the Cambridge Herbarium during his professorship.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Elected to the chair of botany at Cambridge in 1861 following Henslow's death, which he held until his death in 1895.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Ray Club; Ray Society; Entomological Society; Cambridge Antiquarian Society; Linnean Society; Royal Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Leading member of the Ray Club, which developed into the Ray Society (founded 1844); helped with its publications including Memorials of John Ray and Correspondence of John Ray. Founding member of the Entomological Society in Cambridge and the Cambridge Antiquarian Society. Elected fellow of the Linnean Society in 1830 and was its senior fellow at his death. Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1851.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Apprenticed to a medical practitioner in Londonderry; completed medical training at Guy's Hospital, London; awarded M.D. by Aberdeen University in 1795; qualified as licentiate of the College of Physicians, London in 1796.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Published Systematic Arrangement of Minerals (1795) and New System of Mineralogy (1799), classifying minerals by chemical composition and crystal form using a Linnaean system; this advanced upon the Wernerian system. Active in promoting mineralogical and geological science through the Geological Society of London.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant surgeon at Haslar Naval Hospital (1777); apothecary, assistant physician, and full physician at Guy's Hospital (1781–1811), where he also lectured on chemistry; established successful private medical practice from 1796.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; British Mineralogical Society; Geological Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1805; member of the British Mineralogical Society (formed 1799); founding member of the Geological Society of London (13 November 1807) and served as president from 1822 to 1824.

Father_Notes: None

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Studied heart and pleural diseases (1863–1877); illustrated Gaucher's disease (1876); investigated malarial infection and its effects on erythrocytes (1866–1894); pioneered intravenous drug injection, first injecting quinine chlorhydrate for malaria (1890) and strophantine for heart failure (1906); early advocate of oxygen therapy (1870).
Means_of_Support_Notes: Director of the Medical Clinic of Rome from 1863 until his death; practiced as a physician; served as Minister of Public Education (1881, 1893, 1898) and Minister of Agriculture, Commerce, and Industry (1901).
Patronage_Notes: Held ministerial posts under the Italian state; loyal to the house of Savoy.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Italian Society of Internal Medicine; Italian Society of the History of Medicine
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Presided at the first congress of the Italian Society of Internal Medicine (Rome, 1888); elected chairman of the committee drafting the constitution of the Italian Society of the History of Medicine (1907).

Father_Notes: Technician in a distillery who stimulated his son's interest in science.
Education_Notes: Attended Gymnasium in Kiev (1867–1875). Enrolled in natural science section of Department of Physics and Mathematics at Kiev University in 1875, specializing in chemistry. Expelled in 1878 for political activities; resumed studies in 1882. No formal degree is recorded.
Education_Locations: Kiev, Unknown, Russia, 1867, 1875; Kiev, Unknown, Russia, 1875, 1878; Kiev, Unknown, Russia, 1882, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in slow oxidation and biological oxidation; developed the peroxide theory of oxidation (Bach-Engler theory). Investigated carbon assimilation by plants, enzymology, and industrial biochemistry. Conducted fundamental research on oxidation-reduction reactions and biological catalysis.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked in Paul Schützenberger's laboratory at Collège de France (1890–1894). Conducted independent research in Geneva (1894–1917). After 1917 directed the L.Y. Karpov Institute of Physics and Chemistry and the Institute of Biochemistry within the Academy of Sciences of the U.S.S.R. Held positions in Soviet scientific institutions and government bodies.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by Lev Yakovlevich Karpov's recommendation for directorship of the chemical laboratory. Elected member of Central Executive Committee of U.S.S.R. (1927). Organized and directed major Soviet scientific institutes under state auspices.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected chairman of Société de Physique et d'Histoire Naturelle de Genève in 1916. Elected member of Academy of Sciences of the U.S.S.R. in 1929 and academician-secretary of the chemical sciences section in 1939. Chosen honorary member of Imperial Society of the Chemical Industry (London) and American Chemical Society in 1943. Permanent president of Dmitrii Ivanovich Mendeleev All-Union Chemical Society from 1932 until his death.

Father_Notes: Great-grandson of Benjamin Franklin and related to leading Philadelphia families.
Education_Notes: Graduated from West Point at the head of his class in 1825. Studied primary and secondary education during a two-year sojourn in Europe (1836–1838), observing German Gymnasium and French lycée systems.
Education_Locations: West Point, Unknown, United States, Unknown, 1825
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Terrestrial Magnetism; Meteorology; Astronomy; Chemistry; Geology; Seismology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work in chemical analysis and heat radiation/absorption. Conducted significant investigations of steam boiler explosions. Primary focus shifted to terrestrial magnetism and meteorology, establishing American magnetic observatory network. Directed Coast Survey expansion into astronomical research, tidal observations, Gulf Stream studies, and seismic wave analysis from earthquakes.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served in Corps of Engineers for two years after West Point (1825–1827). Professor of natural philosophy and chemistry at University of Pennsylvania (1827–1836). Organized and directed Girard College (1836–1842). Returned to University of Pennsylvania (1842–1843). Head of U.S. Coast Survey (1843–1867) and successor to Hassler as head of Office of Weights and Measures.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed head of Coast Survey by federal government. Served on informal Commission on Conference planning naval strategy during Civil War (1861). Vice-president of U.S. Sanitary Commission. Member of Permanent Commission advising navy on technical matters (1863–1864). First president of National Academy of Sciences (1863).
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Philosophical Society; Franklin Institute; American Association for the Advancement of Science; National Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Assumed leading roles in American Philosophical Society and Franklin Institute affairs in Philadelphia. Directed significant steam boiler investigation at Franklin Institute (1836). President of American Association for the Advancement of Science (1851). First president of National Academy of Sciences (1863).

Father_Notes: None

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the epistemology of modern science, analyzing the conceptual ruptures between classical and contemporary physics. Examined mathematical physics, thermodynamics, and the role of instruments (Wilson cloud chamber, spectroscope, particle accelerator) in embodying theory. Applied psychoanalytic method to epistemology and developed analyses of imagination, space, time, and the classical elements.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught physics and chemistry in the collège of Bar-sur-Aube; later became a philosopher, presumably in an academic capacity.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Obtained the bachelor of sciences degree in 1898; defended his doctoral dissertation on the theory of speculation two years later (1900).
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in the mathematical theory of speculation and probability. Introduced continuity into probability problems by making time a variable; examined movements and chains of probabilities applied to market fluctuations and light propagation. First to examine stochastic methods of Markovian type, foundational to Kolmogorov's theory. Work anticipated Einstein-Wiener theory of Brownian motion.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Named lecturer at Besançon in 1919; taught at Dijon and Rennes; professor at Besançon from 1927 to 1937, when he retired.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Jean Bachet was appeals judge of Bresse and counselor to the duke of Savoy; the family was ancient and noble, with his grandfather a counselor to King Henry II.
Education_Notes: Orphaned at age six; received early education in a Jesuit house in the duchy of Savoy. Presumably studied in Padua as a young man; may have taught in a Jesuit school in Milan or Como. Spent time in Paris and Rome.

Religion_Notes: Educated by the Jesuit order; elected to the Académie Française in 1635.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in mathematical recreations and theory of numbers. Produced the first edition of the Greek text of Diophantus's Arithmetica with extensive Latin commentary (1621), establishing the foundation for modern study of Diophantine analysis. Authored Problèmes plaisans et delectables (1612), containing arithmetical problems ranging from parlor tricks to sophisticated problems of weights and river crossings.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Member of the Académie Française from 1635. Came from a wealthy noble family and appears to have lived on personal means while pursuing scholarly and literary work.
Patronage_Notes: Belonged to an ancient noble family; his grandfather was counselor to King Henry II and his father counselor to the duke of Savoy.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie Française in 1635, though too ill with rheumatism and gout to attend the inaugural ceremony in 1634.

Education_Notes: Studied humanities and medicine at Leipzig; took his medical degree at the University of Helmstedt in 1676.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Medical practitioner in Leipzig from 1676; lecturer in medicine at University of Leipzig from 1677; appointed chair of physiology and botany in 1691; professor of pathology in 1701; professor of therapeutics and dean perpetual in 1719.

Father_Notes: Pastor at the Jacobi Kirche in Berlin; instilled in Bachmann a pious Lutheran view of life and modesty.

Education_Notes: Attended Gymnasium where his mathematical talent was discovered by teacher Karl Schellbach. Studied mathematics at University of Berlin, then transferred to Göttingen in 1856 to attend Dirichlet's lectures, where he became close friends with Dedekind. Completed studies in Berlin and received doctorate in 1862 under Ernst Kummer for a thesis on group theory. Completed habilitation in Breslau in 1864 with a paper on complex units.
Education_Locations: Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1856; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, 1856, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1862; Breslau, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1864
Religion_Notes: Inherited a pious Lutheran view of life from his father.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: From 1856 onward, Bachmann's interests were centered almost exclusively upon number theory. His major work was a comprehensive survey of number theory, Zahlentheorie (1892–1923), which reviewed known results, evaluated various methods of proof and approach, and synthesized the contributions of Dirichlet, Kummer, Dedekind, and Hensel. Also published works on irrational numbers, lower number theory, and Fermat's problem.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as extraordinary professor in Breslau, then appointed to a professorship in Münster. Around 1890 resigned his professorship. In Weimar, combined mathematical writing with composing and serving as music critic for various newspapers.

Father_Notes: None

Education_Notes: Studied law at Strasbourg, Berlin, and Munich for four years; passed first state examination and served as law clerk 1906–1908. In 1908 abandoned law and began experimental physics at Tübingen under Friedrich Paschen, specializing in atomic spectroscopy. Doctoral dissertation on Preston's rule accepted February 1913, published 1921.
Education_Locations: Strasbourg, Unknown, Germany, 1902, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Munich, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Tübingen, Unknown, Germany, 1908, 1913
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Devoted his career to improving spectrographs for studying Zeeman effects and atomic structure. Made major technical innovations in light-source design and vacuum-arc construction. Discovered hyperfine structure of bismuth spectrum and provided first firm evidence of nuclear angular momentum in even-Z nuclei.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant to Paschen at Tübingen until 1914. Employed in service corps during World War I. Head of physical laboratory at Veifa-Werke (electrical and X-ray equipment manufacturer) in Frankfurt am Main, 1918–1920. Returned to Tübingen as assistant 1920–1923. Privatdozent at Tübingen from spring 1923. Extraordinary professor at Landwirtschaftliche Hochschule Hohenheim 1926 (ordinary professor 1929), though scientific work continued at Tübingen. Professor at Tübingen from 1936; retired 1948.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and fabricated improved spectrographs of unparalleled quality for Zeeman-effect studies. His most important innovation was the vacuum arc light source, featuring elaborate electrode advancement by clockwork and motor-driven oscillation, packed into four millimeters between electromagnet pole pieces to achieve unprecedented spectral resolution.

Father_Notes: Born in poverty.
Education_Notes: Left school at an early age but prepared himself for entrance to the University of Uppsala, where he received a Ph.D. in 1875.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Devoted his career to the study of Encke's comet, demonstrating that its long-term acceleration is subject to irregular changes attributable to nongravitational forces. Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked at the observatory of Dorpat for three years after his Ph.D., then at Pulkovo Observatory under Otto von Struve. Elected to the Imperial Academy of Sciences of Petrograd in 1883 and served as director of Pulkovo Observatory from 1895 until his death.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Awarded the Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society in 1909 for his work on Encke's comet.

Father_Notes: Sir Nicholas Bacon was lord keeper of the great seal; mother was Ann, daughter of Sir Anthony Cooke, indicating gentry connections.
Education_Notes: Educated at Trinity College, Cambridge from 1573 to 1575; entered Gray's Inn and became a barrister in 1582. No university degree is recorded.

Religion_Notes: Adhered to the middle road of the Church of England, neither authoritarian nor sectarian.
Scientific_Disciplines: Philosophy; Natural Philosophy; Philosophy of Science
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal contributions were in natural philosophy, philosophy of scientific method, and projects for the practical organization of science. His inductive method and vision of science profoundly influenced later seventeenth-century science. Works include The Advancement of Learning, Novum organum, and New Atlantis.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a barrister from 1582; held government positions including lord chancellor (1618) and viscount St. Albans (1621). In his final years after dismissal from office, devoted himself to natural philosophy and writing.
Patronage_Notes: Knighted on the accession of James I; held high offices under the Crown including lord chancellor. Sought Crown support throughout his life for his scientific projects, as evidenced by his 1592 letter to Cecil.

Father_Notes: Family impoverished as a result of support for Henry III against the baronial party.

Education_Notes: Early instruction in Latin classics, particularly Seneca and Cicero. Acquired interest in natural philosophy and mathematics at Oxford. Took M.A. either at Oxford or Paris, probably around 1240. Lectured in the Faculty of Arts at Paris between 1241 and 1246 on Aristotelian works. Returned to Oxford around 1247 where he came under the influence of Robert Grosseteste and Adam Marsh.
Education_Locations: Oxford, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1241, 1246
Religion_Notes: Franciscan friar, entered the order around 1257. Condemned and imprisoned by his order between 1277 and 1279, possibly related to heretical Averroist propositions condemned by the bishop of Paris, Stephen Tempier, in 1277.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural Philosophy; Optics; Mathematics; Astronomy; Astrology; Alchemy; Philosophy; Calendar Reform; Geography
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work in optics, particularly on lenses and magnification; developed geometrical theory of physical causation based on Grosseteste's multiplication of species; advanced understanding of the eye as an image-forming device; contributed to calendar reform with accurate calculations of the Julian year error; wrote extensively on astrology, alchemy, and natural magic; emphasized mathematics as fundamental to all sciences.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lectured in the Faculty of Arts at Paris; taught at Oxford; supported by the Franciscan order after entering around 1257.
Patronage_Notes: Sought patronage from Cardinal Guy de Foulques (later Pope Clement IV), who requested his philosophical writings in 1265 and issued a papal mandate in 1266 requesting copies of his works. Composed his three major works (Opus maius, Opus minus, Opus tertium) in response to papal request.
Instruments_Notes: Developed optical constructions for convex and concave spherical lenses for magnification to aid vision; described use of spherical astrolabe; conducted experiments with lodestones and floating magnets to investigate magnetic orientation.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the industrial synthesis and manufacture of phenol-formaldehyde condensation products (Bakelite resins), beginning in 1907. Surveyed industrial utilization of condensation reactions and distinguished three stages of reaction with soluble intermediate products.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of chemistry and physics at the Government Normal School of Science in Ghent; employee and later head of a photographic firm in the United States; founder and operator of the Bakelite Corporation, which by 1930 occupied a 128-acre plant at Bound Brook, New Jersey; consultant in electrochemistry.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected president of the American Chemical Society in 1924; delivered a lecture before the society on 8 February 1909 on phenol-formaldehyde condensation.

Father_Notes: Magnus Johann von Baer was an Estonian landholder with a modest estate; served as a district official (Landrat) and official of the Estonian knighthood.
Education_Institution: Cathedral School; University of Dorpat; University of Berlin; University of Vienna; University of Würzburg; University of Berlin
Education_Notes: Attended cathedral school for nobility in Reval (1807–1810); matriculated at University of Dorpat as medical student in August 1810; received M.D. in September 1814. Continued studies in Berlin and Vienna (1814–1815) and Berlin (winter 1816–1817). Studied comparative anatomy under Ignaz Döllinger at Würzburg (1815–1816).
Education_Locations: Reval, Unknown, Estonia, 1807, 1810; Dorpat, Unknown, Estonia, 1810, 1814; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1814, 1815; Vienna, Unknown, Austria, 1814, 1815; Würzburg, Unknown, Germany, 1815, 1816; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1816, 1817

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of embryology; discovered the mammalian egg (1826) and described vertebrate development from conception to birth. Identified the notochord, neural folds, and primary brain vesicles. Established the epigenetic principle of development from general to special. Proposed four fundamental animal types based on symmetry. Later devoted himself to physical and ethnographic anthropology, geography, and natural history expeditions across Russia. Contributed to founding of Russian Geographical Society and Russian Entomological Society.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Prosector in anatomy at Königsberg (1817); extraordinary professor of anatomy (1819); ordinary professor of zoology (1826); served as dean of medical faculty and rector of university. Entered Academy of Sciences in St. Petersburg as full member in zoology (1834); academician for comparative anatomy and physiology (1846); ordinary professor at Medico-Chirurgical Academy in St. Petersburg (1846–1852); librarian for foreign division of academy.
Patronage_Notes: Instructed the two daughters of Grand Duchess Helen Pavlovna (wife of Grand Duke Michael Pavlovitch) in natural history and enjoyed her friendship for many years beginning in 1839–1840. Supported by the Academy of Sciences in St. Petersburg for scientific expeditions and research.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Academy of Sciences (St. Petersburg); Royal Society of London; Paris Academy; Russian Geographical Society; Russian Entomological Society; German Anthropological Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of Academy of Sciences in St. Petersburg (1826); entered as full member in zoology (1834); retired from active membership (1862) but continued as honorary member until 1867. Elected member of Royal Society of London and Paris Academy. First president of Russian Entomological Society (1860). Instrumental in founding Russian Geographical Society (beginning 1845) and German Anthropological Society (1861).

Alt_Name: Adolf Johann Friedrich Wilhelm von Baeyer; Adolf von Baeyer
Father_Notes: Lieutenant general in the Prussian army; participated in government projects to measure degrees of latitude and longitude and in a general European measurement program on the shape of the earth.
Education_Institution: Friedrich-Wilhelms Gymnasium; University of Berlin; University of Heidelberg; Kekulé's Private Laboratory; University of Ghent
Education_Notes: Early education at Friedrich-Wilhelms Gymnasium and University of Berlin under P.G. Dirichlet and G. Magnus, emphasizing mathematics and physics. After military service in 1856, studied experimental chemistry with R. Bunsen at Heidelberg, then entered Kekulé's private laboratory in Heidelberg in 1858. Followed Kekulé to Ghent and remained until 1860. Received doctoral degree from Berlin in 1858 for work on arsenic methyl chloride.
Education_Locations: Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1856; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, 1856, 1858; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, 1858, 1858; Ghent, Unknown, Belgium, 1858, 1860
Religion_Notes: Mother was Jewish but converted to the Evangelical faith and was confirmed by Schleiermacher. Baeyer was of the same faith as his parents.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in synthetic organic chemistry and structural determination. Major contributions include work on uric acid derivatives and barbiturates, discovery of phenolphthalein and phthalein dyes, complete synthesis of indigo with determination of its exact structural formula, development of strain theory relating ring stability to bond bending, investigation of polyacetylenes and oxonium compounds, and elucidation of benzene structure. Empirical approach to chemistry focused on test-tube analysis and structural determination rather than theoretical speculation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held various teaching positions at the technical institute and military academy in Berlin after 1860. Appointed ordinary professor of chemistry at the imperial university at Strasbourg in 1872. Moved to Munich as successor to Justus von Liebig, where he established a chemical laboratory in 1877 and directed extensive research with numerous students and assistants.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Berlin Academy of Sciences; German Chemical Association
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of both the Berlin Academy of Sciences and the German Chemical Association.

Father_Notes: Blasius Armeno, probably of Armenian origin, was a merchant of modest means who died in 1670 when Georgius was two years old.
Education_Institution: Jesuit College of Dubrovnik; University of Naples; University of Salerno; University of Pisa
Education_Notes: Educated first by his uncle and then at the Jesuit College of Dubrovnik, where he received classical training and studied Peripatetic philosophy. Completed medical studies in Naples and received the M.D. degree, probably from Salerno in 1688. Attended Bellini's lectures at Pisa.
Education_Locations: Dubrovnik, Unknown, Croatia, Unknown, Unknown; Naples, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1688; Salerno, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1688; Pisa, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Educated by Jesuits; served as papal physician and was introduced to the papal court.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in experimental physiology and anatomical research using microscopy. Studied muscle fiber structure, blood circulation, and the properties of bodily fluids. Conducted vivisection experiments on animals and performed numerous autopsies. Developed iatrophysical theory explaining life phenomena through the mechanical properties of fibers and fluids. Contributed to understanding of smooth versus striated muscle and histological fiber classification.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Began medical practice with his foster father in Lecce. Worked in hospitals across Italian cities from 1689 onward. Became professor of anatomy at the Sapienza in Rome in 1696 and professor of theoretical medicine there in 1701. Served as the pope's second physician from 1695 and as papal archiater's assistant from 1692.
Patronage_Notes: Invited to Rome in 1692 by Marcello Malpighi, who was the pope's archiater; lived in Malpighi's house as scientific secretary. Introduced to the papal court and patronized by Pope Innocent XII, to whom he dedicated De praxi medica. Confirmed in his court position by Pope Clement XI.
Instruments_Notes: Used microscopy extensively to study the fine structure of muscles, brain membranes, and other tissues, perfecting his anatomical observations through microscopic examination.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Academia Naturae Curiosorum; Arcadia; Accademia dei Fisiocritici
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Royal Society in 1697, Academia Naturae Curiosorum and Arcadia in 1699, and Accademia dei Fisiocritici in 1700.

Father_Notes: Father was Johann Wilhelm Baier, professor of Protestant theology at the University of Jena.
Education_Notes: Matriculated at University of Jena in 1693 and studied philosophy, classical languages, mathematics, medicine, and natural science. Traveled in northern Germany and Baltic provinces (1699–1700) to enrich knowledge through scholarly conversations and examination of collections. Completed studies and received degrees in 1700. Made an educational trip to mining facilities in the Hartz Mountains and northern German university towns before settling in Nuremberg.
Religion_Notes: Son of a Protestant theology professor; no conversion or change of affiliation mentioned.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Practiced medicine as a physician and professor. His principal scientific fame rests on studies of minerals and fossils, particularly oryctography (geology and paleontology). His Oryctographia norica (1708) presented a systematic study of fossils and minerals in the Nuremberg region, with exact descriptions and illustrations that helped disprove the notion that fossils were merely sports of nature and laid foundations for investigation of Jurassic fauna and scientific paleontology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Settled in 1701 as a practicing physician in Nuremberg. From 1704 held a professorship at the medical faculty of the University of Altdorf until his death, and was twice elected rector of the University.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of the Leopoldina (Academy of Natural Scientists) in 1708; chosen as its president in 1730.

Father_Notes: John Batters By Bailey was a medical practitioner.

Education_Notes: Educated at Kendal Grammar School and Clare College, Cambridge, where he graduated with First-class Honors in geology and physics in 1902.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Made notable contributions to tectonics and metamorphism, igneous and general geology, and the history of geological ideas. Revolutionary reinterpretation of Dalradian schists in Scottish Highlands using recumbent folds and fold faults. Major work on Tertiary volcanic complex of Mull. Pioneering studies of submarine landslips and turbidity currents. Extensive work on Alpine and Caledonian mountain systems.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Geologist and district geologist with Geological Survey of Great Britain (Scotland) from 1902 to 1929. Professor of geology at Glasgow University 1929–1937. Director of Geological Survey and Museum 1937–1945. Military service 1915–1919 interrupted his geological work.
Patronage_Notes: Served as director of the Geological Survey and Museum, a government scientific institution.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected Fellow of the Royal Society. Received six honorary doctorates and seven scientific medals. Knighted in 1945.

Alt_Name: L.H. Bailey; Liberty Hyde Bailey, Jr.

Education_Notes: Entered Michigan State Agricultural College at nineteen; trained in compound microscopy and began plant experiments. Received B.S. in 1882. Received M.S. from Michigan State no later than 1886. Studied Darwinian evolution and worked under William James Beal, a pioneer in laboratory teaching of botany.
