Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Authority on Carex, Rubus, Cucurbita, palms, Vitis, and cultivated Brassica. Pioneered classification and nomenclature of fruits and vegetables, hybridization, and cross-fertilization. Published hundreds of papers and more than sixty books on horticulture, agriculture, plant breeding, evolution, and cultivation principles. Founder of the Bailey Hortorium and editor of Baileya and Gentes herbarum journals.

Patronage_Notes: Appointed chairman of President Theodore Roosevelt's Country Life Commission in 1908, which investigated rural improvement possibilities until 1911.

Awarded Wilder Medal by American Pomological Society (1885). Honorary degrees from Alfred University and universities of Wisconsin, Vermont, and Puerto Rico.

Father_Notes: Father was a mathematician and noted architect.

Brought rheumatism into nosology and described rheumatic diathesis with variable painful localizations.

Father_Notes: Jacques Bailly was keeper of the king's paintings at the Louvre and owned a house in Chaillot; the position had been held by the family since Bailly's great-grandfather.
Education_Notes: Received schooling to prepare him for his father's office. Around age twenty received mathematics lessons from Montcarville of the Collège Royal; subsequently studied with Nicolas de Lacaille and Alexis Clairaut, France's greatest observational and theoretical astronomers respectively.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted observational and theoretical astronomical research on Halley's comet, Jupiter's satellites, and their light variations. Published a four-volume history of astronomy (1775–1782) that became his most lasting achievement. Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1763.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Succeeded to his father's position as keeper of the king's paintings in 1768, relieved of functions in 1783 but continued to receive the pension and honorary title. Conducted astronomical research and published within the Académie des Sciences. Served as first mayor of Paris (1789–1791).
Patronage_Notes: Held a hereditary court position as keeper of the king's paintings at the Louvre. Served as first mayor of Paris following the French Revolution, appointed by unanimous proclamation in July 1789.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Académie Française; Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in January 1763 to fill the vacancy created by Lacaille's death. Elected to the Académie Française in 1783 and to the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres in 1785, making him a triple academician, a distinction shared only with Bernard de Fontenelle among Frenchmen.

Father_Notes: Third son of a banker; family had means sufficient to apprentice him to a mercantile firm.
Education_Notes: Received only elementary education; apprenticed to a London mercantile firm at age fourteen for seven years.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in practical astronomy and standardization; calculated positions of 2,881 stars; worked on standard pendulum, standard yard, and earth's ellipticity; famous for describing Baily's beads phenomenon during solar eclipses; revised and published multiple historical star catalogs.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as a stockbroker and prospered on the stock exchange before retiring at age fifty to devote full time to astronomy. Published actuarial tables and astronomical papers while engaged in commerce.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Astronomical Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Royal Society from 1821; one of the founders of the Astronomical Society of London (later Royal Astronomical Society); served as president for four two-year terms, first beginning in 1825.

Father_Notes: George Bain was a handloom weaver; poverty forced him to remove Alexander from school at age eleven.
Education_Notes: Largely self-taught in Latin, Greek, mathematics, and mechanics during seven years of manual labor; won a bursary to Marischal College in 1836 and excelled there for four years, receiving his M.A. in 1840 as the best candidate of the year.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in philosophical psychology, emphasizing the unity and active nature of the mind; correlated mental processes with physiological processes; developed utilitarian ethics following Mill; founded and edited the journal Mind (1876–1892), which became a major philosophical publication.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught mental and moral philosophy at Marischal College for five years after 1840; held various lectureships for fifteen years; elected to the chair of logic at Aberdeen University in 1860 and remained until retirement in 1880; founded and edited the journal Mind for sixteen years.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Read papers to the Aberdeen Philosophical Society on classification of sciences, human senses, and terrestrial heat between 1843 and 1844; served as rector of Aberdeen University from 1882 to 1886.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Jagdish N. Hattiangadi. Autobiography (London, 1904). Articles in Westminster Review and manuscripts in Aberdeen University Library.

Father_Notes: Samuel Baird was a lawyer of local prominence in Reading, Pennsylvania.
Education_Notes: Entered Dickinson College in 1836, received B.A. in 1840 and M.A. in 1843. Briefly studied medicine in New York City in late 1841 but abandoned it after two months. Received informal instruction from established naturalists including James Dwight Dana, John James Audubon, and George N. Lawrence.
Religion_Notes: Gradually drifted from his Protestant upbringing; after 1875 did not attend religious services.
Scientific_Disciplines: Zoology; Ornithology; Mammalogy; Ichthyology; Herpetology; Anthropology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Leading vertebrate zoologist of mid-nineteenth-century America. Conducted taxonomic studies of birds and mammals, often in collaboration with Charles Girard. Published comprehensive monographs on mammals (1857) and birds (1858) describing seventy new mammal species and 216 new bird species. Wrote on reptiles, amphibians, and fishes. Authored 'The Distribution and Migrations of North American Birds' (1865), demonstrating support for organic evolution and defining biological zones. Co-authored A History of North American Birds (1874), a three-volume study notable for first comprehensive information on Arctic bird breeding grounds.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of natural history at Dickinson College from 1846. Assistant to Joseph Henry at the Smithsonian Institution from 1850. Directed the U.S. Fish Commission from 1871. Succeeded Joseph Henry as secretary of the Smithsonian in 1878, a position held until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Secured appointment to the Smithsonian through recommendations from politicians and scientists. Directed the U.S. Fish Commission under congressional authority.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member of the National Academy of Sciences in 1864, over the opposition of Louis Agassiz.

Father_Notes: One of three children in a modest artisan family; parents sacrificed to provide his education.
Education_Institution: Lycée Lakanal; Lycée Henri IV; École Normale Supérieure; University of Italy; Faculté des Sciences, Paris
Education_Notes: Won scholarship competition for Paris in 1886 and entered Lycée Lakanal as boarding student, completing advanced classes in 1890 with two honorable mentions in the Concours Général de Mathématiques. Entered special mathematics section at Lycée Henri IV in 1891. Accepted to both École Polytechnique and École Normale Supérieure in 1892; chose the latter and studied there for three years. Placed first in written part of 1895 agrégation in mathematics but ranked third overall due to oral examination performance. Defended doctoral thesis on theory of functions of real variables on 24 March 1899 before Appell, Darboux, and Picard.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1886, 1890; Paris, Unknown, France, 1891, 1892; Paris, Unknown, France, 1892, 1895; Unknown, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1899
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on theory of functions of real variables, particularly limit functions of continuous functions and discontinuous functions. Developed concept of semicontinuity and Baire classes. Contributed to theory of sets and transfinite methods. Work on partial differential equations and functions of several variables. Later interest in calendar reform.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at lycées in Troyes, Bar-le-Duc, and Nancy. Lecturer at Faculty of Sciences of Montpellier from 1902. Awarded Peccot Foundation fellowship in 1904 to teach at Collège de France. Appointed professor of analysis at Faculty of Science in Dijon in 1905. Granted pension in 1925.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of the Academy of Sciences on 3 April 1922. Received ribbon of the Legion of Honor.

Father_Notes: None

Religion_Notes: Muslim philosopher writing in Arabic; worked within Islamic intellectual tradition of the Almoravid period.
Scientific_Disciplines: Philosophy; Scholastic Philosophy; Physics; Astronomy; Natural History
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered systematic study of Aristotelian philosophy in Muslim Spain. Developed dynamic theory of motion and force, rejecting Ptolemaic epicycles. Wrote commentaries on Aristotle's Physics, Organon, Meteorologica, and other works; treatises on the soul and the Active Intellect; and works on astronomy and botany.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as vizier to an Almoravid prince. Engaged in philosophical teaching and writing.
Patronage_Notes: Served an Almoravid prince as vizier.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: William Baker was a Clerk in Chancery; mother Mary Pengry was a midwife of great practice.
Education_Notes: Apprenticed to a bookseller at age fifteen; no formal institutional education is recorded.
Religion_Notes: The entry notes his pious approach to nature and reverence for the microscope as revealing God's creation, but does not state a specific religious affiliation.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the popularization of microscopy through two widely translated books; conducted microscopical examinations of water creatures, fossils, and crystals; received the Copley Medal for observations of crystal morphology; examined and measured Leeuwenhoek's bead microscopes.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught the deaf and dumb, amassing a considerable fortune from this practice; published books and contributed frequently to the Philosophical Transactions; served as first honorary secretary of the Society for the Encouragement of Arts Manufactures and Commerce.
Patronage_Notes: Fellow of the Society of Antiquaries (1740) and the Royal Society (1741); received the Copley Medal from the Royal Society in 1744.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and improved microscopes; published detailed instructions on their construction and use; examined and measured twenty-six bead microscopes bequeathed to the Royal Society by Antony van Leeuwenhoek.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Society of Antiquaries; Royal Society; Society for the Encouragement of Arts Manufactures and Commerce
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Society of Antiquaries in January 1740 and the Royal Society in March 1741; frequent contributor to the Philosophical Transactions for seventeen years; first honorary secretary of the Society for the Encouragement of Arts Manufactures and Commerce, established in 1754.

Father_Notes: None

Education_Locations: Ackworth, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Bootham, York, England, Unknown, 1847
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Expert on vascular cryptogams and ferns; monographic work on British roses and other plant families; pioneer investigator in plant ecology; contributed to major floras including Flora Brasiliensis, Flora of Tropical Africa, Flora Capensis, and Flora of British India.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked in drapery business in Thirsk from 1847 to 1865; lectured on botany at London Hospital Medical School from 1869 to 1881; appointed lecturer in botany at Chelsea Physic Garden in 1882; appointed keeper of herbarium and library at Kew in 1890, serving until retirement in 1899.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Royal Horticultural Society; Linnean Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1878; received Victoria Medal of Honour from the Royal Horticultural Society in 1897; received Linnean Medal in 1899.

Father_Notes: None

Published widely on geological and biological subjects, with particular interest in rock formations, stratigraphy, and geological revolutions. Engaged critically with contemporary theories including Hutton's plutonism and Wernerian geognosy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as a mineralogical surveyor and taught mineralogy and geology, primarily in London.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Geographer and philologist who devoted much time to geography despite never traveling outside the Iberian Peninsula. Means_of_Support_Notes: Member of al-Muʿtasim's court at Almeria for much of his life. Also a poet and man of wide-ranging knowledge.
Patronage_Notes: Served at the court of al-Muʿtasim in Almeria; acquainted with the writer Ibn Khāgān late in life.

Developed quantitative methods for determining catalyst activity and proposed a classification of organic catalytic reactions. Made fundamental contributions to chemical kinetics, including work on activation energy and reaction rates in flow systems.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of chemistry from 1934. Elected corresponding member of the Soviet Academy of Sciences in 1943 and full member in 1946.

Father_Notes: Parents were wine-growers of modest circumstances.

Education_Notes: Attended lycée in Montpellier after 1819; trained in pharmacy in Montpellier under Jacques Étienne Bérard; received pharmacy degree in 1826 with thesis on cyanogen and its compounds.

Discovered bromine (ca. 1825); studied iodine detection, bleaching agents (Javelle water), extraction of salts from seawater, oxamic acid, and amyl alcohol. Developed reliable test for iodine presence and prepared hypochlorous acid and chlorine monoxide.

Father_Notes: German-born of Italian descent; established a banking firm in Haiti.
Education_Institution: Not Specified; Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle; University of Paris
Education_Notes: Attended law school briefly in Paris before turning to natural sciences. Studied under de Blainville at the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle. Licencié ès sciences naturelles in 1845; M.D. awarded 30 August 1854 for a thesis on skin physiology.
Education_Locations: Frankfurt am Main, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1840, 1845; Paris, Unknown, France, 1845, 1854
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in microscopic studies and protozoology. Discovered sexual reproduction in ciliata and established laws of binary fission in infusoria. Conducted microsurgical experiments elucidating the role of the nucleus and introduced merotomy technique. Investigated germ-cell autonomy through study of Chironomus sexual-organ formation and aphid reproduction. Studied pebrine disease in silkworms.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Private wealth from his father's banking firm allowed him to forgo medical practice and pursue research. Patronage_Notes: Claude Bernard, who praised his work, asked him to direct histological research at the Museum laboratory in 1867.
Instruments_Notes: Pioneered microscopic techniques including the introduction of merotomy and microsurgical experiments on infusoria and other organisms.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Founded the Société de Micrographie; faithful member of the Société de Biologie. Secretary of the Journal de physiologie.

Religion_Notes: Became abbot of Guastalla in 1585, indicating ecclesiastical affiliation.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal contribution was a commentary on the pseudo-Aristotelian Questions of Mechanics, emphasizing centers of gravity and equilibrium; translated Hero of Alexandria's Automata and Belopoieca; compiled biographies of approximately 200 mathematicians; worked on geography in later years.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Abbot of Guastalla from 1585; served the duke of Urbino as historian and biographer from 1609 until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Entered service of Ferrante II Gonzaga in 1580, who secured his abbacy in 1585; later served the duke of Urbino as historian and biographer from 1609.

Father_Notes: James Maitland Balfour; mother was Lady Blanche, daughter of the marquis of Salisbury. Family of considerable prominence and wealth.
Education_Notes: Attended preparatory school at Hoddesdon, Hertfordshire, and Harrow School (1865), where he won a prize for an essay on the geology and natural history of East Lothian, judged by Thomas H. Huxley. Matriculated at Trinity College, Cambridge in 1870 and took a first in Natural Science Scholarships in 1871. Worked under physiologist Michael Foster from 1872.
Education_Locations: Harrow, Unknown, England, 1865, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1870, 1871
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in comparative embryology, particularly the study of elasmobranch development. Conducted detailed microscopic examinations of germ-layer formation, organ system development, and excretory system evolution. Authored the first comprehensive comparative embryology treatise. Investigated phylogenetic links between major animal taxa.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Began lecturing on morphology and embryology at Trinity College, Cambridge in autumn 1873. Became director of the university's morphological laboratory. In 1882, Cambridge created a professorship of animal morphology for him to hold for life.
Instruments_Notes: Conducted painstaking microscopic examinations of embryological specimens, particularly elasmobranch development, which formed the basis of his detailed descriptive work.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; British Association for the Advancement of Science
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Royal Society in 1878. Became vice-president of the biological section of the British Association for the Advancement of Science in 1880. Won the Royal Society's Royal Medal in 1881.

Father_Notes: John Hutton Balfour was professor of botany at Edinburgh University. Family ancestry included George H. Baird, principal of Edinburgh University, and geologist James Hutton.
Education_Institution: University of Edinburgh; University of Würzburg; University of Strasbourg
Education_Notes: Obtained B.S. from Edinburgh University in 1873 and M.B. in 1877. Continued botanical studies, particularly morphology and physiology, at universities of Würzburg and Strasbourg. Accompanied transit of Venus expedition to Rodriguez Island in 1874 as botanist and geologist.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Taxonomist of considerable promise; concentrated on Rhododendron and Primula genera. Authority on vegetation of the Himalayas and western China. Modernized teaching methods and established Edinburgh as main center for teaching of taxonomy. Accomplished reforms in horticultural practice and garden design.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Chair of botany at Glasgow University (1879–1884); Sherardian professor of botany at Oxford (1884–1888); professor of botany at Edinburgh University (1888–1922), also serving as queen's botanist in Scotland and Regius keeper of the Royal Botanic Garden.

Father_Notes: Andrew Balfour was an army surgeon who later became a printer and publisher in Edinburgh.

Education_Notes: Attended High School in Edinburgh and universities of Edinburgh and St. Andrews. Graduated M.D. from Edinburgh in 1832. Pursued further medical study in Paris before returning to Edinburgh in 1834.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Became seriously interested in botany around age eighteen. Pioneered the use of the microscope in botanical demonstrations and emphasized botanical excursions for instruction and ecological understanding. Explored much of Scotland with students, studying flora and ecological diversity. Published influential botanical textbooks and botanico-religious works.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced medicine in Edinburgh from 1834 until 1841. Appointed professor of botany at Glasgow University in 1841, then at Edinburgh in 1845, where he served until retirement in 1879. Also held posts as queen's botanist in Scotland and Regius keeper of the Royal Botanic Garden.
Instruments_Notes: Made extensive use of the microscope in botanical demonstrations, a practice not common at the time.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Founding member of the Botanical Society of Edinburgh in 1836 and founder of the Edinburgh Botanical Club in 1838. Elected fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh in 1835 and served as its secretary for many years. Elected fellow of the Linnean Society in 1844 and of the Royal Society in 1856. Acquired the secretaryship of the Royal Caledonian Horticultural Society.

Father_Notes: Father was a senator; family was patrician (patrizio genovese).
Education_Notes: Trained in the law; no university degree is named.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted experiments on falling bodies, motion on inclined planes, and pendulums. Investigated atmospheric pressure through correspondence with Galileo. Speculated on terrestrial motion as cause of tides. Discussed elastic shock, vacuum, and light in unpublished works.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Spent most of his life in public service; served as perfect of the fortress at Savona (ca. 1611), governor of Savona's fortress (1647–1649), and member of Genoa's principal governing body until his death. Pursued scientific interests as an amateur alongside public duties.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Investigated aromatic hydrocarbons and elucidated structures of retene, chrysene, pyrene, and picein. Discovered alicyclic compounds and isodiazo compounds. Extended benzene centric formula to naphthalene. Studied nitrogen compounds, hydrazones, and diazo compounds. Engaged in major controversy with Arthur Hantzsch over diazo compound formulation. Later investigated oxidation and reduction of nitrogen compounds, optical properties of anthranil derivatives, and photochemical properties of benzaldehyde derivatives.

Father_Notes: Railway official; Banach was raised by a laundress who became his foster mother.
Education_Notes: Graduated from secondary school in Krakow in 1910. Studied at the Institute of Technology in Lvov but did not graduate from that institution. Received his doctorate in 1919 with an unusual exemption from complete university education; thesis published in Fundamenta mathematicae in 1922.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Functional Analysis; Analysis; Topology; Set Theory
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founded functional analysis as a comprehensive theory of normed linear spaces (Banach spaces). Made significant contributions to orthogonal series, general topology, descriptive set theory, measure and integration theory, and derivation and absolute continuity. Proved the Hahn-Banach theorem, Banach-Steinhaus theorem, and theorems on continuous linear mappings.
Means_of_Support_Notes: From 1916 supported himself by private lessons. Appointed lecturer in mathematics at the Institute of Technology in Lvov in 1919; became associate professor and then full professor at the University of Lvov in 1927. Dean of the faculty at Lvov from 1939 to 1941. Wrote college and secondary-school texts.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Polish Academy of Sciences and Arts; Ukrainian Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected corresponding member of the Polish Academy of Sciences and Arts in 1924. Elected member of the Ukrainian Academy of Sciences. Co-founded the journal Studia mathematica with Steinhaus.

Education_Notes: Received bachelor's degree in astronomy from Warsaw University in 1904, where one of his papers won a gold medal. Continued studies under Schwarzchild at Göttingen and at Pulkovo. Received master's degree in astronomy from Moscow University in 1910.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Theoretical and observational astronomer whose work encompassed orbital mechanics, the three-body problem, parabolic orbit determination, spherical polygonometry, and photometric problems. Developed the cracovian calculus for numerical computation. Contributed to lunar libration studies, occultation prediction, and eclipsing binary observations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Junior assistant at Warsaw Observatory (1908–1909); assistant at Engelhardt Observatory near Kazan (1910–1915); taught at Dorpat (1915–1918); Dozent of geodesy at Warsaw Polytechnic High School (1918); professor of astronomy and director of Krakow Observatory (1918–1954).
Instruments_Notes: Carried out precise observations of the moon's libration using a four-inch heliometer while at Kazan. Advocated for and installed the first Polish radio telescope at Fort Skala, a branch station of the Krakow Observatory.

Education_Notes: Received B.A. from Harvard in 1888 and assisted in the chemistry department there in 1888–1889. Studied at Strasbourg, Berlin, and Leipzig, where he received his Ph.D. under Wilhelm Ostwald in 1892. Also studied under van't Hoff in Amsterdam.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: One of the early physical chemists in the United States. Specialized in electrochemistry, heterogeneous equilibria, and the phase rule. Later focused on colloid chemistry, including emulsions, photography chemistry, dyeing theories, and colloidal phenomena in anesthesia and other medical conditions. Clarified contact catalysis and placed it on a theoretical foundation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught chemistry at Harvard from 1893 to 1895 and at Cornell from 1895 to 1937. Founded the Journal of Physical Chemistry in 1896, supported it financially, coedited it until 1909, and edited it until 1932.

Father_Notes: Father was John Bannister, described as 'pleb.' in matriculation record.
Education_Notes: Matriculated at Magdalen College, Oxford on 21 June 1667; received B.A. in 1671 and M.A. in 1674. Served as chorister and clerk (possibly librarian) for two years; chaplain from 1676 to 1678. Assembled a labeled herbarium with author citations while at Oxford.
Religion_Notes: Arrived in Virginia as an Anglican minister in 1678; served as chaplain at Oxford from 1676 to 1678.
Scientific_Disciplines: Botany; Natural History; Entomology; Malacology; Anthropology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: First resident, university-educated naturalist of eastern United States. Contributed approximately 340 plant descriptions and at least eighty plant drawings cited in Ray's Historia, Morison's Historia, and Plukenet's Phytographia. Described internal anatomy of snails and explained function of balancers in Diptera. Compiled 'Collectio insectorum' of about one hundred specimens and composed significant 'Natural History of Virginia.'
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as Anglican minister in Virginia from 1678, though financially insecure and absent from Bristol Parish register by 1680. Received encouragement and hospitality from William Byrd I and Theodorick Bland. In 1690 patented 1,735 acres near Appomattox River by importing thirty-five persons, becoming a planter to secure income and time for natural history work.
Patronage_Notes: Received encouragement and hospitality from William Byrd I, a trader at the falls of the James River, and from Theodorick Bland of Westover. Corresponded with and sent specimens to Bishop Compton, Martin Lister, Leonard Plukenet, Samuel Doody, and John Ray, who called him 'eruditissimus.' Probably received assistance from the Temple Coffee House Botany Club in London.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Probably received assistance from the Temple Coffee House Botany Club in London; corresponded with its members including Bishop Compton, Lister, Plukenet, and Doody.

Father_Notes: William Banks of Revesby Abbey, Lincolnshire; took particular interest in the drainage of the Fenland; died in 1761.
Education_Notes: Entered Harrow in 1752, transferred to Eton in 1756. At age fifteen developed passion for botany. Entered Christ Church, Oxford in 1760 as a gentleman commoner; studied botany under Israel Lyons, brought from Cambridge at Banks's expense. Left Oxford without a degree.
Education_Locations: Harrow, Unknown, England, 1752, 1756; Eton, Unknown, England, 1756, 1760; Oxford, Unknown, England, 1760, 1764
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Devoted himself to botany from age fifteen. Collected over 800 previously unknown specimens during the Endeavour voyage (1768–1771). Maintained extensive herbarium and library. Advised on botanical research at Kew Gardens and promoted cultivation of plants throughout the British Empire.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Inherited well-managed estate at majority in 1764; yearly income estimated between £6,000 and £30,000. Supported scientific research and expeditions from his own fortune. Served as president of the Royal Society from 1778 to 1820. Advised King George III on Kew Gardens and agricultural matters.
Patronage_Notes: Introduced to King George III in 1771; the two men developed a close friendship based on shared interest in horticulture and agriculture. Banks became the king's chief adviser on Kew Gardens. Made a baronet in 1781, knight of the Order of the Bath in 1795, and member of the Privy Council in 1797.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1766. Elected president of the Royal Society in 1778 at age thirty-five and served until his death in 1820, presiding over 417 of 450 council meetings. One of the founders of the Linnean Society. Assisted in founding the Royal Institution. Took active interest in the Board of Longitude. Elected to membership in the Institute of France in 1802.

Also credited with an epistle on the astrolabe and an early almanac.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught arithmetic, algebra, geometry, and astronomy at the madrasa al-ʿAṭṭārīn in Fez.

Education_Notes: Studied medicine at the University of Pisa; graduated from the Medical School of Florence in 1877.
Education_Locations: Pisa, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Florence, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1877
Religion_Notes: Described as a devout Roman Catholic with a deep belief in science.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Eminent Italian pathologist of the early twentieth century. Made fundamental contributions to pathological anatomy, bacteriology, and histology. Pioneered understanding of leukemia, Banti's disease (splenomegaly with anemia and cirrhosis), hemolysis, and the spleen's role in blood cell destruction. Studied infectious diseases, pneumonia, typhoid fever, cancer cells, endocarditis, and aphasia.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at the Archihospital of Santa Maria Nuova in Florence from 1877; chief of hospital medical service from 1882; temporary professor of pathological anatomy in 1890 and ordinary professor from 1895 at the Medical School of Florence. Medical service at the hospital ended in 1924 after forty-seven years.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Accademia Medico-Fisica Fiorentina; Italian Society of Pathology
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Presented works to the Accademia Medico-Fisica Fiorentina and reported findings to the Italian Society of Pathology.

Father_Notes: William Thompson Banting; family lived on a small Ontario farm.
Education_Notes: Initially entered University of Toronto to study for the ministry but registered as a medical student the next year. Completed medical degree. Attracted to anatomy during medical school; inspired by C.L. Starr to pursue orthopedic surgery.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on the isolation and clinical application of insulin for diabetes treatment. Early research on cerebellar cortex excitability under F.R. Miller. Later research focused on cancer, coronary thrombosis, and silicosis.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Demonstrator in anatomy and physiology at Western University medical school; surgical practice at London, Ontario (brief); professor of medical research at University of Toronto from 1923; director of Banting-Best Department of Medical Research; chairman of Medical Research Committee of National Research Council during World War II.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by J.J.R. Macleod at University of Toronto, who provided laboratory space, assistant, and dogs for initial research. Canadian Parliament awarded him an annuity in 1923.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Became an honorary member of most major scientific and medical societies of the world following insulin discovery.

Education_Notes: Enrolled by Caliph al-Maʾmūn in the House of Wisdom, the first scientific institution in the Abbasid Empire, where they excelled in mathematics, astronomy, and mechanics.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Excelled in mathematics and astronomy; especially interested in geometry and the measurement of plane and spherical figures. Aḥmad focused on mechanics. Muḥammad also worked in astronomy. Led astronomical observations in Baghdad and organized a school of translators of Greek scientific manuscripts.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Supported by Caliph al-Maʾmūn through enrollment and leadership roles at the House of Wisdom, where they conducted scientific research and led translation efforts.
Patronage_Notes: Recognized and enrolled by Caliph al-Maʾmūn in the House of Wisdom, which he had founded.
Instruments_Notes: Constructed an instrument from hinged rules for solving the problem of two mean proportionals, similar to an instrument devised by Plato.

Studied with Kraepelin at the psychiatric-neurological clinic at Heidelberg and at the neurological clinic in Freiburg im Breisgau until April 1902. Received surgical training at Vienna General Hospital until September 1903.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in the clinical investigation of the human equilibrium system and vestibular apparatus. Discovered caloric nystagmus and developed objective methods for diagnosing vertigo and equilibrium disturbances. Established the connection between the equilibrium organ and brain centers, creating the foundation for otoneurology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Entered service at the University of Vienna ear clinic in 1903 under Adam Politzer. Appointed director of the University of Uppsala otorhinolaryngology clinic in 1917, a post he held until his death.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member or honorary member of numerous scientific societies. Received the Erb Medal of the German Neurological Society in 1913.

Education_Notes: Sent by the Church to Peru in 1588; no formal degree recorded. Gained practical knowledge through extensive travel and observation in Peruvian mining regions.
Religion_Notes: Sent to Peru by the Church in 1588 and combined priestly duties with metallurgical studies; served as a parish priest in San Bernardo, Potosí after 1624.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in silver ore treatment by amalgamation; authored El arte de los metales, the first significant treatise on metals in Spanish and the only major original seventeenth-century work on the subject. Emphasized laboratory control of industrial processes and cost computation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Sent by the Church to Peru in 1588 and served as a parish priest; combined ecclesiastical duties with practical metallurgical work and consultation on mining operations.
Patronage_Notes: Dedicated El arte de los metales in 1637 to Juan de Lizarazu, president of the Real Audiencia de la Plata of Peru, who transmitted it to Spain with approval of the mayor and Amalgamators Guild of Potosí.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Published memoirs on spherical geometry and trigonometry, infinitesimal calculus, elementary and infinitesimal geometry, calculus of probabilities, polyhedra theory, Dupin's indicatrix, integral calculus, and number theory. Recognized as a good unspecialized mathematician of the late nineteenth century.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught mathematics at the lycée of Nice after passing his agrégation in 1860. Served as assistant astronomer at the Paris Observatory under Le Verrier. From 1880 received regular financial help from a foundation connected with the Académie des Sciences.
Patronage_Notes: Le Verrier, director of the Paris Observatory, offered him a position as assistant astronomer. Joseph Bertrand, permanent secretary of the Académie des Sciences, encouraged his return to scientific writing and secured regular financial support from an Academy-connected foundation.
Instruments_Notes: Perfected a new type of thermometer during his work at the Paris Observatory.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Connected to the Académie des Sciences through Bertrand's patronage and support from an Academy-connected foundation.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primary contribution was delineation of the temperature-regulating center in the brain and its physiological mechanisms. Became a leading authority on body temperature regulation and the effects of pyretic and antipyretic drugs. Demonstrated the existence of two temperature control centers in the hypothalamus and their roles in thermoregulation and water-balance control.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught pharmacology at Yale University (1912–1921), McGill University (1921–1923), and University of Louisville (1923–1931). Returned to Yale in 1931 as associate professor and in 1940 as research associate in pharmacology.

Education_Notes: Attended Leys School, Cambridge from 1888. Obtained B.S. from University of London while still a student at Leys. Took a year off in 1892–1893 due to overstrain. Entered King's College, Cambridge to study natural science and graduated in 1896.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on blood gas analysis and the oxygen dissociation curve of hemoglobin. Means_of_Support_Notes: Elected fellow of King's College, Cambridge in 1899 and became lecturer in 1905, holding both positions for nearly fifty years. Became professor of physiology in 1925 upon the death of John Newport Langley.

Education_Notes: Attended Gymnasium in Bremen; brief engineering apprenticeship at a railway maintenance depot; studied engineering at Bremen, then physics at Munich, Berlin, and Göttingen. Received doctorate from Göttingen in 1907 for dissertation on oscillation generation.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Made foundational contributions to nonlinear switching elements and spontaneous oscillation theory. Formulated electron-tube coefficients and their governing equations. Developed standard four-volume text on electron tubes and applications. Proposed subjective loudness measurement and the phon as a unit. Discovered Barkhausen effect—discontinuities in ferromagnetic magnetization revealed by acoustic methods, supporting domain theory. Co-developed the Barkhausen-Kurz oscillator for ultrahigh-frequency continuous-wave generation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Research worker at Siemens & Halske laboratories in Berlin after 1907. Appointed professor of communications electrical engineering at Technische Hochschule Dresden in 1911, where he remained until his death, directing the Institute of High-Frequency and Electron-Tube Technology.
Instruments_Notes: Co-developed with Karl Kurz in 1920; an electron tube for continuous-wave oscillation at ultrahigh frequencies, forerunner of microwave tubes and foundational to understanding velocity modulation.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Vice-president of the Institute of Radio Engineers in 1935.

Father_Notes: John Martin Barkla was secretary of the Atlas Chemical Company in Widnes; mother Sarah Glover came from a local family of watch manufacturers.
Education_Institution: Liverpool Institute; University College Liverpool; Trinity College, Cambridge; King's College, Cambridge; University of Liverpool
Education_Notes: Entered University College Liverpool in 1895 with scholarships, concentrating on mathematics and physics under Oliver Lodge. Received B.Sc. (First-Class Honours) in 1898 and M.Sc. in 1899. Served as first president of the University Physical Society. In autumn 1899 entered Trinity College Cambridge as advanced student with 1851 Exhibition scholarship, attending lectures by George Stokes and conducting research at the Cavendish Laboratory. Moved to King's College Cambridge after eighteen months to sing in the chapel choir; scholarship exceptionally renewed for a third year in 1901. Returned to University of Liverpool as Oliver Lodge Fellow for three years, receiving D.Sc. in 1904.
Education_Locations: Liverpool, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Liverpool, Unknown, England, 1895, 1899; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1899, 1901; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1901, 1902; Liverpool, Unknown, England, 1902, 1904
Religion_Notes: A deeply religious man and faithful adherent of the Methodist Church, following his ancestors.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in X-ray physics, particularly the discovery and characterization of characteristic X-ray spectra. Demonstrated that secondary X rays scattered by light elements have the same wavelength as the primary beam, supporting the ether pulse theory. Discovered the polarization of X rays and established the Thomson scattering distribution. Identified homogeneous groups of characteristic X rays (K and L series) from heavy elements and established the condition that they could be excited only by harder X rays. Later pursued the controversial J-Phenomenon.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Demonstrator, assistant lecturer, and special lecturer at University of Liverpool (1905–1909). Wheatstone professor of physics at King's College London (1909–1913). Professor of natural philosophy at University of Edinburgh (1913–1944).
Instruments_Notes: Developed and refined X-ray apparatus for investigating secondary radiation and polarization. Used an ionization chamber with gold-leaf electroscope to measure ion density and detect radiation properties.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1912. Appointed Bakerian lecturer for 1916.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Self-educated; competed successfully for position of assistant mathematics master at Royal Military Academy, Woolwich in 1801.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Published mathematical tables and treatises on theory of numbers. Conducted experiments on timber strength and stress. Investigated terrestrial magnetism and compass deviation caused by iron in ships, developing a method to correct ships' compasses. Attempted to develop an electric telegraph using electromagnetism. Developed an achromatic telescope lens (the Barlow lens). Conducted experiments on railroad design, including optimal rail shape and effects of gradients and curves.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant mathematics master at Royal Military Academy, Woolwich from 1801. Conducted experiments at Woolwich dockyard and arsenal. Served as royal commissioner of railroads on several occasions in the 1830s and 1840s.
Instruments_Notes: Developed a telescope lens consisting of a colorless liquid between two pieces of glass. The Barlow lens, a modification of his telescope lens, is a negative achromatic combination of flint glass and crown glass.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Institution of Civil Engineers
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Made honorary member of the Institution of Civil Engineers in 1820. Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1823.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Harold I. Sharlin. Father_Notes: Father's inheritance provided Barlow with leisure to pursue scientific work in his early thirties.
Education_Notes: Privately educated; took a course in crystallography from H.E. Armstrong in the mid-1880s; largely self-taught in advanced crystallography through independent study and associations with H.A. Miers and W.J. Pope.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in mathematical crystallography and crystal structure theory. Developed theories of close-packed atomic arrangements in crystals; derived the 230 space groups independently (published 1894); investigated symmetry, optical properties, and the relationship between crystal morphology and chemical composition. Work bridged classical crystallography and modern X-ray diffraction.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Inherited wealth from his father enabled him to pursue scientific research as a private scholar without formal institutional employment.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Royal Society in 1908; served as president of the Mineralogical Society from 1915 to 1918.

Father_Notes: Father Reuben Barnard died before Edward's birth; family was impoverished.
Education_Notes: Only two months of formal schooling in childhood. From 1883 to 1887 attended Vanderbilt University as both student and instructor with an irregular curriculum suited to his lack of prior schooling and astronomical needs; received no degree at that time. Six years after leaving Vanderbilt, awarded D.Sc. in recognition of scientific contributions and earlier studies.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Foremost observational astronomer of his time, ranking with Herschel. Discoveries and contributions spanned nearly all branches of astronomy: comets (17 discoveries), nebulae, Jupiter's fifth satellite, double stars, variable stars, novae, planetary observations, Milky Way photography, stellar parallax and proper motion, and dark nebulae. Pioneered wholesale use of photography in astronomical observing.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked in portrait studio 1866–1883 to support family. From 1883–1887 student and instructor at Vanderbilt University. September 1887–1895 at Lick Observatory; October 1895–1923 professor of practical astronomy at University of Chicago and observer at Yerkes Observatory. Received five $200 Warner prizes for comet discoveries (1889, 1901, 1902) and numerous medals and awards from learned societies.
Instruments_Notes: Used five-inch telescope purchased in 1876; six-inch telescope at Vanderbilt; thirty-six-inch great refractor at Lick Observatory; Bruce telescope at Yerkes Observatory. Pioneered use of small telescopic camera (2½-inch portrait lens) for Milky Way photography; developed long-exposure photographic techniques for astronomical observing.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Astronomical Society; American Academy of Arts and Sciences; American Philosophical Society; National Academy of Sciences; Astronomical Society of the Pacific
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Foreign associate of Royal Astronomical Society; member of American Academy of Arts and Sciences and American Philosophical Society; director of B. A. Gould Fund of National Academy of Sciences; vice-president of American Association for the Advancement of Science (1898). Recipient of Lalande gold medal (1892), Arago gold medal (1893), Gold Medal of Royal Astronomical Society (1897), Janssen gold medal (1900), Janssen Prize of French Astronomical Society (1906), and Bruce gold medal (1917).

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Received a humanistic education with command of Greek and Latin. Studied at the University of Padua and lectured there around 1559 on Sacrobosco's Sphere.
Religion_Notes: Brought before the Inquisition in 1587 on charges of sorcery and causing a torrential rainstorm in Crete; sentenced to provide silver crosses at 100 ducats and condemned to remain in prison at the pleasure of the Holy Office, apparently a suspended sentence.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Edited Proclus' commentary on Euclid's Elements (1560), based on superior manuscripts. Translated Hero's work on war machines (1572) and corrected Commandinus' translation of Pappus' Collectio. Wrote on rhythmomachia, parallel lines, and cosmography; noted eighty-four errors in Sacrobosco's Sphere, though rejected heliocentric theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lectured at the University of Padua around 1559. As a Venetian patrician, likely supported by family wealth and patronage.

Father_Notes: None

Education_Notes: Educated in Paris at the École Polytechnique and the École des Ponts et Chaussées. No degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Collected, described, and drew fossils of the central Bohemian basin from 1840 onward. Named and analyzed over 4,000 new fossil species. Distinguished metamorphosis in trilobites and identified embryonic states. Studied the Silurian fauna and its geographical distribution.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Initially took a position as engineer for the construction of a horse-drawn railway in Prague. From 1840 onward, fossil collection and paleontological research became his chief occupation.
Patronage_Notes: Served as tutor to the grandson of Charles X and left France with the exiled royal family after the July Revolution of 1830.

Father_Notes: None

Education_Notes: Studied engineering at Lehigh University, graduating with high honors in 1892; earned M.S. in 1893 and M.S. in 1897 at Lehigh; received Ph.D. in geology from Yale in 1900; earned D.Sc. from Lehigh in 1916. Supported extended education through part-time teaching positions in mathematics, mining and metallurgy, geology, zoology, and astronomy.

Scientific_Disciplines: Geology; Isostasy; Sedimentology; Metamorphism; Paleoclimatology; Structural Geology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Chief contributions were in isostasy, sedimentology, and metamorphism. Pioneered dry-land geology and stratigraphic analysis; developed theory of magmatic stoping; recognized causal relationships between climatic variation and sedimentation; proposed cyclic models of geological processes; contributed to geodesic theory and understanding of the lithosphere and aesthenosphere.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held part-time teaching positions in mathematics, mining and metallurgy, geology, zoology, and astronomy while pursuing advanced degrees. Joined the U.S. Geological Survey in Montana in 1901 to study mining districts and granite batholiths. Became professor of structural geology at Yale from 1908 to 1919.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Delivered lecture 'The Origin of the Earth' to Yale's Sigma Xi Society in 1916.

Father_Notes: None

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered improvements in chemical analysis and analytical reagents; collaborated extensively with Claude Bernard on physiological chemistry, particularly digestion and sugar metabolism; later focused on industrial applications including dyes, photographic chemistry, and sulfuric acid manufacture.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of chemistry at École Municipale Turgot and later at École Supérieure de Commerce in Paris; conducted industrial chemistry research; served as inspector of child labor in factories of the Department of the Seine.

Father_Notes: Member of a wealthy industrial family; parents were liberals under the Restoration and became conservatives and ardent Catholics under the Second Empire.
Education_Notes: Studied with the Jesuits in Lille. Wrote a second doctoral thesis on the development of living Spongiae (1876). First doctoral thesis on Cretaceous formations of England, presented in Paris in 1876 under Hébert's supervision. Studied optical petrography in the laboratory of Fouqué and Michel-Lévy at the Collège de France.
Religion_Notes: Ardent Catholic; among the militants of the Catholic party; religious convictions inhibited him from speaking freely on evolution; made a member of the Pontifical Scientific Academy by the pope in the last year of his life.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in stratigraphic and paleontological research on Cretaceous formations; extended Hébert's zones to England; discovered axes of deformations in English Cretaceous matching Primary era activity, later developed as theory of posthumous flections. Mapped geological formations of Brittany (1880–1909), publishing twenty maps covering 25,000 square kilometers. Studied fossil corals, sponges, bryozoa, brachiopods, and graptolites; wrote monograph on Devonian fauna of Erbray (1888). Translated Zittel's Handbuch der Palaeontologie into French (1883–1894).
Means_of_Support_Notes: Named assistant at the Faculté des Sciences of Lille in 1871, where he spent his entire career. Became lecturer in 1878 and professeur adjoint in 1888. Director of the Institute of Geology of Lille from 1902, following Gosselet. Retired from teaching in 1926.
Patronage_Notes: Mentored by Jules Gosselet, whose enthusiasm for geology shaped his career; devoted disciple for half a century. Befriended by American geologist James Hall, who took him to the United States and conducted him through important stratigraphic sequences in New York State.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Pontifical Scientific Academy
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected a titular member of the Académie des Sciences after several defeats; also a corresponding member of numerous academies. Made a member of the Pontifical Scientific Academy by the pope in 1939.

Father_Notes: Thomas Barrow was a prosperous linendraper with court connections.
Education_Institution: Charterhouse; Felsted School; Trinity College, Cambridge
Education_Notes: Attended Charterhouse as a dayboy, then Felsted School under headmaster Martin Holbeach, where he studied Greek, Latin, logic, and rhetoric. Entered Trinity College, Cambridge in 1643 as a pensioner, graduating B.A. in 1648 and receiving M.A. in 1652. Spent four years touring the Continent (1655–1660) before returning to Cambridge.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Felsted, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1643, 1648
Religion_Notes: Took holy orders in 1660 upon the Restoration. Served as royal chaplain in London and was known for his theological sermons, which were published posthumously by Tillotson (1683–1689).
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Barrow's scientific fame rests on three series of Lucasian lectures: Lectiones mathematicae (1664–1666) on mathematical foundations; Lectiones geometricae (1670) on higher geometry, tangents, quadratures, and rectification, developing a method for finding tangents through composition of motions; and Lectiones opticae on catoptrics and dioptrics. His optical work was rendered obsolete by Newton's lectures but influenced Newton's geometrical optics. His mathematical lectures, though containing early formulations related to the calculus, were little read and had limited impact.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Elected college fellow at Trinity in 1649 and served as college lecturer and university examiner. Held the Regius professorship of Greek (1660), the Gresham professorship of geometry in London (1662), and the Lucasian professorship of mathematics at Cambridge (1663–1669). Served as royal chaplain in London (1669–1673) and returned as Master of Trinity College (1673–1677), also serving as university vice-chancellor (1675).
Patronage_Notes: Rewarded with the Regius professorship of Greek upon the Restoration of Charles II in 1660. Appointed royal chaplain in London in 1669 and chosen by the king for the mastership of Trinity College in 1673.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected one of the first fellows of the Royal Society after its incorporation in 1662, but never took an active part in its meetings.

Father_Notes: Father owned a Nova Scotia-based mercantile concern with ships trading to North America and the West Indies.

Education_Notes: Studied medicine at London, Paris, Erlangen, and Berlin before receiving M.D. from Edinburgh in 1833. After graduation, specialized in anatomy and physiology under Friedrich Tiedemann at Heidelberg for about a year. Attended Royal Infirmary, Edinburgh, to further medical knowledge.

Conducted extensive histological studies on blood corpuscles and tissue formation, attempting to demonstrate the unity of animal structures.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Had private income and never practiced medicine or held a permanent appointment. In 1843 presented a course of physiological lectures at St. Thomas' Hospital, London. In 1844 became house surgeon at Royal Maternity Hospital, Edinburgh, but resigned due to ill health.
Instruments_Notes: Conducted extensive microscopical research in embryology and histology, producing numerous detailed illustrations of embryological stages and tissue structures.

Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1840. Received the Royal Medal in 1839 for his embryological papers of 1838 and 1839. Active member of the Royal Society of Edinburgh and the Wernerian Society.

Father_Notes: Guillaume Barthez de Marmorières was chief engineer of Languedoc, a position of considerable authority and status.
Education_Notes: Entered medical school at Montpellier at age sixteen and completed his degree in three years. Later studied in Paris under the patronage of Falconnet, physician to Louis XV.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed vitalistic doctrines distinguishing matter, life, and soul as separate phenomena requiring distinct scientific principles. Advocated clinical teaching and inductive methods based on Hippocratic principles. Demonstrated through anatomical analysis that hydraulic explanations of muscle motion were inadequate.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as physician with the French army (1755–1757); worked as royal censor and editor of the Journal des savants in Paris; professor of medicine at Montpellier (ca. 1760–1781), becoming chancellor of the medical school in 1773; personal physician to Napoleon at the time of his death.
Patronage_Notes: Protégé of Falconnet, physician to Louis XV. Later served as personal physician to Napoleon and held positions in Napoleon's consular government alongside Corvisart.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Société Royale de Médecine; Institut National
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences and Société Royale de Médecine; appointed to the Institut National under the Directorate. These honors were temporarily stripped during the Revolution.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Ruth Schwartz Cowan. Father_Notes: Father Bertel Jespersen was court chaplain; mother Ane Rasmusdotter Tinckel was daughter of a clergyman from Skåne.
Education_Institution: University of Copenhagen; University of Wittenberg; University of Leiden; University of Basel; University of Padua; University of Naples
Education_Notes: Sent to grammar school at age three; delivered lectures in Greek and Latin by age eleven. Matriculated at University of Copenhagen in 1603, transferred to Wittenberg in 1604 where he studied philosophy and theology for three years, elected master of philosophy and humane arts in 1608. Studied medicine at Leiden without abandoning theology. Studied anatomy at Padua and Naples 1608–1610. Defended thesis for M.D. at Basel in 1610. Received D.Th. in 1626.
Education_Locations: Copenhagen, Unknown, Denmark, 1603, 1604; Wittenberg, Unknown, Germany, 1604, 1607; Leiden, Unknown, Netherlands, 1606, 1607; Basel, Unknown, Switzerland, 1607, 1610; Padua, Unknown, Italy, 1608, 1610; Naples, Unknown, Italy, 1608, 1610
Religion_Notes: Lutheran orthodoxy marked his personal life and theological writings; mild religious tone in his works, particularly urging study of Holy Writ in vernacular and original languages.
Scientific_Disciplines: Anatomy; Medicine; Philosophy; Theology; Physics; Logic
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Anatomical manual Anatomicae institutiones corporis humani (1611) made him famous; first to describe olfactory nerves as first pair of cerebral nerves; identified suprarenal glands as capsulae atrabiliares. Wrote numerous manuals on logic, physics, ethics, and metaphysics. Lectured on medicine, physics, and religion at Copenhagen; published theological works including De natura theologiae and De auctoritate Sacrae Scripturae.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor of eloquence at University of Copenhagen in 1611; became professor of medicine in 1613; accepted professorship of theology at University of Copenhagen in 1624. Practiced medicine and performed dissections in Italy; performed no dissections at Copenhagen.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Father was Caspar Bartholin (1585–1629), a scholar and academic.
Education_Institution: University of Leiden; University of Padua
Education_Notes: Matriculated at University of Leiden in 1646 and studied mathematics in Holland for several years. Traveled in France, Italy, and England. Received M.D. from University of Padua in 1654.
Education_Locations: Leiden, Unknown, Netherlands, 1646, Unknown; Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1654
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Worked in pure mathematics, particularly the theory of equations in the Cartesian tradition. Made major contributions to physics through his study of double refraction in Icelandic spar. Observed comets of 1664–1665 and worked on Tycho Brahe's astronomical observations. Wrote little on medicine but contributed to medical journal.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor of mathematics at University of Copenhagen in 1656, transferred to extraordinary chair of medicine in 1657 and ordinary chair in 1671. Served as dean of faculty of medicine, librarian, and rector of the university. Appointed royal physician and privy councilor.
Patronage_Notes: Directed by Frederick III of Denmark to prepare Tycho Brahe's manuscript observations for publication. Appointed royal physician and privy councilor by the crown.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: In fairly close touch with the Royal Society through German scientists; sent copy of Experimenta crystalli Islandici to Henry Oldenburg.

Father_Notes: Father Caspar Bartholin was professor of anatomy and religion at the University of Copenhagen.
Education_Institution: University of Copenhagen; University of Leiden; University of Padua; University of Basel
Education_Notes: Entered University of Copenhagen in 1634; studied medicine at Leiden from 1637 under Sylvius and Johannes de Wale; studied anatomy at Padua under Johan Rhode and Johann Vesling; obtained medical degree at Basel in 1646.
Education_Locations: Copenhagen, Unknown, Denmark, 1634, Unknown; Leiden, Unknown, Netherlands, 1637, Unknown; Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, 1646; Basel, Unknown, Switzerland, Unknown, 1646
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Revised and published editions of his father's anatomical treatise; discovered the lymphatic system as a separate physiological system in 1652; made extensive anatomical studies and recognized the significance of Malpighi's work on capillaries; wrote on comparative anatomy, fossil sharks' teeth, and medical philosophy.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught mathematics briefly, then held the chair of anatomy at University of Copenhagen from 1649; became Professor honorarius in 1661, freeing him from academic duties; practiced as a physician and was the most distinguished physician in Denmark.
Patronage_Notes: Held in high esteem by the Danish king, who sometimes observed dissections and donated cadavers for research; responsible for the royal decree of 1672 organizing Danish medicine.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by C. D. O'Malley. Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: Jesuit School; Jesuit School; Not Specified; University of Bologna
Education_Notes: Entered the Society of Jesus at age fifteen; studied with the Jesuits at Piacenza and Parma; taught rhetoric at Parma; proceeded to Milan and Bologna for theological studies, where he studied under G. B. Riccioli; took vows in 1643. No degree is named.
Education_Locations: Piacenza, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Parma, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Milan, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Bologna, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Member of the Society of Jesus; took vows in 1643.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Expounded and popularized the work of contemporary physicists, particularly barometric experiments and atmospheric pressure; wrote on physical analysis of sound, sound waves, and hearing; investigated phenomena of freezing. Sought to link speculative and experimental approaches in science.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Member of the Society of Jesus with vows in 1643; taught rhetoric at Parma; served as rector of the Collegio Romano from 1671 to 1673; served as historian of the Jesuits from 1650 onward, residing principally in Rome.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by the Society of Jesus as a member and officer; served as rector of the principal Jesuit university.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Father Pellegrino was competent in both pharmacy and surgery.
Education_Institution: University of Bologna; University of Ferrara
Education_Notes: Studied philosophy and medicine at Bologna and Ferrara. At Ferrara was a pupil of Antonio Cittadini and Sebastiano Dell'Aquila. Witnessed degree conferrals in 1494 and attended an anatomical dissection in 1497. No degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Bologna, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Ferrara, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Taught medical theory at Ferrara from 1498, prefacing courses with historical lessons. Authored Opusculum de antiquitate medicinae, a treatise on the history of ancient medicine analyzing the origins of medical thought and demonstrating knowledge of classical medical literature. Also wrote on the nature of demons and complexions.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught a course on Ibn Sīnā's Canon at Ferrara from 1498, though not on the regular professorial list. Practiced medicine toward the close of the fifteenth century and in the early sixteenth century at Venice.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Thomas Barton attended Trinity College, Dublin, was ordained in the Anglican Church, worked as a missionary with Indians around Carlisle, and settled on Conestoga Creek. Married Esther Rittenhouse, sister of David Rittenhouse, in 1753.
Education_Institution: Academy; University of Edinburgh; Lisbon Academy
Education_Notes: Educated by his older brother William and at an academy in York, Pennsylvania. Commenced medical training at age eighteen under Dr. William Shippen of Philadelphia. Studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh (1786–1787), where he won the Harveian Prize for his dissertation on black henbane and served as one of four annual presidents of the Royal Medical Society of Edinburgh. Received a diploma from Lisbon Academy, Portugal; did not receive a degree from Edinburgh or confirmed degree from Göttingen. Sought a German university degree in 1796 but no confirmation of receipt.
Education_Locations: York, Pennsylvania, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, 1786, 1787; Lisbon, Unknown, Portugal, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Inferred from his father's Anglican ordination and family background; no explicit statement of Barton's own affiliation in the entry.
Scientific_Disciplines: Botany; Zoology; Natural History; Ethnography; Medicine
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Author of the first American botanical textbook, Elements of Botany (1803). Assembled the largest herbarium of native plants of his time (1,674 specimens, 1797–1807). Patron of Frederick Pursh and Thomas Nuttall; worked toward a flora of North America. Published observations on natural history, physical geography, and ethnographic topics. Left unfinished a natural history of the Lewis and Clark expedition.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of natural history and botany at the University of Pennsylvania from 1789; succeeded to the professorship of materia medica in 1795 and added the professorship of the practice of physic in 1813. Served as curator of the American Philosophical Society (1790–1800) and vice-president (1802–1815).
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Philosophical Society; Royal Medical Society of Edinburgh
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected one of four annual presidents of the Royal Medical Society of Edinburgh during his studies (1786–1787). Served the American Philosophical Society as curator (1790–1800) and vice-president (1802–1815).

Father_Notes: William Bartram owned a farm near Darby, Pennsylvania; John inherited a farm from an uncle and later purchased another of 102 acres at Kingsessing.
Education_Notes: Had only common country schooling. Self-taught in botany and natural history from age twelve; briefly considered medicine and surgery but devoted himself to natural history and botanical study.
Religion_Notes: Born into the Society of Friends (Quaker); became a deist through his studies of nature, expressing disbelief in the divinity of Jesus. Disowned by the Friends in 1757 but continued attending meetings. Contemptuous of ecclesiastical formalities and theological points.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal focus on botanical collecting and identification of American plant species; introduced over a hundred American species to Europe. Also collected and described shells, insects, hummingbirds, terrapin, wild pigeons, mussels, rattlesnakes, wasps, and the seventeen-year locust. Made extensive botanical journeys throughout the American colonies and Florida, discovering Franklinia altamaha.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Farmed 102 acres at Kingsessing, converting marshy lands into productive meadows through drainage and intelligent crop rotation. Supported by annual fund raised by Collinson and patrons for plant collecting. Named king's botanist in 1765 with annual stipend of fifty pounds.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by dukes of Richmond, Norfolk, Argyll, and Bedford; Lord Petre; Sir Hans Sloane; and Thomas Penn, who enriched their gardens with American plants. Peter Collinson served as principal patron and advisor, raising annual funds and introducing Bartram to European naturalists including Linnaeus, Gronovius, and Buffon. Named king's botanist by royal appointment in 1765.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: American Philosophical Society; Royal Academy of Sciences of Sweden
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Especially devoted to the American Philosophical Society, established by Franklin in 1743. Made a member of the Royal Academy of Sciences of Sweden in 1769. Awarded a gold medal in 1772 by a Society of Gentlemen in Edinburgh for his services to arts and sciences.

Father_Notes: John Bartram was a botanist and naturalist; encouraged William's botanical and artistic pursuits from childhood.
Education_Notes: Attended the Academy of Philadelphia from 1752 to 1756, where he studied Latin and French alongside his preferred subjects of botany and drawing. No formal degree recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Made detailed observations and drawings of plants, birds, animals, and fishes during his travels through the Carolinas, Georgia, and Florida (1773–1778). Recorded Indian life and natural phenomena. His Travels became influential in romantic literature.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Apprenticed to a merchant in 1757 and opened a trading store in Cape Fear, North Carolina (1761), which failed. Attempted planting rice and indigo in Florida. Received fifty pounds annually from Dr. John Fothergill (1773 onward) to travel and make drawings. Declined a professorship of botany at the University of Pennsylvania in 1782. Worked in his brother's garden and nursery after returning to Kingsessing in 1778.
Patronage_Notes: Peter Collinson, his father's London patron, encouraged his early work and sent drawings to George Edwards. Dr. John Fothergill succeeded Collinson as patron, offering fifty pounds yearly and purchasing Bartram's drawings from 1773 onward.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Philadelphia Society for Promoting Agriculture; Academy of Natural Sciences; American Philosophical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Philadelphia Society for Promoting Agriculture in 1785 and contributed observations on the pea-fly. Made a member of the Academy of Natural Sciences at its founding in 1812. Elected to the American Philosophical Society but took no active interest and never attended meetings.

Father_Notes: Father Carl Barus Sr. was a musician and choirmaster; family experienced persistent financial difficulties.
Education_Institution: Columbia University School of Mines; University of Würzburg
Education_Notes: Attended Columbia University's School of Mines 1874–1876; studied at University of Würzburg 1876–1879 under Friedrich Kohlrausch.
Education_Locations: New York, Unknown, United States, 1874, 1876; Würzburg, Unknown, Germany, 1876, 1879
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed methods of measuring temperatures over 1,000° C using thermocouples, independently of Châtelier. Internationally recognized authority on pyrometry. Later studied effects of X rays and radioactivity on water vapor condensation in fog chambers.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked for United States Geological Survey 1880–1892, United States Weather Bureau 1892–1893, and Smithsonian Institution 1893–1894. Appointed Hazard professor of physics at Brown University in 1895, became dean of graduate school in 1903, taught until retirement in 1926.
Instruments_Notes: Developed thermocouple methods for high-temperature measurement. Designed and improved fog chambers to study condensation of water vapor under X rays and radioactivity, though his wooden chamber with resin impregnation proved less reliable than C. T. R. Wilson's glass design.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: National Academy of Sciences; American Physical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to National Academy of Sciences in 1892. Founder of American Physical Society in 1899; served as president 1905–1906. Awarded Rumford Medal of American Academy of Arts and Sciences in 1900.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: University of Padua; University of Paris; University of Vienna; University of Munich
Education_Notes: Studied geology at Padua under Giuseppe Meneghini and Giovanni Omboni, who introduced him to fossil fishes. Continued studies in Paris in 1877 under Hébert, Gaudry, and Sauvage; in Vienna in 1878 with E. Suess and M. Neumayr; and in Munich with Zittel. No degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Padua, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1877, Unknown; Vienna, Unknown, Austria, 1878, Unknown; Munich, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primarily a student of fossil fishes, particularly Eocene, Cretaceous, Miocene, and Pleistocene faunas of Italy and the Mediterranean basin. Investigated stratigraphic relations, volcanic phenomena at Vesuvius and Solfatara, marine mammals, and the contemporaneity of man and extinct animals on Capri. Conducted faunal revisions of Mesozoic and Cenozoic fossil fishes. Published a secondary-school textbook of zoology in 1885.
Means_of_Support_Notes: From 1879 to 1887 taught natural history, geology, and mineralogy in secondary schools in Padua, Modena, and Milan. In 1887 appointed to the chair of geology at Naples, which he held until his death. As director of the Geological Institute in Naples, improved laboratory facilities and collections.

Father_Notes: Onorato Bassi owned a farm at Mairago; Agostino returned to manage it after failing eyesight forced him to leave public service.
Education_Notes: Studied law at University of Pavia as his parents wished, but also pursued physics, chemistry, mathematics, natural science, and some medicine. Attended lectures by Lazzaro Spallanzani. Received doctorate in jurisprudence in 1798.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Botany; Medicine; Mycology; Parasitology; Agriculture
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Discovered the fungal cause of muscardine (silkworm disease) through microscopic investigation and experimental inoculation, demonstrating that a living fungus parasite caused disease in animals. Proposed that parasites were the source of various human contagions including plague, smallpox, syphilis, and cholera. Maintained agricultural interests including merino sheep breeding and potato cultivation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as provincial administrator and police assessor in Lodi under French administration, holding various civil service positions. Managed his father's farm at Mairago for most of his life. Presented research at University of Pavia and engaged in agricultural experimentation and publication.
Instruments_Notes: Used microscopic investigation to identify the fungal parasite Botrytis bassiana (now Beauvaria bassiana) as the cause of muscardine; increasing loss of eyesight eventually precluded further microscopic observations.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: University of Cincinnati; George Washington University
Education_Notes: Worked as technical assistant to E. O. Ulrich after high school. Withdrew from University of Cincinnati to follow Ulrich to Washington. Completed graduate work at George Washington University, earning M.S. and Ph.D.
Education_Locations: Cincinnati, Unknown, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Washington, D.C., Unknown, United States, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: World authority on Silurian and Ordovician Bryozoa. Assembled outstanding collection of bryozoan fossils. Published major bibliographic indexes on Ordovician and Silurian fossils, Paleozoic ostracods, and paleozoic echinoderms. Also studied tetra corals, Cystoidea, and conodonts.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Employed by United States National Museum and affiliated with George Washington University for nearly four decades. Conducted graduate work and research at these institutions.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Served as president of the Paleontological Society; delivered presidential address in 1933.

Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant physician and lecturer on pathology at St. Mary's Hospital, London; professor of pathological anatomy at University College London from 1867; physician to University College Hospital from 1878; held chair of principles and practice of medicine from 1887 to 1898; appointment at National Hospital, Queen Square, London from 1868 to 1902. Crown referee in cases of supposed insanity from 1884 to 1898.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of London; Royal College of Physicians of London; Royal College of Physicians of Ireland
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society of London in 1868 at age thirty-one. Served as censor of the Royal College of Physicians of London from 1897 to 1898. Received honorary fellowship of the Royal College of Physicians of Ireland.

Education_Notes: Refused ecclesiastical career despite scholarship to petit séminaire of Vaux-sur-Poligny. Passed baccalauréat ès lettres in 1882 and baccalauréat ès sciences. Obtained licencié ès sciences naturelles. Studied experimental embryology under Laurent Chabry at University of Lyons. Presented doctoral thesis in 1891 on amphibian metamorphosis.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Discovered traumatic parthenogenesis in batrachians through experimental manipulation of frog eggs. Clarified the complex phenomena of fertilization through elegant experimental analysis.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Master of special functions and their application to partial differential equations. Major contributions to mathematical physics including conformal transformations preserving electromagnetic equations, integral equations, Laplace transforms, and solutions to equations of mathematical physics. Later work focused on hydrodynamics and aerodynamics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Liverpool University and Manchester before emigrating to the United States in 1910.
