Father_Notes: Henry Bates was a hosiery manufacturer at Leicester.
Education_Notes: Elementary education at Leicester schools; attended Mr. H. Screaton's boarding school at Billesden; formal education terminated in midsummer 1838. Apprenticed to a hosiery manufacturer and took night classes at the local Mechanic's Institute, excelling in Greek, Latin, French, drawing, and composition. Later taught himself German and Portuguese while in South America.
Religion_Notes: Unitarian religious views, which did not hinder his acceptance of natural selection.
Scientific_Disciplines: Natural History; Entomology; Zoology; Botany; Geography
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Avid entomologist from youth, collecting beetles in Charnwood Forest. Published first scientific paper on beetles in 1843. Spent eleven years in South America collecting specimens and observing natural phenomena. Developed the theory of Batesian mimicry, explaining how unprotected species resemble protected ones for survival advantage. Contributed extensively to systematic entomology, particularly on Coleoptera (Adephaga, Lamellicornia, Longicornia) and Lepidoptera (Heliconidae, Erycinidae). Authored The Naturalist on the River Amazon, a major scientific travel work.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Apprenticed to hosiery manufacturer until 1844; worked as clerk in Burton-on-Trent. From 1848 to 1859 supported himself through collecting and selling specimens in South America (though profit was modest, about £73 per year). From 1864 served as assistant secretary of the Royal Geographical Society for twenty-eight years, editing its Journal and Proceedings. Published numerous scientific papers and edited travel works.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Entomological Society of London; Linnean Society; Zoological Society; Royal Society; Royal Geographical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to Entomological Society of London in 1861; served as president in 1868, 1869, and 1878. Elected fellow of Linnean Society in 1871, Zoological Society in 1863, and Royal Society in 1881. Served as assistant secretary of Royal Geographical Society from 1864 for twenty-eight years; was secretary of the Geographical Section of the British Association but declined the presidency.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in establishing Mendelian genetics; named the discipline 'genetics' in 1905–1906. Early work focused on heredity, variation, and evolutionary mechanisms. Father_Notes: Father was Jābir ibn Sinān al-Ḥarrānī, a famous instrument maker mentioned by Ibn al-Nadīm, which explains the son's astronomical interest and proficiency in devising new instruments.
Education_Notes: No formal degree is recorded. Al-Battānī began his observational work in 877 and continued until 918, conducting astronomical observations and developing his astronomical knowledge through practice and study of Ptolemy's Almagest.
Religion_Notes: Al-Battānī was Muslim, as indicated by his personal name Muḥammad and his kunya Abū ʿAbd Allāh. His ancestors professed the Ḥarranian Ṣabian religion, which preserved ancient Mesopotamian astral theology and was tolerated by Muslim rulers until the eleventh century.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: One of the greatest Islamic astronomers. Composed the Zīj, a major astronomical treatise with his own observations of the sun and moon and corrections to Ptolemy's Almagest. Determined the obliquity of the ecliptic, the motion of the solar apogee, and the eccentricity of the solar orbit. Improved lunar mean motion, measured apparent diameters of celestial bodies, and developed new methods for computing lunar eclipses. Also wrote on astrology and composed a commentary on Ptolemy's Tetrabiblos.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Traveled to Baghdad with the Banū al-Zayyāt, a prominent family from al-Raqqa, suggesting patronage support. Spent much of his life in al-Raqqa conducting observations. Also engaged in astrological practice and writing.
Instruments: Armillary Sphere; Mural Quadrant; Triquetrum; Sundial
Instruments_Notes: Devised a new type of armillary sphere called al-bayḍa (the egg). Also designed a mural quadrant and a triquetrum for astronomical observations. Constructed a sundial indicating unequal hours (rukhāma).

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Traveled extensively across Asia, Africa, and the Mediterranean world, documenting geographical features, climate, flora, and fauna. Means_of_Support_Notes: Made his living from gifts and stipends from rulers and high officials in the places he visited. Exercised judicial functions as a Mālikite judge in India and on his way from Morocco to Egypt. Undertook occasional commercial ventures and benefited from strategic marriages.
Patronage_Notes: Received support from various rulers and high officials throughout his travels. Served as a judge under rulers' authority, including in Delhi and at the court of Sultan ʿInān of Fez.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Originally trained as a civil engineer. Studied at the University of Berlin from 1892 to 1895 and earned the Ph.D. for a thesis on the secular variation of the earth's magnetism.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founder of the department of terrestrial magnetism at the Carnegie Institution of Washington. Conducted extensive mapping of the earth's magnetic field, promoted establishment of magnetic stations, developed mathematical theory of magnetism, and investigated atmospheric electricity and extraterrestrial influences on the earth's magnetism, including effects of solar eclipses.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as a computer for the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey (1887–1892, 1899–1906). Taught at the University of Chicago (1895–1896) and the University of Cincinnati (1897–1899). Appointed head of the department of terrestrial magnetism at the Carnegie Institution of Washington in 1904, where he remained until his death.
Patronage_Notes: Supervised geomagnetic work of the U.S. Coast and Geodetic Survey. Appointed head of the Carnegie Institution of Washington's department of terrestrial magnetism in 1904 and proposed the worldwide research program that the Institution funded.
Instruments_Notes: Promoted the establishment of magnetic stations for observational data collection and was active in the mathematical analysis of observations from these instruments.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: International Union of Geodesy and Geophysics
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Very active in various international geophysical organizations. Founded the periodical Terrestrial Magnetism (later Terrestrial Magnetism and Atmospheric Electricity) in 1896 and edited it until 1927; the periodical became the Journal of Geophysical Research.

Father_Notes: Jean Bauhin, a French Protestant physician and surgeon from Amiens, sought refuge from religious persecution and settled in Basel in 1541, becoming attached to the university. He taught his son anatomy from childhood.
Education_Institution: University of Basel; University of Padua; University of Montpellier; Not Specified; Not Specified; University of Bologna
Education_Notes: Received Bachelor of Philosophy in 1575 from University of Basel. Studied anatomy under Girolamo Fabrizio at Padua for eighteen months from October 1577, attended teaching of Marco de Oddi and Emilio Campolongo at the Hospital of St. Francis, and probably Melchior Wieland in the botanical garden. Visited Bologna and received instruction in anatomy from Giulio Cesare Aranzio. Attended University of Montpellier in spring 1579 and spent time in Paris attending anatomies conducted by Sévérin Pineau. Was in Tübingen in May 1580. Received doctorate on 2 May 1581 after disputation on 19 April on the subject De dolore colico.
Education_Locations: Basel, Unknown, Switzerland, 1572, 1575; Padua, Unknown, Italy, 1577, 1579; Montpellier, Unknown, France, 1579, 1579; Paris, Unknown, France, 1579, 1580; Tübingen, Unknown, Germany, 1580, 1580; Bologna, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Son of a French Protestant physician who sought refuge from religious persecution.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Made major contributions to anatomical nomenclature, particularly of muscles, veins, arteries, and nerves. Described the ileocecal valve (valvula Bauhini). Published influential anatomical textbooks including Theatrum anatomicum (1605), which William Harvey used as the basis for his Lumleian Lectures. In botany, was primarily a taxonomist concerned with collecting and classifying plants; separated botany from materia medica. Distinguished between genus and species and introduced binomial nomenclature in his Pinax (1623). Also wrote on bezoar stone, Caesarean section, hermaphrodites and monstrous births, and the pulse.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of Greek from April 1582; held special chair in anatomy and botany from September 1589. Continued to teach anatomy and botany, holding public anatomies in winter and leading botanical expeditions in summer. Served as dean of the Faculty of Medicine nine times beginning in 1586, and as rector of the university four times (1592, 1598, 1611, 1619). Maintained a private medical practice that grew considerably. In 1597 was associated with his brother Jean as physician to Duke Frederick of Württemberg. Succeeded Felix Plater as archiater to the city of Basel in 1614. Appointed professor of the practice of medicine in 1615.
Patronage_Notes: Associated with Duke Frederick of Württemberg as physician from 1597.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Protestant from Amiens; physician to Margaret of Navarre; exiled to Basel in 1541 due to religious persecution under Francis I.
Education_Institution: University of Montpellier; University of Tübingen
Education_Notes: Basic education in Basel under Coelius Secundus Curione and Conrad Gesner. Visited foreign universities between 1560 and 1563, with prolonged stay at Montpellier from 1561 to 1562. University records do not confirm the M.D. from Montpellier, but he established medical practice at Lyons in 1563.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, 1561, 1562; Tübingen, Unknown, Germany, 1561, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Protestant from Amiens; family exiled due to religious persecution under Francis I; sought refuge in Geneva in 1568; second wife Anne Grégoire was a Protestant refugee from Besançon.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primary interest was botany from youth; collaborated with Conrad Gesner on Historia plantarum and pioneered study of alpine flora. Conducted systematic explorations of Montpellier region, Provence, Languedoc, and north Italy. Compiled encyclopedic Historia plantarum universalis describing 5,226 plants. Also studied mineral waters, fossil collections, and insects; illustrated apple and pear varieties.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Established medical practice at Lyons in 1563; practiced medicine in Geneva from 1568; appointed professor of rhetoric at Basel in 1570; became physician to Duke Frederick of Württemberg in 1571 and was appointed archiater; instrumental in establishing College of Medical Practitioners at Montbéliard in 1575.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Duke Frederick of Württemberg, an enlightened and sympathetic ruler of the dual principality of Württemberg–Montbéliard, from 1571 onward.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Guillaume Baumé ran two inns in Senlis; the family appears to have been fairly well-to-do.
Education_Institution: Not Specified; C. J. Geoffroy's dispensary
Education_Notes: Apprenticed to a pharmacist in Compiègne around 1743; by 1745 was working in C. J. Geoffroy's dispensary in Paris, where he developed his interest in theoretical chemistry and pharmacy. Became maître apothicaire in 1752.
Education_Locations: Compiègne, Unknown, France, 1743, 1745; Paris, Unknown, France, 1745, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered large-scale production of sal ammoniac in France (1767); designed the areometer with a calibrated scale (1768); won first prize in 1777 for an essay on furnaces, alembics, and distillation apparatus. Published numerous works on chemistry and pharmacy; contributed to the Dictionnaire des arts et métiers (1766). Remained a phlogistonist throughout his life, resisting new chemical theories.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Opened his own dispensary in Paris (1753), which supplied drugs in bulk to pharmacies and hospitals and manufactured chemicals on a large scale. Supplied industrial and laboratory apparatus. From 1757 taught chemistry and pharmacy courses with Macquer for sixteen years. Elected to the Académie des Sciences (1772–1785); received a pension from the Academy until the Revolution.
Instruments_Notes: Designed an areometer (1768) with a calibrated scale fixed at two points (density of distilled water and a salt solution of known concentration), enabling properly calibrated instruments to be produced.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Institut de France
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected adjoint-chimiste to the Académie des Sciences on 25 December 1772; became associé in 1778 and pensionnaire in 1785. After the Revolution, obtained a place as associé non résidant at the Institut de France.

Father_Notes: Father was solicitor-general at the High Court of Justice, Brussels.
Education_Institution: University of Utrecht; University of Utrecht
Education_Notes: Attended the Latin School of Brussels; studied classical literature and natural sciences at Utrecht, graduating in classical literature in 1843 and natural sciences in 1844.
Education_Locations: Utrecht, Unknown, Netherlands, Unknown, 1843; Utrecht, Unknown, Netherlands, 1843, 1844
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Primarily a teacher and practical chemist. Developed methods for quantitative determination of oxygen in organic substances (1853 onwards); analyzed drinking water, milk, and alcohol strength; published on diamonds, marine pileworms, and meteorology. Analyzed meteorites and proposed theories on their origin and atmospheric phenomena.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of physics and chemistry at the Royal Athenaeum in Maastricht (1845–1847); professor of chemistry at the Athenaeum Illustre in Amsterdam (1848–1865); perpetual secretary of the Dutch Society, Haarlem (1865–1885). Edited the Archives néerlandaises des sciences exactes et naturelles.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Perpetual secretary of the Dutch Society, Haarlem, from 1865 until his death.

Father_Notes: Son of a lithographer and merchant.
Education_Institution: University of Bonn; University of Göttingen
Education_Notes: Studied chemistry under Kekulé at Bonn, earning his degree in 1869 with a dissertation on the reduction of nitrobenzene. Further study at Göttingen for one year.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Trained as a chemist but became primarily a mineralogist and crystallographer. Early work on atomic weights and periodic table arrangement; later focused on etch figures on crystal faces as a method for determining crystal symmetry, and comparative crystal morphology. Authority on sulfosalts of the Binnental occurrence.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held three brief teaching posts after graduation; taught chemistry at the agricultural school of Lüdinghausen, Westphalia, from 1873 to 1896; called to the University of Fribourg in 1896 as its first professor of mineralogy, also teaching inorganic chemistry for the first ten years.

Father_Notes: None

Education_Notes: Early education at Collège de Troyes; apprenticed to pharmacist Faciot in Rheims; studied under P. de Chamousset and G. F. Rouelle in Paris from 1749. No formal degree is named.

Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted systematic analyses of French mineral waters; published important memoirs on mercury precipitates (1774–1775) that challenged phlogiston theory through quantitative observation; analyzed minerals and investigated arsenic content in commercial tin; helped revive knowledge of Jean Rey's calcination theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a pharmacist; served as apothicaire-major des camps et armées du roi from 1763 to 1793; became pharmacien inspecteur to the Conseil de Santé in 1793; member of the Institut de France from 1795.
Patronage_Notes: Commissioned by the government in 1753 to analyze mineral waters of France; sent as chief pharmacist on an army expedition in 1755; later commissioned by the Paris College of Pharmacy to report on arsenic in tin (1781).
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected member when the Institut de France was founded in 1795; never elected to the Academy.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Enrolled at Ingolstadt University on 19 October 1592 as a student of philosophy; later moved to Augsburg. No degree is named.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Amateur astronomer who established modern nomenclature for naked-eye stars by assigning Greek and Latin letters to stars in constellations. Created the Uranometria, a comprehensive star catalogue with copper-plate engravings that standardized stellar identification and remains in use.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a lawyer; appointed legal adviser to the city council of Augsburg on 13 December 1612 at an annual salary of 500 gulden. Received an honorarium of 150 gulden from Augsburg in 1603 for dedicating the Uranometria to the city council.

Father_Notes: Joshua Bayes, F.R.S., was a respected theologian of dissent and one of the first six ministers publicly ordained as Nonconformists.
Education_Notes: Privately educated; became his father's assistant at the presbytery in Holborn, London.
Religion_Notes: Member of the first secure generation of English religious Nonconformists; served as minister at a chapel in Tunbridge Wells.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Established foundations for statistical inference through his Essay on the Doctrine of Chances; defended Newton's calculus against Berkeley's logical critique in his Introduction to the Doctrine of Fluxions.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as minister at the chapel in Tunbridge Wells; was a wealthy bachelor with independent means.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society of London in 1742.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: None
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Author of the Kanz al-tujjār, a mineralogical work on the knowledge of minerals. Evidence suggests involvement with mathematics through manuscript copies (1260, 1269/1270) related to mechanical clocks. First Arabic author to document the use of the magnetic needle as a ship's compass, describing its application during sea travel.
Means_of_Support_Notes: None
Patronage_Notes: The Kanz al-tujjār was dedicated to either the Ayyübid ruler al-Malik al-Muẓaffar II (1229–1244) or his son al-Malik al-Manṣūr II (1244–1284), indicating court patronage.
Instruments_Notes: First Arabic author to describe the magnetic needle as a navigational compass. Documented the use of a needle threaded through straw, floated in water and oriented by a magnet to determine north-south direction. Also noted the use of hollow iron fish as compasses in the Indian Ocean.

Father_Notes: Sir William Maddock Bayliss was a professor of physiology at University College, London, and maintained a private laboratory and workshop. The family entertained generously and attracted many overseas physiologists.
Education_Institution: University College School; Trinity College, Cambridge; University of Cambridge; University of Pennsylvania
Education_Notes: Graduated from University College School, then entered Trinity College, Cambridge, graduating in physiology in 1922. Remained as Michael Foster Student and received Ph.D. in 1925 with thesis on tone in plain muscle.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1922, 1922; Cambridge, Unknown, England, 1922, 1925; Philadelphia, Unknown, United States, 1928, 1929
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted research on blood pH, heart-lung metabolism, kidney perfusion, serotonins, water diuresis, glomerular permeability, blood rheology, and instrumentation for physiological research. Made significant contributions to understanding blood viscosity in narrow tubes and developed pump-oxygenator perfusion techniques.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held positions as Michael Foster Student at Cambridge (1922–1925), Sharpey Scholar at University College (1926–1929), physiologist at Marine Biological Station Plymouth (1933–1934), lecturer in physiology at University of Edinburgh (1934–1939), and reader at University College (1945–1950). During World War II served in the Army Operational Research Group directing research on antiaircraft gunnery. Later held honorary research associate position at University College.
Instruments: Glass electrode; Electrometer; Micropipettes; Pump-oxygenator; Roller pump
Instruments_Notes: Developed and refined pump-oxygenator perfusion techniques for kidneys and heart-lung preparations. Designed and built micropipettes for blood viscosity studies. Worked with newly developed glass electrodes and electrometers for pH measurement. Designed a roller pump for long-continued infusion and various recording and control devices.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society of Edinburgh; Physiological Society; Society for Experimental Biology; Marine Biological Association
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Royal Society of Edinburgh; member of the Physiological Society, Society for Experimental Biology, and Marine Biological Association.

Alt_Name: W. M. Bayliss; William Maddock Bayliss
Father_Notes: Moses Bayliss was a manufacturer of galvanized goods and founder of the Wolverhampton firm Bayliss, Jones and Bayliss.
Education_Institution: University College London; Wadham College, University of Oxford
Education_Notes: Apprenticed to a local general practitioner in Wolverhampton; studied at University College, London from 1880, gaining a medical entrance exhibition and science exhibition in 1881; took B.Sc. with scholarship in zoology and physics in 1882; studied physiology and anatomy but failed anatomy at second M.B. examination and relinquished medical studies to concentrate on physiology; influenced by John Burdon-Sanderson and Ray Lankester; followed Burdon-Sanderson to Oxford in 1885 as undergraduate of Wadham College and took first-class degree in physiology in 1888.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, 1880, 1882; Oxford, Unknown, England, 1885, 1888
Religion_Notes: Attended an Anglo-Catholic church but was largely tolerant in religious matters.
Scientific_Disciplines: Physiology; General Physiology; Biochemistry; Physical Chemistry; Enzyme Action; Electrophysiology; Colloid Chemistry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in general physiology and the application of physical chemistry to biological problems. Major contributions include discovery of hormones (secretin) with Starling, elucidation of peristaltic waves, studies of enzyme kinetics and adsorption, investigation of colloid osmotic pressure, and work on wound shock. Authored the landmark Principles of General Physiology (1914).
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant at University College London, then assistant professor from 1903, and professor of general physiology from 1912 onward. Worked at University College for the remainder of his life.
Instruments_Notes: Used Thomson galvanometer in early electrophysiology work on secretion; employed Lippmann's capillary electrometer (introduced 1873) in studies of mammalian heart electrical phenomena.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Physiological Society; Royal Society; Royal Danish Academy of Science; Royal Academy of Belgium; Société de Biologie of Paris
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to Physiological Society in 1890; served as secretary 1900–1922 and treasurer 1922–1924. Elected fellow of Royal Society in 1903; served on council 1913–1915. Croonian lecturer (jointly with Starling) in 1904. Awarded Royal Medal (1911) and Copley Medal (1919). Received honorary degrees from Oxford, St. Andrews, and Aberdeen. Elected to Royal Danish Academy of Science, Royal Academy of Belgium, and Société de Biologie of Paris. Awarded Baly Medal of Royal College of Physicians (1917). Editor of Physiological Abstracts (1923–1924) and joint editor of Biochemical Journal (1913–1924).
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Charles L. Evans. Alt_Name: Ḍiyāʾ Al-Dīn Abū Muḥammad ʿAbdllāh Ibn Aḥmad; Ibn al-Bayṭār al-Mālaqī; Abdallah ibn Ahmad
Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Studied in Seville under Abu'l-ʿAbbās al-Nabātī, ʿAbdallah ibn Ṣāliḥ, and Abu'l-Hajjāj, gathering herbs with them. Preferred the works of al-Ghāfiqī, al-Zahrāwī, al-Idrīsī, Dioscorides, and Galen. No formal degree is named.
Religion_Notes: Embedded in Islamic scholarly culture; worked under Ayyūbid sultans in Cairo and Damascus.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Chief herbalist under Sultan al-Kāmil and al-Ṣāliḥ. Systematized Arab medicinal discoveries, adding 300–400 medicines to the ancient pharmacopoeia. Authored the Jāmiʿ, an alphabetical enumeration of some 1,400 animal, vegetable, and mineral medicines with synonyms across multiple languages. Wrote commentaries on Dioscorides and treatises on simple medicines and foodstuffs.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Named chief herbalist by Sultan al-Kāmil and retained the post under al-Ṣāliḥ. Taught disciples, most notably Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa, and traveled through Arabia, Palestine, Syria, and Iraq accompanied by followers.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed chief herbalist by Ayyūbid Sultan al-Kāmil; his major work al-Jāmiʿ was dedicated to Sultan al-Ṣāliḥ.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by J. Vernet. Original works: inventory in C. (Stuttgart, 1840–1842); French edition by Lucien Leclerc, Notices et Extraits, XXIII, XXV, XXVI (Paris, 1877–1883). Secondary: César E. Father_Notes: Lionel John Beale (1796–1871) was a prominent London surgeon and medical author.
Education_Institution: King's College School; King's College, University of London; University of Oxford
Education_Notes: Attended Highgate private school, then King's College School from 1840 to 1844, during which he was apprenticed to apothecary-surgeon Joseph Ross. Studied medicine at King's College, University of London from 1845, matriculating with honors in chemistry and zoology in 1847. Spent two years at Oxford as assistant to Henry Acland in the Anatomical Museum. Licensed by the Society of Apothecaries in 1849; graduated M.B. in 1851.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, 1840, 1844; London, Unknown, England, 1845, 1847; Oxford, Unknown, England, 1847, 1849
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in teaching microscopy applied to pathological anatomy. Conducted histological studies on tissue structure and vital staining techniques. Developed unique terminology distinguishing germinal matter (protoplasm) from formed matter. Engaged in controversies over nerve endings, disease germs, and mechanistic interpretations of life.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as resident physician at King's College Hospital (1850–1851). Established private laboratory in Carey Street (1852) where he taught microscopy. Professor of physiology and general and morbid anatomy at King's College (1853–1869), professor of pathological anatomy (1869–1876), and professor of principles and practice of medicine (1876–1896). Honorary consulting physician to King's College Hospital after retirement.
Instruments_Notes: Pioneered practical teaching of microscope use in pathological anatomy. Developed Beale's solution (carmine in ammonia) as a histological stain. Authored influential laboratory manuals on microscope use and technique.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Royal College of Physicians; Microscopical Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1857. Member of Royal College of Physicians (1856), fellow (1859), awarded Baly Medal (1871), and served as Lumleian lecturer (1875). Delivered Croonian lecture in 1865. President of the Microscopical Society from 1879 to 1880.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Gerald L. Geison. Original works: The Microscope, and Its Application to Clinical Medicine (London, 1854; 4th ed., 1878); How to Work With the Microscope (London, 1857; 5th ed., 1880); Protoplasm; or Life, Matter, and Mind (London, 1870; 4th ed., 1892); On Disease Germs (1870); On Slight Ailments (London, 1880; 4th ed., 1896); Kidney Diseases, Urinary Deposits, and Calculous Disorders (London, 1869); and papers listed in Royal Society Catalogue of Scientific Papers. Secondary: Bulletin de l'Académie royale de médecine de Belgique (1906); Dictionary of National Biography, Supp. 2; Journal of the American Medical Association (1906); Lancet (7 Apr. 1906); Medical History (1958); Nature (1905–1906); Proceedings of the Royal Society (1907).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Gerald L. Geison.

Father_Notes: May have been the son of Jean Beaugrand, author of calligraphy treatises, who taught calligraphy to Louis XIII.
Education_Notes: Studied under Viète. Visited England before 1630. Spent a year in Italy from February 1635 as part of Bellièvre's entourage, visiting mathematicians including Castelli, Cavalieri, and Galileo.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Published Viète's In artem analyticam isagoge with scholia and mathematical compendium (1631). Authored Géostatique (1636), proposing that weight varies with distance from center of gravity. Engaged in mathematical correspondence and polemics on geometry and mechanics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Became mathematician to Gaston of Orléans in 1630. Assumed the functions of secrétaire du roi in 1635 under Chancellor Pierre Séguier.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Gaston of Orléans as mathematician from 1630. Supported by Chancellor Pierre Séguier in his secretarial appointment.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

(1922); letter to Desargues in Taton, L'oeuvre mathématique de Desargues (Paris, 1951); writings against Descartes in Descartes, Oeuvres and Correspondance; anonymous pamphlets in Tannéry, Mémoires scientifiques, VI (Paris, 1896); contributions to Mersenne, Harmonie universelle and Correspondance. Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Self-educated in medicine through apprenticeship and reading. Apprenticed to Dr. Benjamin Chandler in St. Albans, Vermont for two years; received a license to practice from the Medical Society of Vermont in June 1812. No formal degree recorded.
Education_Locations: Champlain, Unknown, United States, 1807, 1810; St. Albans, Unknown, United States, 1810, 1812
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in gastric physiology through systematic experimental investigation of digestion using Alexis St. Martin's gastric fistula. Demonstrated digestion as a chemical process, established presence of free hydrochloric acid in gastric juice, and made foundational observations on gastric secretion, mobility, and the effects of psychic influences on digestion. First American physiologist to make a major contribution to the development of the science.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as acting surgeon's mate in the U.S. Army from September 1812 to 1815; commissioned as post surgeon at Fort Mackinac from 1820 onward, stationed at multiple army posts (Mackinac, Niagara, Crawford, St. Louis) until resignation in 1839; thereafter engaged in general medical practice.
Instruments_Notes: Employed a thermometer to track gastric temperature and movement during digestion experiments, demonstrating that the thermometer was subject to the same gastric contractions as food.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Odoardo Beccari was a learned naturalist who explored the interior regions of Borneo.
Education_Notes: Studied in Florence and received his M.D. in 1907. Obtained a teaching diploma in human anatomy in 1911.
Scientific_Disciplines: Anatomy; Comparative Anatomy; Neurology; Cytology; Embryology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work in comparative anatomy of vertebrates, particularly the rhombencephalon and Mauthner fibers. Conducted systematic cytological studies on germ cell genesis and sex differentiation in amphibians (Bufo viridis). Made precise observations on human neuroanatomy including the rhinencephalon, olfactory structures, and hippocampal gyrus. Defended the neuron doctrine and clarified the role of the rhombencephalon in static extrapyramidal motility.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Substitute teacher of anatomy at Florence until 1915. Director of the Institute of Human Anatomy at Catania University from 1921. Director of the Institute of Comparative Anatomy at the University of Florence from 1925 until his seventieth year. Presided over the Faculty of Natural and Physical Sciences at the University of Florence from October 1944 until his death.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Italian Society of Anatomy; Italian Society of Experimental Biology; National Academy of the Lincei
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Secretary of the Italian Society of Anatomy from 1929. Associate founder of the Italian Society of Experimental Biology. Member of the National Academy of the Lincei.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Pietro Franceschini. Beccari's books include Elementi di tecnica microscopica (Milan, 1915, 1927, 1940); La inversione sperimentale del sesso nei vertebrati (Pavia, 1930); Nevrologia comparata anatomo-funzionale dei vertebrati e dell'uomo (Florence, 1943); Genetica (Florence, 1945); Il problema del neurone, 2 vols. Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Entered the Piarist novitiate in 1732 and studied at Rome and Narni. No university degree is named in the source.
Education_Locations: Rome, Unknown, Italy, 1732, Unknown; Narni, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Member of the Piarists (Clerks Regular of the Pious Schools), a Catholic teaching order. Christened Francesco and took the name Giambatista upon joining the order.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering experimental physicist who studied electricity systematically, particularly natural electricity in the atmosphere. Conducted observations of thunderstorms, cloud formation, and electrical states of the air using metal poles, kites, and rockets. Investigated electrical phenomena including discharge appearances, insulators, condensers, and induction effects. Also worked on measuring longitude in Piedmont and geophysical subjects.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed to the chair of physics at the University of Turin in 1748, which he held with distinction for over twenty years. As a Piarist priest, received ecclesiastical support from the order.
Patronage_Notes: Recommended for his Turin appointment by the marchese G. Morozzo, who also suggested electricity as a research focus. Received financial support increases from Benjamin Franklin's letters of praise and patronage.
Instruments_Notes: Designed the electrical thermometer, an invention usually wrongly ascribed to Ebenezer Kinnersley. Constructed parallel plate condensers from insulators other than glass and attempted to estimate their relative powers.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by John L. Heilbron. Father_Notes: Protestant pastor who died when Becher was eight years old.
Education_Notes: Largely self-educated; recalled only one teacher, De bus, rector of the Speyer Retscher-Gymnasium. Received M.D. from University of Mainz on 16 November 1661.
Religion_Notes: Converted to Roman Catholicism by 1657 while at Mainz.
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Alchemy; Medicine; Iatrochemistry; Economics; Natural Philosophy
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Major contributions to chemical theory, particularly the concept of terra pinguis (fatty earth) and its influence on phlogiston theory through Georg Ernst Stahl. Wrote extensively on alchemy, fermentation, metallurgical transmutation, and chemical processes. Also published on economics and mercantilist theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor of medicine at Mainz (1663) and physician to the elector. Served as Hofmedicus und Mathematicus to Ferdinand Maria, elector of Bavaria (1664). Held post of imperial commercial counsellor to Emperor Leopold I in Vienna (1666). Organized imperial arts and crafts center and proposed educational reforms.
Patronage_Notes: Served Ferdinand Maria, elector of Bavaria, and Emperor Leopold I. Married Maria Veronika, daughter of imperial councillor Ludwig von Hörnigk (1662).
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Unsuccessfully sought membership in the Royal Society in 1680; submitted a book on clock design but was not elected.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Allen G. Debus. Original works: Physica subterranea (Frankfurt, 1669, with supplements 1671, 1675, 1680); Oedipus chimicus (Frankfurt, 1664); Naturkündigung der Metallen (Frankfurt, 1661); Parnassus medicinalis illustratis (Ulm, 1662–1663); Politischer Discurs (Frankfurt, 1668); Chymischer Glückshafen (Frankfurt, 1682); Tripus Hermeticus fatidicus (Frankfurt, 1689). Father_Notes: Originally a bookseller in Prague; became a railway employee at Pilsen in 1866 and later at Vienna.
Education_Notes: Attended several schools before enrolling at the University of Vienna in 1874, where he studied under geologist Gustav Tschermak. Became Tschermak's assistant in 1878. No formal degree is named in the source.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work on metamorphic rocks and petrography; developed the Becke line method for determining refractive indices (1893); introduced the Becke volume rule (1896); classified plutonic rocks and lavas; developed terminology for crystalline transformations (crystalloblastic, granoblastic, porphyroblastic, etc.); originated the term diaphtoresis for regressive metamorphism (1909); contributed to classification of metamorphic rock facies and graphic representation of rock analyses.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Associate professor (later full professor) of mineralogy at the University of Czernowitz from 1882; called to the University of Prague in 1890; moved to the University of Vienna in 1898, where he served as director of the Mineralogical Institute from 1906 to 1927.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Appointed secretary-general of the Viennese Academy of Sciences in 1911; received the Wollaston Medal of the Geological Society of London in 1929.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Hans Baumgärtel. Original works include 'Krystalline Schiefer des niederösterreichischen Waldviertels' (1882); 'Beziehungen zwischen Dynamometamorphose und Molekularcolumen,' Neues Jahrbuch für Mineralogie, II (1896); 'Fortschritte auf dem Gebiete der Metamorphose,' Fortschritte der Mineralogie (1911, 1916); Das Wachstum und der Bau der Kristalle (1918); numerous articles in Mineralogische und petrographische Mitteilungen (1883–1928). Secondary: A. Himmelbauer, obituary in Mineralogische und petrographische Mitteilungen, 42 (1932); obituary in Verhandlungen der Geologischen Bundesanstalt Wien (1931); Walther Fischer, Neue deutsche Biographie, 1 (1953).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Hans Baumgärtel.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: Harvard University; University of Heidelberg; Royal Academy of Mines
Education_Notes: Studied at Harvard for undergraduate work; earned advanced degrees in chemistry and mathematics at the University of Heidelberg and the Royal Academy of Mines, Berlin.
Education_Locations: Cambridge, Unknown, United States, Unknown, Unknown; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted detailed studies of mining districts and Pacific Coast ranges; developed mathematical, geophysical, and geochemical approaches to mining geology; published theoretical papers on the structure and rigidity of the earth, elastic stress-strain functions, and rock deformation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Instructor of mining and metallurgy at University of California, Berkeley (1874–1879); employed by the U.S. Geological Survey; worked one year at the German Royal Iron Works.
Patronage_Notes: Associated with the U.S. Geological Survey under Clarence King; instrumental in establishing the Carnegie Geophysical Laboratory, which he directed.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the National Academy of Sciences; biographical memoir published in its Memoirs.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Mathab. Kendall. Becker's publications include 'Reconnaissance of San Francisco, Eureka and Bodie Districts Nevada,' U.S. Geological Survey First Annual Report (Washington, D.C., 1880); Geology of the Comstock Lode and Washoe District, U.S. Geological Survey Monographs III (Washington, 1882); 'An Elementary Proof of the Earth's Rigidity,' American Journal of Science 39 (1890); 'The Finite Elastic Stress-Strain Function,' ibid. 46 (1893); 'Finite Homogeneous Strain, Flow and Rupture of Rocks,' Bulletin of the Geological Society of America 4 (1896). Father_Notes: Johannes Friedrich Wilhelm Beckmann established a dye and emery works in Solingen and independently discovered Paris green in 1814.
Education_Notes: Spent one year in laboratory work with Remigius Fresenius in Wiesbaden before entering university. Completed degree at Leipzig in 1878 under Hermann Kolbe and Ernest S. C. Meyer. Later studied with Johannes Wislicenus and Wilhelm Ostwald at Leipzig.
Education_Locations: Wiesbaden, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Leipzig, Unknown, Germany, 1875, 1878
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered the Beckmann transformation (1886), converting ketoximes into amides; investigated isomerism of benzoldoxime and nitrogen bonding; developed the Beckmann thermometer for molecular weight determination via freezing-point depression; identified SCI4 and investigated furfurol properties.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant to toxicologist Robert Otto at Technische Hochschule Brunswick; extraordinary professor at Giessen (1891); ordinary professor at Erlangen (1892–1897); ordinary professor and laboratory organizer at Leipzig (1897–1912); director of Kaiser Wilhelm Institute of Applied and Pharmaceutical Chemistry (1912–1923).
Patronage_Notes: Appointed director of the newly founded Kaiser Wilhelm Institute of Applied and Pharmaceutical Chemistry in 1912.
Instruments_Notes: Developed a thermometer with variable mercury bulb capacity to adjust measurement range; used for determining molecular weight based on freezing-point depression and boiling-point elevation of solutions.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Ruth Anne Gienapp. Original works: "Zur Kenntneiss der Isonitrosovebindungen," Berichte der Deutschen chemischen Gesellschaft 19–21 (1886–1888); "Ueber die Methode der Molckular-gewichtsbestimmung durch Gefrierpunktserniedrigung," Zeitschrift für physikalische Chemie 2–3 (1888–1889); "Untersuchungen in der Campherreihe," Annalen der Chemie 250 (1889); Das Laboratorium für angewandte Chemie der Universität Leipzig (1908); "Ueber die verbindung des Schwefels mit Chlor," Zeitschrift für physikalische Chemie 55, 61 (1923, 1928). Father_Notes: Director of taxation and custodian of postal services; died in 1745 when Johann was six years old.
Education_Institution: Gymnasium at Stade; University of Göttingen
Education_Notes: Enrolled at Gymnasium in Stade in 1754; entered University of Göttingen in 1759 where he studied theology, mathematics, natural sciences, public finance and administration, and philology. Completed studies by 1762. Studied with Linnaeus in Sweden in 1765–1766.
Education_Locations: Stade, Unknown, Germany, 1754, Unknown; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, 1759, 1762
Religion_Notes: Mother was daughter of a Protestant parson; taught at St. Peter's Gymnasium, a Lutheran school in St. Petersburg.
Scientific_Disciplines: Agriculture; Chemistry; Physics; Natural History; Botany; Mineralogy; Technology; Mathematics; Philology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Founded agricultural science as an independent discipline with his 1769 textbook, establishing that agriculture required scientific foundations in natural history, mineralogy, chemistry, physics, and mathematics. Created technology as a separate academic subject with his 1777 Anleitung zur Technologie, the first advanced textbook in the field. Pioneered the history of inventions and technology. Conducted meteorological observations and studied natural sciences throughout his career.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at St. Peter's Gymnasium in St. Petersburg for two years (1763–1765). Appointed extraordinary professor of philosophy at Göttingen in 1766; ordinary professorship of economic sciences established for him in 1770, which he held until his death. Lectured on mineralogy, agriculture, technology, materials science, commerce, and public administration.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Troitzsch, Ansätze technologischen Denkens bei den Kameralisten (Berlin, 1966).

Father_Notes: Antoine-César Becquerel was an experimental physicist and professor at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle.
Education_Notes: At age eighteen admitted to both the École Polytechnique and the École Normale Supérieure but declined both to assist his father. Received Doctor of Science degree from the University of Paris in 1840.
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Electricity; Magnetism; Optics; Spectroscopy; Luminescence
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Measured electrical current properties and discovered that Joule's law applied to liquids as well as solids. Investigated diamagnetism and developed an 'Archimedean law' of magnetic action. Demonstrated light-induced electrical currents and invented the actinometer. Revealed Fraunhofer lines in ultraviolet spectra. Made pioneering discoveries in luminescence and phosphorescence; invented the phosphoroscope to measure phosphorescent duration and identify new phosphorescent substances.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as assistant at the University of Paris, professor of physics at the Institut Agronomique de Versailles, and from December 1852 held the chair of physics at the Conservatoire des Arts et Métiers. Taught chemistry at the Société Chimique de Paris from 1860 to 1863. Served as aide-naturalist at the museum before succeeding his father as director in 1878.
Instruments_Notes: Used his father's electrostatic balance to measure electromotive force of voltaic piles. Constructed the actinometer to measure light intensity through photochemical reactions. Invented the phosphoroscope, a device with two perforated disks on the same axis that allowed observation of phosphorescent substances in darkness and measurement of phosphorescent duration; could be fitted with a prism to examine spectra of luminescent bodies.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1863.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by J. B. Gough. Original works: Traité d'électricité et de magnétisme, leurs applications aux sciences physiques, aux arts et à l'industrie, 3 vols. (Paris, 1855–1856, with Antoine-César Becquerel); Recherches sur les divers effets lumineux qui resultent de l'action de la lumière sur les corps (Paris, 1859); La lumière, ses causes et ses effets, 2 vols. (Paris, 1867–1868). Secondary: Henri Becquerel, 'La chaire de physique du Muséum,' Revue scientifique 49, no. 22 (28 May 1892), 673–678; Jules Violle, 'L'oeuvre scientifique de M. Edmond Becquerel,' ibid., no. 12 (19 March 1892), 353–360; E. N. Harvey, A History of Luminescence From the Earliest Times Until 1900 (Philadelphia, 1957), 207–219, 351–360.

Father_Notes: Royal lieutenant at Châtillon-sur-Loing.
Education_Notes: Entered the École Polytechnique in 1806 and graduated; no degree is named in the source.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in electrochemistry and the study of electrical phenomena in minerals. Investigated piezoelectricity in crystals, thermoelectric effects, and the voltaic cell. Demonstrated that electricity is generated only through chemical reaction, temperature difference, or friction. Performed synthesis of mineral substances through electrolysis, obtaining crystals of sulfides and other compounds. Invented an electromagnetic balance and differential galvanometer.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Military career in the Corps of Engineers, promoted to captain in 1812. Appointed sous inspecteur of the École Polytechnique in 1813; returned to active service in 1814. After 1815 devoted himself entirely to science. Became first occupant of the chair of physics at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle in 1838.
Patronage_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1829. Appointed to the chair of physics at the Muséum d'Histoire Naturelle when it was founded in 1838.
Instruments_Notes: Invented an electromagnetic balance and a differential galvanometer for his electrical and magnetic investigations.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Royal Society of London
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences in 1829. Awarded the Copley Medal of the Royal Society of London in 1837. Took an active and regular part in the Academy's proceedings throughout his life.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by David M. Knight. Father_Notes: Alexandre-Edmond Becquerel was a renowned physicist, member of the Academy of Sciences, and professor of physics at the Museum of Natural History.
Education_Institution: Lycée Louis-le-Grand; École Polytechnique; École des Ponts et Chaussées; Faculty of Sciences of Paris
Education_Notes: Educated at Lycée Louis-le-Grand; attended École Polytechnique (1872–1874) and École des Ponts et Chaussées (1874–1877), where he received engineering training. Obtained doctorate from the Faculty of Sciences of Paris in 1888.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1872, 1874; Paris, Unknown, France, 1874, 1877; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1888
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early research focused on optical phenomena, including rotation of plane-polarized light by magnetic fields, infrared spectra, and light absorption in crystals. Discovered radioactivity in 1896 and made fundamental contributions to understanding radioactive radiation, including identification of electrons in radium radiation and evidence of radioactive transformation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held three chairs of physics in Paris: at the Museum of Natural History, École Polytechnique, and Conservatoire National des Arts et Métiers. Also held high rank as an engineer in the National Administration of Bridges and Highways (Ponts et Chaussées), eventually becoming ingénieur en chef.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Academy of Sciences in 1889 after two preparatory nominations (1884, 1886). Became vice-president on 31 December 1906, serving during 1907, and succeeded to the presidency in 1908. Elected permanent secretary on 29 June 1908.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Alfred Romer. Original works: Becquerel, "Recherches sur une propriété de la matière. Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: University of Paris; University of Paris
Education_Notes: Received licentiate in natural sciences at the Faculty of Sciences at Paris in 1903 and doctorate in 1907. Studied under Gaston Bonnier among others.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1903; Paris, Unknown, France, 1903, 1907
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Investigated the physiological nature of plant seeds, protoplasm responses to freezing and dehydration, and suspended life in seeds and microorganisms. Demonstrated that living organisms could survive exposure to liquid hydrogen and helium and be revived by rehydration.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Named assistant at the Faculty of Sciences at Paris in 1907; member of the Faculty of Sciences at Nancy after World War I; appointed professor of general botany at the University of Poitiers in 1927, where he remained until retirement.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Alan S. Kay. Becquerel's work appeared primarily in Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences, Paris, including papers on liquid air effects on seeds (1905), latent life of spores at low temperatures (1910, 1930, 1932), suspended life in vacuum (1925, 1929), and freezing effects on plant cells (1939, 1949). Biographical obituary in Comptes rendus de l'Académie des sciences, Paris, 241 (1955), 137–140.
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Alan S. Kay.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: University College London; University of Edinburgh; University of Vienna
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at University College, London and University of Edinburgh; received M.D. from Edinburgh in 1853 with thesis on the geography of phthisis. After the Crimean War completed medical training in Vienna. Received honorary LL.D. from Edinburgh in 1891.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, 1853; Vienna, Unknown, Austria, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in physical anthropology and synthetic study of the physical, linguistic, and cultural history of Europe. Conducted systematic observations and measurements of human physical variations including hair color, eye color, skin color, height, and cephalic index throughout the British Isles and Europe. Integrated anthropological data with linguistic and cultural history to explain the distribution of European populations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Established a medical practice in Clifton, Bristol in 1857 and maintained it until retirement in 1891. Elected honorary professor of anthropology at the University of Bristol in 1908.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal Society; Ethnological Society; Anthropological Society; Royal Anthropological Institute
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Royal Society in 1873. Founding member of the Ethnological Society in 1857. President of the Anthropological Society in 1869–1870. President of the Royal Anthropological Institute in 1889–1891. Gave the Huxley lecture in 1905 and received the Huxley Medal.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Glyndaniel. Original works: Contributions to Scottish Ethnology (Edinburgh, 1853); The Races of Britain: A Contribution to the Anthropology of Western Europe (Bristol–London, 1885); "Colour and Race," Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute, 35 (1905), 98–140; Memories of Eighty Years (Bristol–London, 1910); The Anthropological History of Europe, Being the Rhind Lectures for 1912 (Paisley, 1912).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Glyndaniel.

Father_Notes: A tanner who wished his son to follow the same trade; the boy's grandfather recognized his abilities and insisted on professional training.
Education_Institution: Bridgnorth Grammar School; Pembroke College, Oxford; University of Edinburgh
Education_Notes: Attended Bridgnorth Grammar School, Shropshire; read medicine at Pembroke College, Oxford, where he also became interested in chemistry and modern languages. Spent three years in Edinburgh from 1784 and visited France, meeting Lavoisier.
Education_Locations: Bridgnorth, Shropshire, England, Unknown, Unknown; Oxford, Unknown, England, 1776, Unknown; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, 1784, 1787
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Translated works on chemistry by Bergman, Scheele, and Spallanzani; adhered to Lavoisier's antiphlogistic chemistry. Investigated the use of gases in treating diseases and established the Pneumatic Institution. Believed true medical science must have a chemical basis. Adhered to the kinetic theory of heat.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Reader in chemistry at Oxford from 1788 until his resignation in 1792. Established and directed the Pneumatic Institution at Clifton from 1798, which treated diseases by gas administration and later became a clinic for preventive medicine advice.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Associated with the Lunar Society during its last years.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by David M. Knight. Original works: The History of Isaac Jenkins (Madeley, 1792); An Essay on the Causes, Early Signs, and Prevention of Pulmonary Consumption (Bristol, 1799); Hygëia, 3 vols. Alt_Name: Bede the Venerable; Venerable Bede; Baeda
Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Entrusted at age seven to Benedict Biscop, founding abbot of Wearmouth and Jarrow monasteries. Spent his entire life in residence at the monastery, devoted to scriptural study, learning, teaching, and writing. Benefited from the monastery's exceptional resources, including a rich library and instruction from scholars brought from Rome and the Continent.
Religion_Notes: Monastic scholar and exegete devoted to scriptural study and Christian theology. His works include scriptural exegesis, homilies, hagiography, and religious verse.
Scientific_Disciplines: Philosophy; Natural History; Astronomy; Mathematics; Geography; Theology; History
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in computus (calculation of time), creating the first perpetual 532-year Easter cycle based on the Metonic lunar cycle. First historian to use the Christian era (anno Domini) systematically. Formulated the tidal principle of establishment of port, described as the only original natural philosophy formulation in the West for eight centuries. Wrote on natural history, cosmology, and chronology. Composed textbooks on grammar, versification, and figurative language.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Monastic life at Wearmouth and Jarrow provided his livelihood. Engaged in teaching within the monastery school and scholarly writing throughout his life.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by Benedict Biscop, founding abbot of Wearmouth and Jarrow, and his successor Ceolfrid, who served as Bede's master and abbot.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Owned a factory producing candles and water conduits; family had sufficient means to support Isaac's education and later business ventures.
Education_Institution: University of Leiden; Academy of Saumur; University of Caen
Education_Notes: Studied letters, philosophy, and theology in preparation for Reformed Church ministry. Privately studied mathematics and nautical science in Amsterdam under Brownist scholar Ainsworth. Received M.D. from Caen in 1618 but never practiced medicine.
Education_Locations: Leiden, Unknown, Netherlands, 1607, 1610; Saumur, Unknown, France, 1612, Unknown; Caen, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1618
Religion_Notes: Prepared for a career in the Reformed Church; associated with Reformed minister Andreas Colvius at Dordrecht.
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Mechanics; Astronomy; Mathematics; Engineering; Hydraulics; Magnetism
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in applying mathematical methods to physics and mechanics. Formulated principle of inertia (1613), law of uniformly accelerated motion of falling bodies (1618), and law of water outflow velocity (1615). Conducted experiments in combustion, pumping, hydrodynamics, and air pressure. Made astronomical observations and established Europe's first meteorological station (1628). Rejected purely rationalistic approaches in favor of mechanistic explanations grounded in experiment.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked in father's candle and water-conduit factory as apprentice and later as independent tradesman in Zierikzee. Served as conrector (assistant headmaster) of Latin schools in Veere (1618–1619), Utrecht (1619–1620), and Rotterdam before becoming rector of the Latin school at Dordrecht (1627), which he expanded to 600 students. Also served as unsalaried adviser to burgomasters on water regulation.
Patronage_Notes: Received support from Dordrecht magistrate in establishing the meteorological station (1628). Mentored by Rudolph Snell and Willebrord Snell at Leiden. Hosted visits from major French philosophers including Descartes (1628, 1629), Gassendi (1629), and Mersenne (1630).
Instruments_Notes: Established the first meteorological station in Europe at Dordrecht in 1628, recording wind velocity and direction, rainfall, temperature, and making astronomical observations.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Founded the Collegium Mechanicum in Rotterdam, a society of craftsmen and scholars focused on scientific problems with technological applications.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by R. Hooykaas. Original works: Theses de febre tertiana intermittente (Caen, 1618); D. Koyré, Études galiléennes, II (Paris, 1939); C. de Waard, L'expérience barométrique (Thouars, 1936).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by R. Hooykaas.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: None
Religion_Notes: Member of a cultivated Jewish family; brother was poet Michael Beer and half-brother was composer Jacob Meyer Beer (Meyerbeer).
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Amateur astronomer who conducted selenographical and solar-system studies with Johann Mädler between 1830 and 1840. Produced the Mappa selenographica (1836), a landmark lunar map based on micrometric observations made with a 9.4-centimeter Fraunhofer refractor. The map contained measurements of 105 fundamental points, 148 lunar crater diameters, and 830 lunar mountain altitudes. Also published Physikalische Beobachtungen des Mars (1830) and Beiträge zur physischen Kenntniss der himmlichen Körper (1839).
Means_of_Support_Notes: Banker by profession; astronomy was an avocation pursued through private means.
Instruments_Notes: Owned a private observatory equipped with a Fraunhofer refractor of 9.4-centimeter free aperture (4-inch), used for selenographical observations. Employed micrometric measurements to determine lunar crater diameters and mountain altitudes.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Father was a fellow of the Royal College of Surgeons.
Education_Institution: Blackheath Proprietary School; University College, London
Education_Notes: Educated at Blackheath Proprietary School, London, and University College, London. Qualified as member of Royal College of Surgeons in 1878. From 1882 to 1883 studied in Austria, Germany, and France under Carl Weigert, Julius Cohnheim, Wilhelm Heinrich Erb, and others.
Education_Locations: London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown; London, Unknown, England, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Clinical neurologist and general physician specializing in diseases of the nervous system. Conducted pioneering neurophysiological research on cerebral cortical function, muscle movements, and cerebral circulation. Published Diseases of the Nervous System (1898) and Croonian Lectures on Muscular Movements (1904).
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant physician at National Hospital, Queen Square, London (1883) and Great Northern Central Hospital (1885), becoming full physician at each. Practiced clinical neurology and internal medicine while conducting neurophysiological investigations.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Royal College of Surgeons; Royal College of Physicians
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Qualified as member of Royal College of Surgeons in 1878; elected member of Royal College of Physicians in 1882; became fellow of Royal College of Physicians of London in 1888.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Edwin Clarke. Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Studied at the École Normale Supérieure from 1894 to 1897 and placed first in the mathematics agrégation in 1897.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialist in rational mechanics, particularly nonholonomic systems, percussion problems, elastic impact, and friction. Extended Carnot's theorem and Painlevé's paradox. Developed theory of gyrostatic compass and servomechanisms for automatic piloting.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught mechanics at the lycée in Brest (1899–1908) and at the École Navale (1908–1921). Held university positions at Montpellier (1921–1924) and Lille (1924–1929). Lectured in fluid mechanics at Paris (1929–1932) and held the chair of physical and experimental mechanics there, directing the mechanics laboratory. Also taught at the École des Beaux-Arts (1924–1930), École Supérieure d'Aéronautique (1930–1939), and École Polytechnique (from 1936).
Instruments_Notes: Published theory of the gyrostatic compass in 1921 and later perfected it; studied compasses of the Anschütz and Sperry types and developed a zenith gyrostatic compass with rotating damper.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the Académie des Sciences on 25 February 1946.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Pierre Costabel. Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Received a good classical education; studied at Sedan is possible but not confirmed.
Religion_Notes: Acknowledged the authority and censorship of the Paris Faculty of Medicine; omitted a Paracelsian quotation possibly due to religious or institutional pressure.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of chemical medicine and iatrochemistry; published influential chemical textbooks; credited with the first mention of acetone; synthesized Galenic and Paracelsian approaches; believed in transmutation.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Gave public lectures on chemical medicaments in Paris; earned 700 crowns by his skill in 1613; served as almoner to Henry IV; received support from royal physician Jean Ribit and Turquet de Mayerne.
Patronage_Notes: Almoner to Henry IV; patronage from royal physician Jean Ribit and Turquet de Mayerne enabled him to establish his laboratory and lecture program.

Father_Notes: Grandson of René-Louis-Maurice Béguyer de Chancourtois, a noted artist and architect.
Education_Notes: Entered École Polytechnique in 1838 and École des Mines in 1840. At age twenty-three left École des Mines to travel through Armenia, Turkestan, the Banat, and Hungary studying mountainous regions. Returned to École des Mines in 1848 as professor.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, 1838, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, 1840, 1843
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in descriptive geometry, subsurface topology, and stratigraphic geology. Formulated a classification method for chemical elements based on their distribution in Earth's crust, creating the telluric screw—a precursor to the periodic table. Advocated for stereographic and gnomonic projections and uniform cartographic systems based on the metric system.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of descriptive geometry and subsurface topology at École des Mines from 1848 until his death; became professor of geology in 1875. Named assistant director of the French Geological Survey by Élie de Beaumont. Appointed director general of mines in France in 1875.
Patronage_Notes: Prince Napoleon invited him to participate in the voyage of the Reine Hortense to polar regions in 1856 following the success of the 1855 Universal Exposition. Served as secretary of Prince Napoleon's Imperial Commission for the 1867 Universal Exposition and as chef de cabinet during Prince Napoleon's administration of Algeria and the African colonies.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Likely learned astronomical instrument use from Regiomontanus; influenced by Regiomontanus's Ephemerides (1475–1506). No formal degree recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Participated in the Council of Mathematicians under John II of Portugal. Contributed to celestial navigation through observations and instrument use. Built the famous Nuremberg globe (1491–1493), a major cartographic work representing world geography with 1,100 localities and medieval geographical traditions.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Engaged in textile business in Flanders and Lisbon from 1480. Member of the Council of Mathematicians in Portugal; undertook official missions for the Portuguese crown.
Patronage_Notes: Served under John II of Portugal as a member of the Council of Mathematicians and was entrusted with official missions.
Instruments_Notes: Used and promoted astronomical instruments including the quadrant for latitude observation and the cross staff (Jacob's staff). Familiar with Regiomontanus's astronomical tables and instruments.

Father_Notes: August Georg Behring was a teacher; Emil was one of twelve children and grew up in simple circumstances.
Education_Institution: Gymnasium of Hohenstein; Friedrich Wilhelms Institute
Education_Notes: Attended Gymnasium of Hohenstein in East Prussia from 1866. Received free medical education at Friedrich Wilhelms Institute in Berlin from 1874 in return for military service; received M.D. in 1878 and passed state board examinations in 1880.
Education_Locations: Hohenstein, Unknown, Germany, 1866, Unknown; Berlin, Unknown, Germany, 1874, 1878
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in serum therapy and antitoxin theory; developed passive and active preventive vaccinations against diphtheria and tetanus; investigated disinfectants and antitoxic blood-serum therapy; conducted research on tuberculosis vaccination.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as military surgeon and assistant surgeon in Prussian Army from 1880–1889; intern at Charité Hospital Berlin (1880); assistant at Institute for Hygiene, University of Berlin under Robert Koch (1889–1894); associate professor of hygiene at Halle (1894); professor of hygiene at Marburg (1895–1917); organized the Behring Institute.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by Friedrich Althoff of Prussian Ministry for Education for Marburg appointment; backed by Farbwerke Meister, Lucius and Brüning (dye works) from 1892 onward; honored by French Académie de Médecine and Académie des Sciences with shared prizes (1895); made officer of Legion of Honor (1895); received Prussian title of Geheimrat (privy councillor, 1895); elevated to hereditary nobility (1901).
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Alt_Name: Konrad Friedrich Beilstein; Conrad Friedrich Beilstein
Father_Notes: Friedrich Beilstein was a salesman and tailor from Lichtenberg near Darmstadt, related to Justus Liebig.
Education_Institution: University of Heidelberg; University of Munich; University of Göttingen; University of Paris; University of Breslau
Education_Notes: Studied under leading German chemists including Bunsen and Kekulé at Heidelberg, Liebig at Munich, and Wöhler at Göttingen. Received doctorate from Göttingen in 1858. Continued studies with Wurtz and Charles Friedel in Paris, and with Löwig in Breslau.
Education_Locations: Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Munich, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1858; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; Breslau, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering work in organic chemistry, particularly structural formulas and isomerism. Investigated chlorination of benzene compounds, aromatic compounds in petroleum fractions, and compound identification. Created the Handbuch der organischen Chemie, a comprehensive reference work that superseded earlier textbooks and became the standard reference for organic chemistry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Göttingen from 1860, appointed extraordinary professor in 1865. Moved to the Technical Institute of St. Petersburg in 1866 and remained there for the rest of his life.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Deutsche Chemische Gesellschaft; St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the Deutsche Chemische Gesellschaft. Elected to the St. Petersburg Academy of Sciences in 1881. Co-edited Zeitschrift für Chemie with Hübner and Fitting from 1865 to 1871.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Ruth Anne Gienapp. Original works include numerous papers in Justus Liebigs Annalen der Chemie and Berichte der Deutschen chemischen Gesellschaft (1859–1880); Handbuch der organischen Chemie, 2 vols. (1880–1883; 2nd ed., 1886–1889; 3rd ed., 1892–1899; 4th ed., 1916–1937). Letters in Kekulé Archiv, Preussische Staatsbibliothek, and possession of Prof. L. Anschutz. Secondary: F. Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Ruth Anne Gienapp.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Graduated from Kazan University in 1849. Worked in Zinin's laboratory at the Academy of Medicine and Surgery in St. Petersburg. Submitted a master's thesis in 1853 and a doctoral dissertation in 1865, though the specific degrees are not named in the entry.
Scientific_Disciplines: Chemistry; Physical Chemistry; Inorganic Chemistry; Organic Chemistry; Thermochemistry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Began with organic chemistry and esterification reactions. Developed concepts of basicity and affinity. Major contributions to physical chemistry, including studies of metal reduction by hydrogen and other metals, establishing an activity series of metals. Discovered alumino-thermal reduction of metals from oxides. Conducted extensive thermochemical research on heats of formation and hydration of metal oxides and halides.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Junior scientific assistant at Kharkov University from 1855; professor of chemistry at Kharkov from 1859 to 1886. Organized the department of chemistry and physics at Kharkov in 1864.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected a member of the Petersburg Academy of Science in 1886.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by G. V. Bykov. Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: Vyatskaya Gymnasium; Medical and Surgical Academy of St. Petersburg
Education_Notes: Graduated from Vyatskaya Gymnasium before enrolling at the Medical and Surgical Academy of St. Petersburg in 1873. Graduated in 1878 and prepared for a teaching career in the clinic of I.P. Merzheevsky. Defended his M.D. dissertation in 1881 on the relation between body temperature and mental illness. Studied with leading European neurologists including Flechsig, Meinert, Charcot, Du Bois-Reymond, and Wundt.
Education_Locations: Sorali, Vyatskaya oblast, Russia, Unknown, Unknown; St. Petersburg, Unknown, Russia, 1873, 1878
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in neuroanatomy and the physiology of the nervous system. Defined the path and separation of posterior spinal cord rootlets, described Bekhterev cells and lateral column bundles, and mapped the reticular formation and taste center in the brain cortex. In nervous diseases, isolated diagnostic reflexes and symptoms, and described numerous conditions including Bekhterev's disease (numbness of the spine), apoplectic hemitonia, and various forms of ataxia and epilepsy. In later life devoted himself to reflexology (objective psychology) and broader psychological research.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of psychiatry at Kazan University from 1885, where he organized the first laboratory for nervous system research. From 1893 to 1913 headed the department of nervous and psychic diseases at the Military Medical Academy in St. Petersburg.
Patronage_Notes: Held academic positions at state institutions (Kazan University and the Military Medical Academy), indicating state sponsorship of his research and teaching.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Father was General T. M. Beliaev.
Education_Notes: Studied at the Mikhailovskoi Artilleriiskoi Akademii (a graduate school of military engineering) from 1902 to 1905. Remained at the academy until 1914, first as tutor and later as professor.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Specialized in metallurgical chemistry and the crystallographic basis of steel structure. Demonstrated that the Widmanstätten structure, previously known only in meteorites, could be produced in steel under controlled cooling conditions. Studied Damascus steel history and manufacture, and the coalescence of iron carbide in engineering steels.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Tutor and professor of metallurgical chemistry at the Mikhailovskoi Artilleriiskoi Akademii from 1902 to 1914. After World War I, worked as an industrial consultant in England and later in Paris.
Patronage_Notes: In 1915 was sent to England by the Russian government in connection with munitions supply during World War I.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by C. S. Smith. Secondary: Robert F. Mehl, "On the Widmanstaätten Structure," The Sorby Centennial Symposium on the History of Metallurgy (New York, 1965), pp. 245–269.

Father_Notes: Jean-Baptiste Forest de Bélidor, a French officer of dragoons on duty in Spain at the time of Bernard's birth; died within five months of Bernard's birth.
Education_Notes: Received practical mathematical training; participated in the survey of the meridian from Paris to the English Channel under Jacques Cassini and Philippe de La Hire, completed in 1718. No formal degree is named in the source.
Religion_Notes: The Duc d'Orléans discouraged him from taking holy orders, suggesting a Catholic upbringing; named chevalier of the Order of Saint Louis.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mechanics; Engineering; Mathematics; Ballistics; Military Engineering; Hydraulics; Architecture
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in engineering mechanics and the application of mathematical principles to practical construction. Authored foundational treatises on fortifications, hydraulic engineering, and ballistics. His works on mechanics, though elementary in theory, proved invaluable to practitioners and influenced subsequent generations of engineer-scientists including Carnot, Coulomb, and Navier.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of mathematics at the artillery school at La Fère in the 1720s–1730s; active military duty in Bavaria, Italy, and Belgium during the War of the Austrian Succession; settled in Paris with the rank of brigadier.
Patronage_Notes: The Duc d'Orléans (regent) arranged his appointment as professor at La Fère and discouraged him from taking holy orders. Elected associé libre of the Academy of Sciences in 1756.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected associé libre of the Academy of Sciences in 1756.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Charles C. Gillispie. Navier 1813); Le bombardier françois (Paris, 1731); Architecture hydraulique (Paris, 1737–1739, ed. Navier 1819); two memoirs in Mémoires de l'Académie Royale des Sciences (1756).
