Father_Notes: Alexander Melville Bell was a teacher of elocution and inventor of Visible Speech, a written code for phonetic notation.
Education_Notes: No formal degree recorded. Early education in Scotland; moved to Canada in 1870 and subsequently to Boston and Washington for his telephone work.
Scientific_Disciplines: Technology; Engineering; Medicine; Natural History; Biology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Inventor of the telephone (1876). Conducted experiments on hereditary deafness, longevity, and selective breeding of sheep to increase nipple number. Made suggestions on medical use of electricity. Experimented with kites and aeronautics through the Aerial Experimental Association.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Wealth derived from telephone patent (granted 10 March 1876) and its broad commercial interpretation. Used fortune to support scientific research and others' work. Organized and financed the National Geographic Society.
Instruments_Notes: Inventor of the telephone. Experimented extensively with kites for aeronautical research and organized the Aerial Experimental Association in 1907.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: National Academy of Sciences; Smithsonian Institution; National Geographic Society
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to the National Academy of Sciences in 1883. Appointed regent of the Smithsonian Institution in 1898. Helped organize and finance the National Geographic Society, serving as its president from 1898 to 1903.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Bernard S. Finn. Original works: complete list in Osborne's article; notebooks, letters, and documentary material at National Geographic Society, Library of Congress, and Bell Telephone Company of Canada; court testimony in The Bell Telephone (Boston, 1908); apparatus at Smithsonian Institution. Secondary: W.C. Langdon, Dictionary of American Biography, II (1928); C.D. Mackenzie, Alexander Graham Bell, the Man Who Contracted Space (New York, 1928); H.S. Osborne, National Academy of Sciences Biographical Memoirs, 23 (1945); B.S. Finn, Smithsonian Journal of History, 1, no. 4 (1966).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Bernard S. Finn.

Father_Notes: Minister of the Church of England; died when Charles was five years old.
Education_Notes: Received basic education from his mother; tutored in art; attended Edinburgh High School for three years. Learned medicine from his brother John Bell's private anatomy classes and from lectures at Edinburgh University. Admitted to the Royal College of Surgeons in 1799.
Education_Locations: Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, Unknown; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Son of a Church of England minister; no conversion or change of affiliation recorded.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered experimental methods for determining functional anatomy of the nervous system by cutting and stimulating nerves and observing behavioral changes. Demonstrated differing functions of spinal nerve roots. Work on peripheral and cranial nerves influenced Müller's laws of sensation and the principle of specific nerve energies.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Opened his own school of anatomy in London in 1804 and built up a surgical practice. Co-owner and principal lecturer at Great Windmill Street School of Anatomy from 1812 to 1825. Instrumental in founding Middlesex Hospital Medical School in 1828. Returned to Edinburgh University as professor of surgery in 1836.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Published papers in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Peter Amacher. Original works: Essays on the Anatomy of Expression in Painting (London, 1806); Idea of a New Anatomy of the Brain (London, 1811); An exposition of the natural System of Nerves of the Human Body (London, 1824); The Nervous System of the Human Body (London, 1830); The Hand, Its Mechanism and Vital Endowments, as Evincing Design (London, 1833). Secondary: Gordon-Taylor and Walls, Sir Charles Bell, His Life and Times (London, 1958); J. M. D. Olmsted, François Magendie (New York, 1944).

Father_Notes: James Bell of a London commercial family; mother Helen Lyndsay Lyall came from a family of classical scholars.
Education_Institution: Stanford University; University of Washington; Columbia University
Education_Notes: Tutored before Bedford Modern School, where teacher E. M. Langley inspired his interest in elliptic functions and number theory. Graduated Phi Beta Kappa from Stanford in two years. M.A. from University of Washington in 1908; Ph.D. from Columbia in 1912. Between degrees worked as ranch hand, mule skinner, surveyor, school teacher, and telephone company partner.
Education_Locations: Stanford, California, United States, Unknown, 1905; Seattle, Unknown, United States, 1905, 1908; New York, Unknown, United States, 1911, 1912
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Number Theory; Analytic Number Theory; Algebra
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Published approximately 250 research papers on numerical functions, analytic number theory, multiply periodic functions, and Diophantine analysis. 'Arithmetical Paraphrases' (1921) won the Bôcher Prize. Also wrote four learned mathematical books and eleven popular works on mathematics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at University of Washington from 1912, lectured at Chicago and Harvard, and held position at California Institute of Technology from 1926 (emeritus after 1953). Published extensively as research mathematician and popular science writer; also wrote seventeen science fiction novels under pseudonym John Taine.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Active in organizations of research mathematicians, teachers, and authors. Served as president of the Mathematical Association of America, 1931–1933.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Kenneth O. May. Original works: 'An Arithmetical Theory of Certain Numerical Functions,' University of Washington Publication no. 1 (1915); 'Arithmetical Paraphrases,' Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 22 (1921), which won Bôcher Prize; Algebraic Arithmetic (1927); Before the Dawn (1934); Men of Mathematics (1937); The Development of Mathematics (1940; 2nd ed. 1945); Mathematics, Queen and Servant of Science (1951); The Last Problem (1961). Father_Notes: Father was Reverend Andrew Bell.
Education_Notes: Began work with the Canadian Geological Survey at age fifteen during high school and college summers. Received civil engineering degree from McGill University in 1861, winning the Governor General's Gold Medal. Studied at Edinburgh for one year following graduation. Earned M.D., C.M. degree in 1878 while employed by the Survey.
Education_Locations: Montreal, Unknown, Canada, Unknown, 1861; Edinburgh, Unknown, Scotland, 1861, 1862
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneering explorer and reconnaissance mapper of northern Canada from Lake Superior to the Arctic and from Saskatchewan to Hudson Bay. Mapped both shores of Hudson Bay and major river systems. Produced over thirty reports on geology of surveyed areas and more than 200 titles on geography, zoology, botany, resources, and indigenous knowledge. First to survey Great Slave, Nipigon, and Amadjuak lakes.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of chemistry and natural history at Queen's University (1863–1867). Chief geologist and acting director of the Canadian Geological Survey (1901–1906), with continuous summer employment by the Survey from age fifteen. Served as medical officer on government ships visiting Hudson Bay.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed to the Canadian Geological Survey as a youth and maintained continuous association with it throughout his career, serving as chief geologist and acting director.
Instruments_Notes: Used compass, sextant, boat log, and Rochon micrometer as his primary instruments during thirty years of canoe-based exploration and reconnaissance mapping of northern Canada.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Geological Society of London; Royal Society of Canada; Geological Society of America; Royal Society of London; Royal Astronomical Society (Canada)
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Fellow of the Geological Society of London (1862), Royal Society of Canada (1882), Geological Society of America (1889), and Royal Society of London (1897). Member of the Royal Astronomical Society (Canada). Received honorary D.Sc. degrees from Queen's and Cambridge universities, the Imperial Science Order (1903), the King's Gold Medal from the Royal Geographic Society (1906), and the Cullum Gold Medal from the American Geographic Society (1906).
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by T. H. Clark. Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: School of Merate dei Somaschi; School of Monza; Seminary of Milan
Education_Notes: Studied rhetoric at the school of the Merate dei Somaschi; philosophy at the school of Monza, run by former Jesuits; and theology at the seminary of Milan, where he was ordained a priest. No university degree is named.
Education_Locations: Merate, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Monza, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown; Milan, Unknown, Italy, Unknown, Unknown
Religion_Notes: Ordained a priest and appointed honorary canon of the basilica of Monza.
Scientific_Disciplines: Physics; Chemistry; Meteorology; Natural History; Agriculture
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneered thermometer design and the thermometergraph; investigated combustion, liquefaction and ebullition of phosphorus, and catalytic properties of platinum sponge. In meteorology, constructed instruments including a hygrometer and perfected the atmidometer; developed a theory of hail formation and critiqued Volta's ideas on the subject. Later turned attention to natural history and agricultural science, particularly silkworm cultivation and plant physiology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Member of the Istituto Lombardo Accademia di Scienze e Lettere and the Società Italiana delle Scienze di Verona. Established and operated a thermometer factory in Milan from 1808, which flourished from the outset.
Instruments_Notes: Designed the thermometergraph with a double scale for automatic registration of maximum and minimum temperatures, inspired the English physicist Six. Constructed a hygrometer from fish bladder (1836) and perfected Landriani's atmidometer. Developed a phosphorus eudiometer to overcome limitations of Giobert's design.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Istituto Lombardo Accademia di Scienze e Lettere; Società Italiana delle Scienze di Verona
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of both institutions; participated actively in congresses of Italian scientists.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Studied law at family's wishes while pursuing natural sciences in leisure time. No university degree is named.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Major focus on Cenozoic Mollusca of Piedmont and Liguria, with detailed monographic work on fossil gastropods, cancellaries, pleurotomes, columbelles, and mitres. Secondary work on diptera of Piedmont and early Italian discussion of phylloxera in viticulture. Embraced evolutionary theory in paleontology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught natural history for thirty years at Liceo Gioberti; served as curator of the paleontological collection of the Royal Geological Museum of Turin.
Patronage_Notes: King Victor Emmanuel requested him to teach natural sciences to his sons.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected honorary member of many academies and scientific societies, but no specific names are given.

Father_Notes: Father was Vincenzo Bellarmino; mother Cynthia Cervini was half-sister of Pope Marcellus II.
Education_Notes: Joined the Jesuit order in 1560. Earned master's degree in philosophy at the Roman College in 1563, where natural philosophy was studied in the Aristotelian tradition. Completed theological studies in Louvain and was ordained priest in 1570.
Education_Locations: Rome, Unknown, Italy, 1560, 1563; Louvain, Unknown, Belgium, 1563, 1570
Religion_Notes: Jesuit priest and cardinal; leading theologian of the Catholic Counter-Reformation.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Studied natural philosophy at the Roman College in the Aristotelian tradition. His principal work was theological polemic defending Catholic doctrine against Protestant interpretation of Scripture, particularly regarding cosmology and the heliocentric theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Ordained priest in 1570. Rector of the Roman College from 1592; cardinal from 1599; archbishop of Capua from 1602. Served as the pope's major theological adviser in his final years at the Vatican.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by successive popes who appointed him to positions of authority. Served as papal theological adviser.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Ernan McMullin. James Brodrick, Robert Bellarmine (Westminster, Md., 1961). Father_Notes: Ernesto Bellavitis was an accountant with the municipal government of Bassano. The family belonged to the nobility but was in modest circumstances.
Education_Notes: Did not pursue regular studies but was tutored by his father, Ernesto Bellavitis, who directed his interest toward mathematics. He surpassed his tutor and pursued studies independently.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Developed the method of equipollencies, a form of geometric calculus enabling operations on geometric entities analogous to algebraic operations on numbers. Contributed to algebraic geometry, introducing new curve classifications and completing Newton's findings on plane cubic curves. Investigated infinitesimal analysis, Eulerian integrals, and elliptic integrals. Studied numerical solutions of algebraic equations following Ruffini, theory of numbers and congruences, and complex numbers. Also explored physics, optics, electrology, and chemistry.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked for the municipal government of Bassano from 1822 to 1843 without pay for the first ten years. Appointed professor of mathematics and mechanics at the lyceum of Vicenza in 1843. In 1845 appointed full professor of descriptive geometry at the University of Padua, transferring in 1867 to the professorship of complementary algebra and analytic geometry. Named senator of the Kingdom of Italy in 1866.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Istituto Veneto; Società Italiana dei Quaranta; Accademia dei Lincei
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected fellow of the Istituto Veneto on 26 September 1840. Became fellow of the Società Italiana dei Quaranta on 15 March 1850. Elected member of the Accademia dei Lincei in 1879.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Ettore Carruccio. Original works: Bibliographies in A. Favaro, Zeitschrift für Mathematik und Physik, Historisch-literarische Abteilung, 26 (1881); E. Nestore Legnazzi, Commemorazione del Conte Giusto Bellavitis (Padua, 1881), pp. 74–88, listing 181 published works. Key works include papers on equipollencies (1835, 1837), geometric calculus, algebraic geometry, descriptive geometry textbook (1851, 1858), and studies on quaternions, elliptic integrals, and universal scientific language. Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: University of Montpellier; University of Avignon
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at Montpellier beginning October 1584; received physician's degree from Avignon on 4 June 1587; received doctorate from Montpellier on 10 July 1595.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, 1584, Unknown; Avignon, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1587
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Held chair of anatomy and botanical studies at Montpellier from 1593. Devoted himself to the establishment and maintenance of the Montpellier botanical garden, comprising medicinal plants, foreign mountain plants, and plants of botanical interest. Was planning a general herbarium of Languedoc with binary nomenclature at his death.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Held chair of anatomy and botanical studies at Montpellier from 1593. Practiced medicine in Avignon and Pézenas before his appointment.
Patronage_Notes: Protected by Henri de Montmorency, governor of Languedoc, whom he met in Pézenas. Appointed to chair by Henri IV in 1593.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Louis Dulieu.

Father_Notes: Born to a family of small businessmen.
Education_Notes: Studied philosophy and mathematics at the University of Pisa under leading scientists including Giovanni Alfonso Borelli. No degree is named in the source.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in applying mechanical philosophy to human physiology and medical theory. Made important anatomical discoveries of renal structure and function, published Exercitatio anatomica de usu renum (1662). Developed hydraulic iatromechanism as alternative to corpuscular medical theory, systematically applying mechanical principles to explain disease and therapeutic methods. Later work on taste, circulation, and contractile physiology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor of theoretical medicine at University of Pisa at age twenty; acquired chair of anatomy five years later. Resigned around age fifty to become first physician to Duke Cosimo III of Tuscany.
Patronage_Notes: Benefited from patronage of Duke Ferdinand II of Tuscany from early youth, enabling his university attendance and early academic appointments. Later served as first physician to Duke Cosimo III.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Theodore M. Brown. Original works: Exercitatio anatomica de usu renum (Florence, 1662); De urinis et pulsibus et missione sanguinis (Bologna, 1683); Opuscula aliquot (Leiden, 1695); complete works ed. 2 vols. (Venice, 1732). Correspondence with Malpighi ed. Gaetano Atti (Bologna, 1847). Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Began naval career as a cadet in Kronstadt in 1789; gained knowledge of physics, astronomy, hydrography, and cartography through naval service and experience.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Led the Russian Antarctic expedition (1819–1821) that discovered Antarctica and conducted the first systematic oceanographic observations of Antarctic waters. Determined the position of the South Magnetic Pole with precision using 203 compass-variation observations. Responsible for maps of the Kruzenstern expedition and corrected inaccuracies on Black Sea charts.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Naval officer commanding various ships on the Baltic and Black seas; from 1839 until his death served as military governor of Kronstadt.
Patronage_Notes: Designated commander of the Antarctic expedition by the Russian government; supported by state resources for the expedition.
Instruments_Notes: Used a bathometer with an internal thermometer to measure water properties at depth (402 meters), demonstrating higher specific weight and lower temperature proportional to depth.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: One of the founders of the Russian Geographic Society in 1845.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Ivan A. Fedoseyev. Bellinsgauzen, Dvukratnye izyskania v Yuzhnom Ledovitom okeane i plavanie vokrug sveta v prodolzhenie 1819, 20 i 21 godov (St. Petersburg, 1821; 3rd ed., Moscow, 1961). M. I. Belov, ed., Pervaya russkaya antarkticheskaya ekspeditsia 1819–1821 gg. i ee otchetnaya navigatsionnaya karta (Leningrad, 1963). M. P. Lazarev, Dokumenty, I (Moscow, 1952).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by Ivan A. Fedoseyev.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Institution: University of Wittenberg; University of Paris
Education_Notes: Apprenticed as a boy to an apothecary at Foulletourte. About 1535 became apothecary to Guillaume Duprat, bishop of Clermont. Studied under botanist Valerius Cordus at the University of Wittenberg. In 1560 obtained the licentiate in medicine from the Paris Faculty of Medicine; never acquired the doctorate.
Education_Locations: Wittenberg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1560
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Originator of comparative anatomy; presented orderly classification of fish and depicted porpoise embryo, setting forth first notions of embryology. First to bring systematic order to classification of birds, distinguishing raptorial, diurnal, web-footed, river, and field birds. Talented botanist who recorded observations of Near Eastern plants and advocated acclimatization of exotic plants in France.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Served as apothecary to Guillaume Duprat, bishop of Clermont, and to François Cardinal de Tournon. Studied at University of Wittenberg and University of Paris. Received pension from Charles IX and was installed at the Château de Madrid.
Patronage_Notes: Protégé of René du Bellay, bishop of Le Mans, who enabled his studies at Wittenberg. Served as apothecary to Cardinal de Tournon. Charles IX granted him a pension and installed him at the Château de Madrid.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by M. Wong. Original works: L'histoire naturelle des estranges poissons marins (Paris, 1551); De admirabili operum antiquorum et rerum suspiciendarum praestantia (Paris, 1553); De aquatilibus libri duo (Paris, 1553); De arboribus coniferis resiniferis (Paris, 1553); Les observations de plusieurs singularitez (Paris, 1553); L'histoire de la nature des oyseaux (Paris, 1555); La nature et diversité des poissons (Paris, 1555); Portraits d'oyseaux, animaux, serpens, herbes, arbres (Paris, 1557); Les remonstrances sur le défault du labour et culture des plantes (Paris, 1558). Alt_Name: A. A. Belopolsky; Aristarkh Apollonovich Belopolsky
Father_Notes: Father Apollon Grigorievich was a gymnasium teacher who did not graduate from the Faculty of Medicine at Moscow University due to lack of funds; family was intellectual but poor.
Education_Notes: Graduated from gymnasium in 1873; entered Moscow University and graduated from Faculty of Physics and Mathematics in 1877. Master's thesis on solar spots completed in 1886. Doctoral dissertation on the spectrum of δ Cephei defended in 1896.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in astrophysics and stellar spectroscopy in Russia. Determined radial velocities of celestial bodies using spectrographs; studied solar rotation, sunspots, and solar corona. Investigated spectra of variable stars, novae, and spectroscopic binary stars. Discovered spectral duality of α Lyrae and variability of α² Canum Venaticorum. Conducted laboratory experiments verifying Doppler principle in optics and studying solar rotation mechanics.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked at Moscow Observatory from 1879 as supernumerary assistant and later in various capacities. Appointed junior assistant in astronomy at Pulkovo Observatory in 1888, staff astrophysicist in 1891. Vice-director of Pulkovo from 1908–1916, director 1917–1919, honorary director from 1933. Elected extraordinary academician in 1903 and ordinary academician in 1906.
Patronage_Notes: Worked under F. A. Bredikhin at Moscow Observatory and later at Pulkovo. Joined editorial board of American Astrophysical Journal in 1902. Participated in International Union for Cooperation in Solar Research organized by G. E. Hale in 1904.
Instruments: Spectrograph; Refractor; Meridional Circle; Transit Instrument
Instruments_Notes: Built and improved spectrographs at Pulkovo; used powerful refractors for spectroscopic observations. Ordered special three-prism spectrograph for solar research. Constructed original device using rotating water wheels with mirror blades to verify Doppler principle. Used dry photographic plates instead of colloidal plates.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Russian Academy of Sciences; International Union for Cooperation in Solar Research
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected extraordinary academician of Russian Academy of Sciences in 1903, ordinary academician in 1906. Joined International Union for Cooperation in Solar Research in 1904; participated in Commission for the Investigation of the Sun in Russia.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by P. G. Kulikovsky. Original works: 'Pyatna na solntse i ikh dvizhenie' (1886); 'Issledovanie spektra peremennoy zvezdy δ Cephei' (1895); 'Astrospektroskopia' (1921); and numerous papers in Izvestiya Imperatorskoi akademii nauk and other journals. Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by P. G. Kulikovsky.

Father_Notes: Father Eugenio painted miniatures; grandfather Giovanni was an engraver of precious stones and cameos.
Education_Notes: Studied mathematics from 1853 to 1856 at the University of Pavia under Francesco Brioschi. No degree is named in the source.
Scientific_Disciplines: Mathematics; Differential Geometry; Applied Mathematics; Geometry
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Early work focused on differential geometry of curves and surfaces, influenced by Gauss, Lamé, and Riemann. Major contribution was the interpretation of non-Euclidean geometry through surfaces of constant curvature, demonstrating that Lobachevski's geometry is realized on pseudospherical surfaces. Later work extended to applied mathematics including elasticity, potential theory, wave theory, thermodynamics, optics, and Maxwell's theory.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked as secretary to a railroad engineer in Verona and Milan (1856–1862). Held successive academic chairs: complementary algebra and analytic geometry at Bologna (1862–1864), geodesy at Pisa (1864–1866), rational mechanics at Bologna (1866–1873), rational mechanics at University of Rome (1873–1876), mathematical physics at Pavia (1876–1891), and mathematics at University of Rome (1891–1900). Became senator of the kingdom in 1899.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Became president of the Accademia dei Lincei in 1898.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by D. J. Struik. Beltrami's works collected in Opere matematiche, 4 vols. (Milan, 1902–1920). Key papers: 'Saggio di interpretazione della geometria non-euclidea,' Giornale di matematiche 6 (1868); 'Richerche di analisi applicata alla geometria,' Giornale di matematiche 2–3 (1864–1865); 'Teoria fondamentale degli spazi di curvatura costante,' Annali di matematica ser. 2 (1868–1869); 'Richerche sulle cinematica dei fluidi,' Opere II (1871–1874). Loria, Bibliotheca mathematica ser. 3, 2 (1901); R. Bonola, Non-Euclidean Geometry (1912; 1955).
Compiler_Details_Notes: Dictionary of Scientific Biography entry by D. J. Struik.

Alt_Name: Edouard Van Beneden; Van Beneden, Edouard
Father_Notes: Father P.J. Van Beneden was a zoologist and professor at the Catholic University in Louvain; organized a modest laboratory on the Belgian seacoast at Ostend.
Education_Notes: No formal degree is named in the entry. Appointed professor at the University of Liège in 1870 with the qualification of chargé de cours.
Religion_Notes: Father was professor at the Catholic University in Louvain; affiliation inferred from institutional context.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Studied protozoa, hydraria, cestodes, nematodes, tunicates, dicyemida, and vertebrates, particularly mammals. Made major contributions to understanding egg maturation, fertilization, and cell lineage in Ascaris and tunicates. Proposed the phylum Mesozoa as a transition between monocellular and multicellular forms. Discovered the individuality of chromosomes and demonstrated the essential nature of fertilization as the union of two half-nuclei.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed professor at the University of Liège in 1870 as chargé de cours, promoted to ordinarius in 1874.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Published numerous papers in the Bulletin and Archives of the Académie royale de Belgique.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Marcel Florkin. Original works: A. Brachet, 'Notice sur Edouard Van Beneden,' Annuaire de l'Académie royale de Belgique 89 (1923), 167–242. Key papers: 'De la distinction originelle du testicule et de l'ovaire' (1874); 'Recherches sur les dicyémides' (1876); 'L'appareil sexuel femelle de l'ascaride mégalocéphale' (1883); 'La segmentation chez les ascidiens' (1884, with C. Alt_Name: Pierre-Joseph Van Beneden; P.J. Van Beneden
Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Apprenticed to pharmacist Louis Stoffels, a natural history collector whose house inspired Van Beneden to pursue zoology. Studied medicine at the University of Louvain, obtaining the M.D. Subsequently studied zoology in Paris to prepare for a professorship.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Naturalist whose work spanned most animal phyla, with emphasis on embryology in systematic classification. Principal contribution was elucidating the life cycle of cestodes (tapeworms) in 1849, demonstrating the relationship between cysticerci and taenias. Later devoted himself to cetacean studies, both living and fossil, and identified fossil Iguanodon remains from Bernissart coal mine in 1878.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of zoology at the Catholic University of Louvain from 10 April 1835 until his death.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the Belgian Royal Academy; received an important prize from the Institut de France in 1853 for a paper on intestinal worms.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Marcel Florkin. Original works: complete list in Notices biographiques et bibliographiques de l'Académie royale de Belgique (1886, 1896). Key publications include 'Les Helminthes cestoïdes' (1849), 'Mémoire sur les vers intestinaux' (1858), and 'Sur la découverte de reptiles fossiles gigantesques' (1878). Secondary: A. Kemna, P.J. Father_Notes: Father was Lorenzo Benedetti; maternal uncle was also a physician, indicating a medical family.
Education_Notes: Received excellent education in both letters and medicine. Studied at Padua; one of his teachers was the historian and humanist Giorgio Merula. No degree is named in the source.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Principal contributions to anatomy through dissection before students and his treatise Historia corporis humani sive anatomice (1502), which described the human body systematically and encouraged anatomical observation. Also compiled a thirty-book codification of diseases (Omnium a vertice ad calcem morborum signa) and worked extensively on Pliny's Natural History.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Taught at Padua; practiced medicine in Venice and served as a physician in the war against Charles VIII of France in 1495. Also served Venice abroad in Greece, Crete, Melos, and the Dalmatian coast.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Dorothy M. Schullian. Original works incl. Alt_Name: Jean Baptiste Benedetti; John Baptist Benedetti
Father_Notes: Described by Luca Guarico as a Spaniard, philosopher, and physician or student of nature; provided most of Benedetti's education, making him a philosopher, musician, and mathematician by age eighteen.
Education_Notes: No formal education beyond age seven except study of the first four books of Euclid's Elements under Niccolò Tartaglia, probably around 1546–1548. Relations with Tartaglia were poor; Tartaglia never acknowledged him as a pupil.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in mechanics and physics, particularly the theory of falling bodies and buoyancy. Made contributions to hydrostatics, musical consonance and vibration theory, perspective, geometry, and astronomical observation. Admirer of Copernicus; explained the ruddy color of the moon during total eclipse through atmospheric refraction.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Court mathematician to Duke Ottavio Farnese at Parma from 1558 for about eight years, serving as astrologer and adviser on engineering. From 1567 remained in Turin in service to Duke Emanuele Filiberto, teaching mathematics and science at court and advising on university affairs. Private means were considerable.
Patronage_Notes: Patronized by Duke Ottavio Farnese at Parma and Duke Emanuele Filiberto of Savoy at Turin. Granted a patent of nobility in 1570 by the duke of Savoy.
Instruments_Notes: Designed and constructed various sundials at Parma and Turin; published the most comprehensive treatise on sundial theory and construction to that time (De gnomonum, 1573).
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Stillman Drake. Father_Notes: Father Edvard Otto Benedicks came from a family involved in the Swedish steel industry for generations.
Education_Notes: Concentrated on natural sciences at Uppsala; received Ph.D. in 1904 with dissertation on physical and physicochemical research on carbon steel.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in metal microscopy and metallography; investigated cooling power of liquids, constituents of steel (troostite and austenite), thermoelectrical phenomena, and physical properties of steel. Also studied meteoritic iron and superconductivity.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of physics at University of Stockholm from 1910; director of the Swedish Institute of Metallography for fifteen years from its founding in 1920; continued research at his private Laboratorium Benedicks for twenty years thereafter.
Patronage_Notes: Swedish Institute of Metallography sponsored by the iron and steel industry and the government.
Instruments_Notes: Pioneered metal microscopy; personally designed and constructed apparatus for his experiments, often in collaboration with assistants.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Awarded the Iron & Steel Institute's gold medal in 1908 for investigations on cooling power of liquids and steel constituents.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Torsten Althin. Father_Notes: Washington Gano Benedict was a businessman of average middle-class background with secondary-school education.
Education_Institution: Massachusetts College of Pharmacy; Harvard University; University of Heidelberg
Education_Notes: Studied chemistry at Massachusetts College of Pharmacy (1888–1889); continued at Harvard University receiving B.A. (1893) and M.A. (1894); additional year at Heidelberg under Victor Meyer leading to Ph.D. magna cum laude.
Education_Locations: Boston, Unknown, United States, 1888, 1889; Cambridge, Massachusetts, United States, 1889, 1894; Heidelberg, Unknown, Germany, 1894, 1895
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Transformed from chemist into world's foremost expert on animal calorimetry and respiratory gas analysis. Pioneered measurement of oxygen consumption, expired air, and heat production. Established standards for basal metabolic rates and investigated lipogenesis, insensible perspiration, and metabolic disorders including diabetes.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lecturer in chemistry at Wesleyan University (1905), professor (1907); physiological chemist for U.S. Department of Agriculture (1895–1907); director of Boston Nutrition Laboratory (1907–1937).
Patronage_Notes: Carnegie Foundation trustees established the Boston Nutrition Laboratory under his direction, influenced by William Welch and John Shaw Billings.
Instruments_Notes: Invented apparatus to measure simultaneously and accurately oxygen consumption, expired air, and heat (1924). Applied mechanical skill to improvement of calorimetry apparatus and established rigorous experimental controls.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: National Academy of Sciences; American Philosophical Society; American Academy of Arts and Sciences; Society of American Magicians
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Elected to National Academy of Sciences (1914), American Philosophical Society (1910), American Academy of Arts and Sciences (1930), Society of American Magicians (1930); honorary member of medical and scientific societies across Europe.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Charles A. Culotta. Original works: Experiments on the Metabolism of Matter and Energy in the Human Body, bull. no. 69, U.S.D.A. Father_Notes: Paolo Benivieni was a nobleman and notary.
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at the University of Pisa; no degree is named in the source.
Religion_Notes: Buried in the chapel of St. Michael in the Church of the SS. Annunziata, Florence; well regarded by Savonarola.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of pathological anatomy; performed at least twenty autopsies and observed gallstones, urinary calculi, scirrhous cancer of the stomach, fibrous tumor of the heart, peritonitis, and transmission of syphilis to the fetus. His De abditis nonnullis ac mirandis morborum et sanationum causis (1507) marked the beginning of a new method of thinking in medical science. Also a competent surgeon.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Practiced as a physician in Florence; had as patients the most important families of the city including the Medici, Bardi, Brunelleschi, Guicciardini, Pazzi, and Strozzi.
Patronage_Notes: Had the Medici family as patients; well regarded by Lorenzo the Magnificent and Ficino.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by Pietro Franceschini. Benivieni's works: De pestilentia ad Laurentium Medicem; Consilium contra pestem; De virtutibus; notes on De opinionibus antiquorum; Liber de cometa ad Julianum Medicem; notes on fossils and minerals; De chirurgia; De abditis nonnullis ac mirandis morborum et sanationum causis (Florence, 1507; Paris, 1528; Basel, 1529; Cologne, 1581; Leiden, 1585; Antwerp, 1585; Naples, 1519). Father_Notes: Justin Benoit was a distinguished surgeon and dean of the faculty at the medical school of Montpellier.
Education_Institution: University of Montpellier; École des Hautes Études
Education_Notes: Studied medicine at Montpellier in compliance with his father's wishes, receiving his medical doctorate in 1869. Subsequently turned to physics and entered the laboratory of the École des Hautes Études, where he conducted experiments on temperature dependence of electrical resistance in metals and received his doctoral ès sciences in 1873.
Education_Locations: Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1869; Paris, Unknown, France, 1869, 1873
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted experiments on temperature dependence of electrical resistance in metals. As director of the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, standardized units of length, temperature, and electrical resistance; determined relationships between the standard meter and wavelengths of light; standardized surveying wires and the standard ohm.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Worked in the electrical industry for four years before joining the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures as assistant director in 1877, becoming director in 1889 and serving until his retirement in 1915.
Patronage_Notes: Appointed assistant director and later director of the Bureau International des Poids et Mesures, a state institution.
Instruments_Notes: Studied various devices for measuring thermal dilation and the relative merits of different thermometers. Associated with standardization of twenty-four-meter Jaderin surveying wires.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Académie des Sciences; Physical Society of London; Société Française de Physique
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Correspondent of the Académie des Sciences; honorary fellow of the Physical Society of London; held the honorary position of president of the Société Française de Physique.

Father_Notes: Robert Daniel Bensley was a prosperous farmer.
Education_Institution: Collegiate Institute; University College of the University of Toronto; University of Toronto
Education_Notes: Graduated from Collegiate Institute in Hamilton in 1883. Entered University College of the University of Toronto in 1884 and received the Governor General's Medal in both arts and sciences upon graduation. Entered the medical department of the University of Toronto in 1889 and received the M.B. three years later.
Education_Locations: Hamilton, Ontario, Canada, Unknown, 1883; Toronto, Ontario, Canada, 1884, Unknown; Toronto, Ontario, Canada, 1889, 1892
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in the study of cell organelles and cellular structure. Differentially stained the cells of the islands of Langerhans in 1906, contributing to Banting's discovery of insulin. Confirmed the presence of the Golgi apparatus in cells in 1910. Demonstrated the mechanism of gastric secretion of hydrochloric acid. Modified freezing-drying techniques to isolate and analyze mitochondria.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Assistant demonstrator in biology at the University of Toronto after receiving his M.B. in 1892. Joined the anatomy department of the University of Chicago in 1901, becoming acting head in 1901 and director in 1907, serving for twenty-six years.
Instruments_Notes: Developed expertise in tissue staining and histological slide preparation. Modified Altman's freezing-drying technique in 1934 with student I. Gersh to isolate mitochondria for microchemical analysis.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Samuel Bentham was inspector-general of naval works and was ennobled in 1809.
Education_Institution: Faculty of Theology at Montauban; Lincoln's Inn
Education_Notes: Early education by private tutors during peripatetic family life. Attended faculty of theology at Montauban, where he studied French and Latin literature, natural philosophy, mathematics, and Hebrew. Studied law at Lincoln's Inn and was called to the bar in November 1831, but abandoned law for botany in 1833. Self-taught in botany and acquired reading proficiency in fourteen languages largely through independent study.
Education_Locations: Montauban, Unknown, France, Unknown, Unknown; London, Unknown, England, Unknown, 1831
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in systematic botany and plant taxonomy. Made outstanding contributions to the classification and description of plant families, particularly Labiatarum. Authored Genera plantarum, a monumental synthesis extending Candolle's taxonomic system based on critical analysis of Kew Herbarium material.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Inherited adequate wealth from his father and uncle in 1833, allowing him to abandon legal practice and pursue botany full-time. Held honorary secretary position at Royal Horticultural Society from 1829 to 1840. Conducted research at Kew Gardens after 1854.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Admitted fellow of the Linnean Society in 1828 and served as its president from 1861. Elected F.R.S. in 1863 and awarded the Royal Medal in 1859. Honorary secretary of the Royal Horticultural Society 1829–1840.
Sources_List: Dictionary of Scientific Biography, entry by George Taylor. Father_Notes: Protestant clergyman and theological writer.
Education_Institution: University of Herborn; University of Marburg; University of Göttingen; University of Duisburg
Education_Notes: Studied theology at Herborn and Marburg; later became interested in natural sciences at Göttingen; received doctorate from University of Duisburg in 1800 with thesis on determining longitude by transiting stars.
Education_Locations: Herborn, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Marburg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Göttingen, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, Unknown; Duisburg, Unknown, Germany, Unknown, 1800
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted pioneering simultaneous observations of meteors with H. W. Brandes using baseline measurements to determine height and velocity; demonstrated Earth's rotation through experiments on falling bodies in Hamburg (1802) and Schlebusch (1804), predating Foucault by fifty years; later pursued ballistic experiments and astronomical observations.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Professor of mathematics at the Lyceum in Düsseldorf from 1805; directed the land survey of the duchy of Berg (1805–1810) and organized its land registry; later devoted himself to science as a private citizen while writing on politics and constitutional law.
Instruments_Notes: Built a small observatory on his property in Bilk two years before his death; bequeathed it to the city of Düsseldorf with an endowment for an resident astronomer, where Schmidt, Brünnow, and Luther subsequently made important astronomical observations.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Étienne Bérard was a chemical manufacturer and associate of Chaptal, who recommended his son to Berthollet.
Education_Institution: University of Paris; University of Montpellier
Education_Notes: Studied at the newly reestablished University of Paris; received bachelier-ès-lettres in 1811 and licencié-ès-sciences; received M.D. from Montpellier on 9 July 1817.
Education_Locations: Paris, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1811; Montpellier, Unknown, France, Unknown, 1817
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Conducted research on salt analysis and solubilities; collaborated on infrared and ultraviolet radiation polarization; best known for work on specific heats of gases with Delaroche; investigated ripening of fruit and oxygen consumption.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Lived in Berthollet's house at Arcueil as a laboratory assistant from about 1807; became a member of the Society of Arcueil; later held a position in the faculty of medicine at Montpellier.
Patronage_Notes: Recommended to Berthollet by Chaptal; lived in Berthollet's household and worked as his laboratory assistant.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Society of Arcueil; Académie des Sciences
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Member of the Society of Arcueil from about 1807; elected correspondent in the chemistry section of the Paris Académie des Sciences on 20 December 1819.

Father_Notes: None
Education_Notes: Earned M.D. with thesis on natural medicine in 1811 at Montpellier.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Physician and medical theorist; contributed articles on cranioscopy and muscle physiology to the Dictionnaire des sciences médicales; wrote extensively on the Montpellier school of medicine and critiqued vitalism and methodological approaches in physiology.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Successful private teacher of medicine; collaborated on the Dictionnaire des sciences médicales in Paris; appointed professor of public health at the Faculté de Médecine of Montpellier in 1823, taking the chair in 1826.

Father_Notes: Faustino Barigazzi was a surgeon of Carpi; Giacomo was one of five children and received rudimentary training in anatomy and surgery from his father.
Education_Notes: Received rudimentary training in anatomy and surgery from his father; possibly some classical education from Aldus Manutius between 1469 and 1477; studied more systematically, perhaps in Ferrara or Bologna, before entering the medical school of the University of Bologna. Studied under Girolamo Manfredi, Lionello dei Vittori, Gabriele Zerbi, and Alessandro Achillini; received his degree on 4 August 1489.
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer in anatomical investigation based on personal dissection and observation. Authored the Commentaria, the first major work since Galen to display considerable anatomical information from direct investigation. Recognized the significance of anatomical illustrations properly related to text. Made numerous anatomical discoveries including the vermiform appendix, arytenoid cartilages, thymus gland, and sphenoidal sinus. Challenged traditional Galenic anatomy on multiple points, including denial of the rete mirabile in the human brain. Also authored an important neurosurgical treatise on skull fractures.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Appointed lecturer in surgery at Bologna in late 1502, becoming one of four eminent foreign faculty members. Likely practiced surgery independently during Italian wars and French invasion of 1494, possibly as a military surgeon. In 1508 placed in charge of treating plague victims in Bologna. Enjoyed great popularity as a teacher. Also practiced medicine as a physician, including consultation at Rome during pontificate of Julius II and medical care for various patrons.
Patronage_Notes: Supported by powerful individuals and families, notably the Medici. Pope Leo X (a Medici) directly enabled his leave of absence in 1513 to provide medical care to Alessandro Soderini. Called to attend Lorenzo de' Medici in 1517 for postoperative care following a gunshot wound and skull fracture. In 1525, at command of Pope Clement VII, went to Piacenza to assist in care of Giovanni dalle Bande Nere (Medici family member). Served as physician to Cardinal Pompeo Colonna in Rome in 1526; accepted a painting by Raphael in lieu of fee.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: None

Father_Notes: Simon Gregor'evich Berg was a notary.
Education_Notes: Graduated from Second Kishinev Gymnasium with gold medal in 1894. Enrolled in natural science section of Faculty of Physics and Mathematics at Moscow University, receiving gold medal and first-degree diploma in zoology in 1898 for dissertation on pike embryology. Received doctorate in geography in 1909 for dissertation on the Aral Sea, and doctorate in zoology in 1934.
Education_Locations: Kishinev, Unknown, Russia, Unknown, 1894; Moscow, Unknown, Russia, 1894, 1898
Scientific_Disciplines: Geography; Ichthyology; Limnology; Zoology; Paleontology; Paleoclimatology; Climatology
Scientific_Disciplines_Notes: Pioneer of limnology in Russia; conducted foundational studies of lakes in Kazakhstan examining salinity, temperature, fauna, and origin. Major contributions to ichthyology including anatomy, embryology, systematics, and geographical distribution of Soviet fishes, and studies of migratory fish spawning and reproduction. Developed system of geographical zones based on climatic, soil, and biological factors. Conducted paleoclimatic and paleogeographic reconstructions linking geological history to landscape development. Studied loess formation, soil development, and biogeographical distribution patterns.
Means_of_Support_Notes: Inspector of fisheries in Aral Sea and Syr-Dar'ya River (1898–1902). Zoologist and director of ichthyology section at Zoological Museum of Academy of Sciences, St. Petersburg (1904–1914). Professor of ichthyology at Moscow Agricultural Institute (1913–1917). Professor of geography at Petrograd University (1917–1950). Head of applied ichthyology section at State Institute of Experimental Agronomy / Institute of Fish Industry (1922–1934). Head of fossil fish section at Zoological Institute of Academy of Sciences (1934–1950). Taught at Pedagogical Institute and Geographical Institute.
Patronage_Notes: Sent by Russian Department of Agriculture to study oceanography in Bergen, Norway (1902–1903). Supported by Academy of Sciences, which elected him associate member in 1928 and academician in 1946.
Scientific_Societies_Membership: Russian Geographical Society; All-Union Geographical Society; Academy of Sciences of the U.S.S.R.
Scientific_Societies_Notes: Awarded P.P. Semenov Gold Medal by Russian Geographical Society in 1909. Awarded Konstantinovsky Medal of Russian Geographical Society in 1915. Elected associate member of Academy of Sciences in 1928 and academician in 1946. President of All-Union Geographical Society from 1940 to 1950.
